# 2  
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization

 

## 2.1 Introduction

Large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems (LSMOPs) refer to a subset of optimization problems which have both a large number of decision variables and multiple conflicting objectives. This class of problems is extensively present in many applications. For example, in the community detection which aims to minimize the inter‐link density and maximize the intra‐link density, the number of network nodes is usually in the order of tens of thousands \[[1](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0001), [2](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0002)\]. In the deep neural network training which aims to minimize the network complexity and maximize the prediction accuracy, there are often millions of weights to be trained [\[3\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0003). Similarly, problems in logistic scheduling \[[4](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0004), [5](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0005)\], power systems [\[6\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0006), radiotherapy planning [\[7\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0007), and many other real‐world applications have also shown the characteristics of LSMOPs.

Up to now, there still does not exist a unified opinion on the minimum number of decision variables for LSMOPs, which may differ for different types of problems. In this book, LSMOPs are defined as the optimization problems which have at least two conflicting objectives and one hundred decision variables. Generally, LSMOPs are more difficult to be handled than the problems with a few decision variables, since the search space is exponentially related to the number of decision variables. On the one hand, with the increasing of the number of decision variables, the number of local optima increases considerably even exponentially. This will easily lead to multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) converging prematurely to a local optimum [\[8\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0008). On the other hand, with the scaling up of the number of decision variables, the probability that decision variables interact with each other increases, which makes the landscape of search space more complicated and the conflicts between multiple objectives more serious [\[9\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0009).

In the past decades, a lot of efforts have been concentrated on studying large‐scale single‐objective optimization problems (LSOPs). A large number of test problems have been designed for large‐scale single‐objective optimization \[[10](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0010)–[14](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0014)\]. The methods for solving LSOPs have also achieved remarkable progress, mainly including the decomposition‐based and non‐decomposition‐based methods \[[15](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0015)–[17](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0017)\]. Recently, with the improvement of computing power, increasing attention has been paid to using MOEAs to address LSMOPs. While different types of benchmark test problems are designed for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, a handful of promising MOEAs have also been customized for solving LSMOPs. In addition, some LSMOPs with specific properties have been extensively investigated, especially those with sparse Pareto optimal solutions. The sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems, namely, sparse LSMOPs, refer to a class of LSMOPs whose decision variables in Pareto optimal solutions are mostly zero‐valued. As an emerging research topic in LSMOPs, some benchmark test problems and a number of MOEAs have also been developed for sparse LSMOPs [\[18\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0018).

The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. [Section 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0002) gives the benchmark test problems for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, and [Section 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0006) presents some commonly used indicators for evaluating the performance of MOEAs in solving LSMOPs. [Section 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0010) introduces the test problems tailored for sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, followed by a performance indicator in [Section 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0022) which can assess the convergence, sparsity, and diversity of solution sets simultaneously. Finally, [Section 2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0023) finishes this chapter with a brief summary.

 

## 2.2 Test Problems for Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization

In this section, some primary concepts related to multi‐objective optimization are first given. Then, we introduce some test problems that are commonly used for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization.

 

### 2.2.1 Primary Concepts

To better mimic the problems in real world, a benchmark test suite should capture as much problem characteristics as possible, including fitness landscape, variable interactions, Pareto front geometries, separability of objective functions, and among many others. In the following, some primary concepts related to large‐scale multi‐objective test problems are introduced in detail.

*   *Fitness landscape*. The goal of solving a multi‐objective optimization problem is to obtain a set of trade‐off solutions in the decision space, and the quality of these solutions is usually assessed in the objective space. The mapping from the decision space to the objective space defines the fitness landscape.

(b) Minimize f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals x squared plus sine left-parenthesis 10 pi x right-parenthesis comma x element-of left-bracket negative 5 comma 5 right-bracket.](images/c02f001.png)
    
    [**Figure 2.1**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0001) Examples of a unimodal function and a multimodal function.     *Modality*. The modality is related to the number of local optima of an objective function. Specifically, an objective function is said to be *multimodal* if it has multiple local optima, and an objective function is *unimodal* if it has only a single optimum. [Figure 2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0001) gives the examples of a unimodal function and a multimodal function. Typically, multimodal functions are more difficult to be optimized than unimodal functions, since solutions are prone to trap into the local optima in multimodal functions.

*   *Deceptive*. For multimodal functions, there exists a special case, namely, the deceptive function, which has at least two optima, i.e., a true optimum and a deceptive optimum. Besides, the majority of the search space must favor the deceptive optimum. [Figure 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0002)(a) gives an example of deceptive function. The true optimum lies in the position of ![x equals 0](images/c02-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> which is very prone to be missed by an optimization algorithm.
*   *Bias*. The bias attribute is used to describe whether an evenly distributed sample of solutions in the decision space maps to an evenly distributed set of solutions in the objective space. If not, the mapping from the Pareto set to the Pareto front is said to be *biased*. [Figure 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0002)(b) plots a large number of objective vectors of a biased multi‐objective optimization problem, where these objective vectors are obtained by randomly sampling 60,000 decision vectors. As can be seen from the figure, these objective vectors get denser toward the Pareto front.
*   *Degenerate*. The Pareto front geometries of different multi‐objective optimization problems are usually diverse (e.g., linear, concave, convex, disconnected, and mixed). Among these geometries, there exists a special kind of Pareto front, namely, the degenerate Pareto front, which is of lower dimension than the objective space where it is embedded. For example, in the bi‐objective optimization problems, a front consisting of a number of points is degenerate, while a front that is a curve is not degenerate. In the three‐objective optimization problems, a front that is a curve is degenerate, while a front that is a two‐dimensional surface is not degenerate. [Figure 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0003) provides examples of Pareto fronts with different geometries.
    
    ![Figure 2.3 Examples of Pareto fronts with different geometries.](images/c02f003.png)
    
    [**Figure 2.3**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0003) Examples of Pareto fronts with different geometries.
    
*   *Nonseparability*. The nonseparability describes the dependency relationship between decision variables. A decision variable ![x Subscript k](images/c02-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> is said to be *separable* on an Otherwise, the decision variable ![x Subscript k](images/c02-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> is *nonseparable* on ![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. If each decision variable is separable, the corresponding objective function is a *separable objective*. Conversely, if each decision variable is nonseparable, the corresponding objective function is a *nonseparable objective*. A special case is that the nonseparable decision variables only interact with some of the other decision variables, and the corresponding objective function is a *partially separable objective*.

 

### 2.2.2 Multi‐Objective Optimization Test Problems

In the earlier years, the performance of MOEAs for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization was usually tested on the problems that were initially designed for multi‐objective optimization, such as the Zitzler, Deb, and Thiele (ZDT) benchmark suite [\[19\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0019), Deb, Thiele, Laumanns, and Zitzler (DTLZ) benchmark suite [\[20\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0020), and Walking Fish Group (WFG) benchmark suite [\[21\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0021).

As one of the first benchmark suites designed for multi‐objective optimization, the ZDT benchmark suite contains six bi‐objective test problems [\[19\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0019). Each of them has the same structure and consists of three functions, namely, the distribution function ![bold f bold 1](images/c02-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, the distance function ![bold g](images/c02-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow></math> and the shape function ![bold h](images/c02-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math>:

The distribution function ![bold f 1](images/c02-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> is used for assessing the diversity maintenance ability of an MOEA, which is only related to the first decision variable of ![bold upper F left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The distance function ![bold g](images/c02-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow></math> is related to the remaining ![n minus 1](images/c02-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> decision variables of ![bold upper F left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which is used to assess the convergence ability of an MOEA. The shape function ![bold h](images/c02-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math> determines the geometries of Pareto fronts, and its inputs are the function values of ![bold f 1](images/c02-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold g](images/c02-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow></math>. [Table 2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0001) gives detailed information of the six ZDT test problems, which contains the features of Pareto front, the features of landscape, the separability of objective functions, and problem formulas. As can be seen from the table, the six ZDT test problems are diverse in terms of the features of Pareto front and landscape, but they are all separable in terms of the separability of objective functions.

![Table 2.1  Detailed Information of the Six ZDT Test Problems.](images/c02-i0024.png)

[**Table 2.1**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-tbl-0001)  Detailed Information of the Six ZDT Test Problems.

While the ZDT benchmark suite is widely used for assessing the performance of MOEAs, one limitation of the six ZDT test problems is that they are not scalable in the objective space. Considering that many problems in the real world have three or more objectives and MOEAs need to demonstrate their efficacy in solving these problems, Deb *et al*. proposed another benchmark test suite, i.e., the DTLZ benchmark test suite [\[20\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0020). All the problems in the DTLZ benchmark suite follow a generic design principle, where the first ![upper M minus 1](images/c02-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> decision variables define the Pareto front and the remaining ![n minus upper M plus 1](images/c02-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> decision variables control the convergence property. The ![n](images/c02-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper M](images/c02-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> represent the number of decision variables and the number of objectives, respectively. The detailed information of the seven DTLZ test problems is presented in [Table 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0002), it is worth noting that in the problem formulas, the last ![n minus upper M plus 1](images/c02-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> decision variables are represented as ![bold x Subscript upper M](images/c02-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub></math>. As can be seen from the table, the DTLZ benchmark suite captures more diverse problem characteristics than the ZDT benchmark suite. For example, while the DTLZ test problems have degenerate Pareto fronts and biased landscapes, the ZDT test problems do not capture these problem characteristics. Besides, from the problem formulas, it can be seen that each DTLZ test problem is scalable to have any number of objectives. But, all the DTLZ test problems are still separable in terms of the separability of objective functions.

![Table 2.2  Detailed Information of the Seven DTLZ Test Problems.](images/c02-i0047.png)

[**Table 2.2**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-tbl-0002)  Detailed Information of the Seven DTLZ Test Problems.

In addition to the ZDT and DTLZ benchmark test suites, some other benchmark test suites have also been designed and used for performance assessment of large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. For example, in the WFG benchmark suite [\[21\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0021), some problems introduce decision variable interactions, which makes them more consistent with the problems in real world. The BT benchmark suite [\[22\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0022) is specially designed to test the performance of MOEAs for solving multi‐objective optimization problems with bias landscape. In the nine BT test problems, two kinds of biases, namely, the position‐related bias and distance‐related bias, are considered. The MaF benchmark suite [\[23\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0023) is designed for assessing the performance of MOEAs on problems with more than three objectives. In the 15 MaF test problems, a variety of problem characteristics that are widely presented in real‐world applications are captured.

Although the benchmark suites as introduced above have effectively promoted the research of evolutionary multi‐objective optimization and some of them are used as the test problems for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, the majority of them are designed by introducing difficulties in the objective space. Few of them pay attention to the challenges brought by the huge decision space. Specifically, on the one hand, some of them are not scalable in the decision space. On the other hand, while some of them are scalable to have any number of decision variables, the decision variables are separable without complex variable interactions. Hence, they are not suitable for evaluating the performance of MOEAs in solving LSMOPs, but these problems just exist widely in many practical applications. To this end, some benchmark test problems have been specially designed for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, which will be elaborated in [Section 2.2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0005).

where ![f 1](images/c02-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> to ![f Subscript upper M](images/c02-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub></math> are the objective functions, ![bold x Superscript f Baseline equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript upper M minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![bold x Superscript s Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript upper M Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are the position‐related part and distance‐related part of the decision vector ![bold x](images/c02-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, respectively. The functions ![h 1](images/c02-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, …, ![h Subscript upper M](images/c02-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub></math> together define the geometry of Pareto front, and they are used to test the diversity maintenance ability of MOEAs. The functions ![g 1](images/c02-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, …, ![g Subscript upper M](images/c02-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub></math> together define the fitness landscape, and they are used to test the convergence ability of MOEAs. Based on the above design formulation, the LSMOP test problems are scalable to have any number of decision variables and objectives. Besides, by strengthening the design of fitness landscape functions, the LSMOP test problems capture some important characteristics that are related to decision variables, which are listed as follows:

1.  (1) The decision variables are nonuniformly divided into multiple groups.
2.  (2) Different groups of decision variables are correlated with different objectives.
3.  (3) The decision variables have mixed separability.
4.  (4) The decision variables have linkages on the Pareto optimal sets.

By introducing the above four characteristics, the LSMOP test problems mimic the problems in real world better, which enables them to comprehensively test the ability of MOEAs in solving LSMOPs. For example, when the ZDT, DTLZ, and WFG test problems are used for performance testing in large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, once a single solution on the Pareto front is obtained, it can be spread along the whole Pareto front by perturbing the variables that are related to the shape functions. By contrast, the LSMOP test problems introduce linkages between position variables in ![bold x Superscript f](images/c02-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></msup></math> and distance variables in ![bold x Superscript s](images/c02-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup></math>, perturbing the position variables of solutions on the Pareto front will affect the distance variables, thus worsening the convergence of solutions.

[Table 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0003) presents detailed information of the LSMOP test problems. As can be seen from the table, despite that the nine LSMOP test problems have simple Pareto front geometries, a wide variety of difficulties brought by decision variables are introduced, such as the mixed landscape and mixed separability of objective functions. It is worth noting that, in the problem formulas, ![c Subscript i comma j](images/c02-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> is used to define the correlation between decision variables and objective functions. The ![u Subscript i](images/c02-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![l Subscript i](images/c02-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> are the upper bound and lower bound of the ![i](images/c02-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th decision variable, respectively. The ![eta 1 comma eta 2 comma ellipsis comma eta 6](images/c02-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></math> are six basic single‐objective optimization problems, and their detailed information is provided in [Table 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0004).

The ![h Subscript i](images/c02-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![g Subscript i](images/c02-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> are the ![i](images/c02-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th shape function and landscape function, respectively. As can be seen from the formula, both the multiplication‐based formulation model and addition‐based formulation model are used in the LMF benchmark test suite, which is obviously different from the benchmarks as introduced above that only use a single formulation model.

To better mimic and reflect the characteristics of LSMOPs in real‐world applications, LMF inherits the common features in the LSMOP benchmark suite, e.g., the nonuniform grouping of decision variables, the mixed separability of objective functions, and variable linkages. Besides, LMF makes the following improvements.

1.  (1) Hybrid linkages between position‐related variables and distance‐related variables are introduced.
2.  (2) More flexible grouping of decision variables is adopted.
3.  (3) The shape functions are strengthened by adding the correlation between position‐related variables.
4.  (4) The imbalanced contribution of decision variables to objective functions is created.

Based on the above design principle and improvements, there are totally 12 problems that have been defined in the LMF benchmark test suite. Tables [2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0005) and [2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0006) present detailed information of the 12 LMF test problems. It can be seen that the 12 test problems are diverse in terms of Pareto front geometries. While the commonly seen concave, convex, and linear Pareto fronts are included, the inverted concave and inverted linear Pareto fronts are also designed. In terms of the features of landscape, the unimodal functions, multimodal functions, and mixed functions are used. Besides, the most objectives of the 12 test problems are partially separable, considering that the partially separable objectives have wider existence in practical applications compared with the two extreme cases, fully separable and nonseparable.

## 2.3 Performance Indicators

With the wide application of MOEAs, a variety of new MOEAs continue to be proposed. In order to investigate their performance, the quality of the solution sets obtained by them needs to be quantified by some performance indicators [\[26\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0026). In this section, they are divided into three categories, namely, the indicators assessing only convergence, the indicators assessing only diversity, and the indicators assessing both convergence and diversity. These indicators are widely adopted to evaluate the performance of MOEAs tailored for both large‐scale multi‐objective optimization and non‐large‐scale multi‐objective optimization.

 

### 2.3.1 Performance Indicators Assessing Only Convergence

The ratio of non‐dominated individuals (RNI) [\[27\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0027), Purity [\[28\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0028), and generational distance (GD) [\[29\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0029) are three representative performance indicators that assess only the convergence of a solution set. Specifically, given a solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>, RNI is mathematically formulated as

(2.6)![RNI left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis equals StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue upper A 1 EndAbsoluteValue Over StartAbsoluteValue upper A EndAbsoluteValue EndFraction comma](images/c02-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>RNI</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![StartAbsoluteValue upper A 1 EndAbsoluteValue](images/c02-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> is the number of non‐dominated solutions in solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and ![StartAbsoluteValue upper A EndAbsoluteValue](images/c02-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> represents the size of solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. Clearly, the larger the RNI, the better the convergence of solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.

Purity is a performance indicator that can compare multiple solution sets simultaneously. Given ![upper N](images/c02-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solution sets ![upper A Superscript 1 Baseline comma upper A squared comma ellipsis comma upper A Superscript upper N](images/c02-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></math> (![upper N greater-than 2](images/c02-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>2</mn></math>), let ![r Subscript i Baseline equals StartAbsoluteValue upper A 1 Superscript i Baseline EndAbsoluteValue left-parenthesis i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma upper N right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denotes the number of non‐dominated solutions in the ![i](images/c02-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th solution set. The spacing (SP) [\[31\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0031), maximum spread (MS) [\[19\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0019), ![upper C upper L Subscript mu](images/c02-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><msub><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></msub></math> [\[32\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0032), and CPF [\[33\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0033) are the most representative performance indicators that assess only the diversity of a solution set. Specifically, SP calculates the standard deviation of the minimum distance of each solution to the others in a solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> as

### 2.3.3 Performance Indicators Assessing Both Convergence and Diversity

The goal of solving an MOP is to obtain a set of uniformly distributed solutions that converge to the Pareto front as closely as possible, thus the indicators that assess both convergence and diversity are usually more desirable. As two representative performance indicators that belong to this category, the inverted generation distance (IGD) [\[34\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0034) and hypervolume (HV) [\[35\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0035) are widely used for performance assessment of MOEAs.

The IGD was first suggested in 2004 [\[36\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0036), and now it has been one of the most commonly used performance indicators. In fact, similar ideas were presented in earlier years \[[37](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0037), [38](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0038)\]. As its name suggested, IGD calculates the average distance from each reference point on the Pareto front to its nearest solution in the solution set. The left of [Figure 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0004) provides a brief example of calculating IGD in the two‐dimensional objective space. Given a set of reference points denoted by ![upper Z equals left-brace z 1](images/c02-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#61;</mo><mo where ![z Subscript j](images/c02-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![a Subscript k](images/c02-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> are the ![j](images/c02-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>th reference point and ![k](images/c02-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>th solution, respectively, ![d left-parenthesis z Subscript j Baseline comma a Subscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the Euclidean distance between reference point ![z Subscript j](images/c02-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> and solution ![a Subscript k](images/c02-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math>.

![Figure 2.4 Brief examples of calculating IGD and HV in two‐dimensional objective space.](images/c02f004.png)

[**Figure 2.4**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0004) Brief examples of calculating IGD and HV in two‐dimensional objective space.

The idea of HV was initially proposed by Zitzler and Thiele [\[39\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0039). In fact, there are also some other terms such as S‐metric [\[40\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0040), Lebesgue measure [\[41\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0041), and hyperarea metric [\[42\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0042), which have a similar meaning as hypervolume. Given a solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and a reference point ![r](images/c02-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>, HV calculates the area covered by solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> with respect to reference point ![r](images/c02-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.

(2.14)![HV left-parenthesis upper A comma r right-parenthesis equals lamda left-parenthesis union Underscript a element-of upper A Endscripts StartSet b vertical-bar a precedes b precedes r EndSet right-parenthesis comma](images/c02-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>HV</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8899;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8826;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8826;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![lamda left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the Lebesgue measure of a solution set: ![lamda left-parenthesis upper Z right-parenthesis equals integral Underscript z element-of upper Z Endscripts 1 upper Z left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis d z](images/c02-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></msub><mn>1</mn><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></math> with *1*Z being the characteristic function of *Z* that equals **1** if ![z element-of upper Z](images/c02-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Z</mi></math> and 0 otherwise, ![a succeeds-or-equal-to b](images/c02-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8829;</mo><mi>b</mi></math> means that ![a](images/c02-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> dominates ![b](images/c02-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. It is worth noting that, compared with IGD, HV has the property of Pareto compliance. That is to say, if a solution set *A* is better than another solution set *B* in terms of Pareto dominance, it can be ensured that ![upper A](images/c02-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> has a better HV value than ![upper B](images/c02-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, but it is not the case in terms of IGD. The right of [Figure 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0004) gives an example of calculating HV in the two‐dimensional objective space, where the value of HV equals the size of the gray region.

Although IGD and HV have been the most popular performance indicators used for performance assessment, they have also some shortcomings. For example, it is often observed that some non‐dominated solutions are ignored in the calculation of IGD, due to the fact that they are not the nearest neighbor of any reference point. This means that these solutions do not have any contribution to the IGD value, and these solutions are called as noncontributing solutions (NSs) in [\[43\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0043). Specifically, given a solution ![y prime](images/c02-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> in the non‐dominated solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>, it is regarded as a NS if the following condition is satisfied:

(2.15)![there-does-not-exist x element-of upper Z colon d i s left-parenthesis x comma y Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis equals min Underscript y element-of upper A Endscripts d i s left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis comma](images/c02-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8708;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![upper Z](images/c02-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math> is a set of reference points that are uniformly sampled from the Pareto front, and ![d i s left-parenthesis x comma y prime right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> represents the Euclidean distance between the reference point ![x](images/c02-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and solution ![y prime](images/c02-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. By taking NSs into consideration, Tian *et al*. [\[43\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0043) proposed an improved indicator, namely, IGD with noncontributing solution detection (IGD‐NS).

(2.16)![IGD hyphen NS left-parenthesis upper A comma upper Z right-parenthesis equals sigma-summation Underscript x element-of upper Z Endscripts min Underscript y element-of upper A Endscripts d i s left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis plus sigma-summation Underscript y prime element-of upper A Superscript prime Baseline Endscripts min Underscript x element-of upper Z Endscripts d i s left-parenthesis x comma y Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c02-math-0016.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>IGD&#8208;NS</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></munder><msub><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![upper A prime](images/c02-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is the set of NSs in population ![upper A](images/c02-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. As can be seen from the definition, the first term in the above formula is similar to IGD. The second term calculates the sum of the minimum distance from each NS to the reference points in ![upper Z](images/c02-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>. In this way, a population can obtain a good IGD‐NS value in the case that it not only shows good convergence and diversity but also contains as few NSs as possible.

There are also other improved indicators that are proposed to address the shortcomings of IGD and HV, such as ![IGD Subscript bold p](images/c02-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mtext>IGD</mtext></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow></msub></math> [\[44\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0044), ![IGD Superscript plus](images/c02-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mtext>IGD</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></math> [\[45\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0045), ![upper I Subscript SDE](images/c02-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>SDE</mtext></mrow></msub></math> [\[46\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0046), and volume measure [\[47\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0047). Although many indicators are available for performance assessment, it is still worth noting that the assessment results of these indicators on a solution set may be inconsistent. While a well‐convergent population with slightly worse diversity has a bad HV value, it may have the best IGD value due to the biased distribution of reference points [\[48\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0048). By the contrary, for a population with good diversity but slightly worse convergence, while it has a bad IGD value, it may have a good value in terms of HV. To address this issue, multiple performance indicators are usually used simultaneously for performance measurement.

 

## 2.4 Test Problems for Sparse Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization

 

### 2.4.1 Synthetic Test Problems

In the academic research and industrial applications, a large number of problems are modeled as LSMOPs, where some of them have a special characteristic, i.e., most of the decision variables in Pareto optimal solutions are zero‐valued. This class of LSMOPs are herein named as sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems (sparse LSMOPs). [Figure 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0005) gives examples of two sparse LSMOPs in the practical applications, namely, the critical node detection problem [\[49\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0049) and neural network training problem [\[50\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0050). The critical node detection problem aims to find the critical nodes in a complex network, the deletion of which will maximize the destruction of the network. If we represent each critical node in the network by 1 and each noncritical node by 0, most decision variables in the optimal solution are zero‐valued. In the neural network training problem, it aims to optimize the weights for improving the prediction accuracy and reducing the network complexity. If we represent each weight in the neural network by a real number, most decision variables in the optimal solution are zero‐valued for sparse network training. The sparse LSMOPs exist extensively in many fields, such as feature selection [\[51\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0051), portfolio optimization [\[52\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0052), sparse signal reconstruction [\[53\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0053), and adversarial attack [\[54\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0054).

![Figure 2.5 Brief examples of two sparse LSMOPs in practical applications. (a) Critical node detection problem. (b) Neural network training problem.](images/c02f005.png)

[**Figure 2.5**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0005) Brief examples of two sparse LSMOPs in practical applications. (a) Critical node detection problem. (b) Neural network training problem.

Despite that sparse LSMOPs are very common in many applications, most of the existing test problems do not consider the sparse nature of Pareto optimal solutions. There exist a few test problems having sparse Pareto optimal solutions, but the majority of them do not have a suitable hardness to assess the ability of MOEAs in solving sparse LSMOPs. For example, although the ZDT1–ZDT4 and ZDT6 test problems have a Pareto optimal set of ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket times StartSet 0 EndSet Superscript upper D minus 1](images/c02-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> with ![upper D](images/c02-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> denoting the number of decision variables, they are easy to be solved since the lower boundary of their decision variables is 0. The DTLZ6 and DTLZ7 test problems have a Pareto optimal set of ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket Superscript upper M minus 1 Baseline times StartSet 0 EndSet Superscript upper D minus upper M plus 1](images/c02-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>, where ![upper M](images/c02-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper D](images/c02-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> represent the number of objectives and decision variables, respectively, but they are too difficult to be solved due to their complicated Pareto fronts instead of the challenge caused by the large number of decision variables. To this end, a sparse multi‐objective optimization benchmark test suite, namely, SMOP, is proposed in [\[55\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0055), which can comprehensively assess the ability of MOEAs in solving sparse LSMOPs.

Each test problem in the SMOP benchmark suite is obtained by the following uniform design formulation:

where ![theta element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c02-i0305.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> is a parameter that controls the sparsity of Pareto optimal solutions.

[Table 2.8](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0008) presents detailed information of the eight SMOP benchmark test problems. Three kinds of Pareto fronts, namely, the linear Pareto front, convex Pareto front, and concave Pareto front are involved. In terms of the features of landscape, unimodal, multimodal, deceptive, and mixed functions are employed, which pose a challenge to most of the existing MOEAs in obtaining sparse optimal solutions.

![Table 2.8  Detailed Information of the Eight SMOP Test Problems.](images/c02-i0306.png)

[**Table 2.8**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-tbl-0008)  Detailed Information of the Eight SMOP Test Problems.

SMMOP [\[56\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0056) is another benchmark test suite tailored for sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. Each SMMOP test problem has multiple equivalent sparse Pareto optimal solutions that are similar in the objective space but completely different in the decision space. This means that SMMOP benchmark test suit is designed for sparse large‐scale multi‐model multi‐objective optimization. Equation ([2.19](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0019)) gives the uniform design formulation of the SMMOP test problems.

where ![g Subscript o n e Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c02-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> can be minimized when the related decision variables are set to specified nonzero values, ![g Subscript z e r o Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to 0](images/c02-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> can be minimized when all the related decision variables are set to zero, and ![upper S](images/c02-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> controls the sparsity of the Pareto optimal solutions. In each landscape function, ![g Subscript o n e](images/c02-i0354.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![g Subscript z e r o](images/c02-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> cannot be minimized simultaneously, which ensures that the equivalent Pareto optimal solutions have different sparse distribution and the number of equivalent Pareto optimal sets is always equal to the number of landscape functions ![n Subscript p](images/c02-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math>.

In the SMMOP benchmark test suite, three types of shape functions and five types of basic landscape functions are defined. Based on these functions, eight benchmark test problems are proposed, namely SMMOP1–SMMOP8. For each SMMOP test problem, the number of decision variables, the number of objectives, and the sparsity of Pareto optimal solutions can be specified flexibly, which are very similar to the SMOP test problems. The main difference lies in that the SMMOP test problems have ![n Subscript p](images/c02-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math> equivalent Pareto optimal sets, where ![n Subscript p](images/c02-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math> can also be specified flexibly.

[Table 2.9](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0009) provides detailed information of the eight SMMOP test problems. ![g Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis x comma t right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0378.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the basic landscape function, where ![x element-of left-bracket negative 1 comma 2 right-bracket](images/c02-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> is a decision variable and ![t element-of left-bracket negative 1 comma 2 right-bracket](images/c02-i0380.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> is a parameter defining the optimal value of ![x](images/c02-i0381.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, i.e., the landscape functions can be minimized when ![x equals t](images/c02-i0382.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi></math>. It is worth noting that, in the eight test problems, the parameter ![t](images/c02-i0383.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> for ![g Subscript o n e](images/c02-i0384.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></math> is set to ![pi slash 3](images/c02-i0385.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, which is a value that cannot be easily found by MOEAs. The parameter ![t](images/c02-i0386.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> for ![g Subscript z e r o](images/c02-i0387.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> is set to 0, which is neither the boundary nor the median of the range ![left-bracket negative 1 comma 2 right-bracket](images/c02-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> of the decision variable. Thus, it is also difficult to be found by MOEAs. By the contrary, if MOEAs take the sparse nature of Pareto optimal solutions into consideration, they may find the optimal decision variables in Pareto optimal solutions easily.

[**Table 2.9**](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-tbl-0009)  Detailed Information of the Eight SMMOP Test Problems.

 

### 2.4.2 Practical Test Problems

Due to the fact that the sparse LSMOPs are generalized from the real problems in real world, a number of problems from different practical applications can also be used to test the performance of MOEAs in addressing sparse LSMOPs, e.g., the fields of machine learning, network science, software engineering, signal processing, data mining, and economics. In [\[57\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0057), 17 sparse LSMOPs in real‐world applications are summarized, and 8 of them are used as practical test problems in the experimental studies, which include feature selection, instance selection, neural network training, community detection, critical node detection, sparse signal reconstruction, pattern mining, and portfolio optimization.

 

#### 2.4.2.1 Feature Selection

This problem aims to select the fewest features for the lowest classification error [\[58\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0058). Thus, it has two optimization objectives, i.e., minimizing the ratio of selected features and minimizing the classification error rate with respect to the selected features. The corresponding problem formula is given in the following:

#### 2.4.2.2 Instance Selection

This problem aims to select the fewest samples for the lowest classification error [\[59\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0059). Thus, its two optimization objectives are minimizing the ratio of selected samples and the classification error rate with respect to the selected samples. The corresponding problem formula is given in the following:

#### 2.4.2.3 Neural Network Training

This problem aims to obtain the optimal weights of a neural network for the lowest classification error and network complexity [\[50\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0050). Thus, it has two optimization objectives, i.e., minimizing the ratio of nonzero weights and minimizing the error rate of the neural network. The corresponding problem formula is given in the following:

#### 2.4.2.4 Community Detection

This problem aims to find the best community structure, where the nodes within the same community have dense connections and the nodes in different communities have sparse connections [\[60\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0060). Its two optimization objectives are minimizing the negative value of the intra‐link density and minimizing the inter‐link density. The corresponding problem formula is given in the following:

#### 2.4.2.5 Critical Node Detection

This problem aims to delete the fewest nodes for the lowest pairwise connectivity of the remaining network [\[49\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0049). Thus, it has two optimization objectives, i.e., minimizing the ratio of deleted nodes and minimizing the ratio of the pairwise connectivity of the remaining network to that of the original network. The corresponding problem formula is given in the following:

#### 2.4.2.6 Sparse Signal Reconstruction

This problem aims to find the most sparse signal for the lowest loss [\[53\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0053). Its two optimization objectives are minimizing the sparsity of the reconstructed signal and minimizing the loss of the reconstructed signal. The corresponding problem formula is given in the following:

## 2.5 Performance Indicator for Sparse Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization

In the past few years, when some MOEAs have been customized for sparse LSMOPs, their performance is usually assessed by the IGD indicator and HV indicator. But, these two indicators are somewhat unsuitable for assessing the performance of MOEAs on sparse LSMOPs, due to the following two facts. On the one hand, a set of reference points on the true Pareto front are needed for calculating IGD, but the true Pareto fronts of real‐world applications are usually unknown. Although HV requires only a single reference point which is not on the true Pareto front, it is still difficult to set this reference point for fair performance comparison [\[65\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0065). On the other hand, the two indicators assess only convergence and diversity of solutions in the objective space, while the sparsity of solutions in the decision space is not considered.

To address the issue as mentioned above, a comprehensive performance indicator, namely, CSD (convergence‐sparsity–diversity) [\[66\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0066), is specifically designed for assessing the performance of MOEAs on sparse LSMOPs. In CSD, both the convergence and diversity of solutions in the objective space and the sparsity of solutions in the decision space are considered. Besides, the CSD indicator does not require any reference point or parameter, which enables it to have wide suitability not only on benchmark problems but also on practical applications.

Considering that the primary goal of solving sparse LSMOPs is to minimize the objectives, and the sparsity is an important factor in decision‐making, CSD first assigns solution sets into different levels according to their convergence and sparsity. Then, the solution sets in the same level are sorted according to their diversity. Algorithm 2.1 presents the procedure of calculating CSD, which consists of four steps, i.e., assigning solution sets according to their convergence, assigning solution sets according to their sparsity, calculating the diversity of each solution set, and calculating the CSD value of each solution set.

In the first step, the superiority between each two solution sets in terms of convergence is first determined by the following formula:

(2.31)![left-brace StartLayout 1st Row StartAbsoluteValue left-brace bold y element-of upper B vertical-bar there-exists bold x element-of upper A colon bold x precedes bold y right-brace EndAbsoluteValue greater-than 0.5 StartAbsoluteValue upper B EndAbsoluteValue 2nd Row StartAbsoluteValue left-brace bold x element-of upper A vertical-bar there-exists bold y element-of upper A colon bold x precedes bold y right-brace EndAbsoluteValue greater-than 0.5 StartAbsoluteValue upper A EndAbsoluteValue EndLayout comma period](images/c02-math-0031.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="." separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8707;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8826;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8707;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8826;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>,</mo></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where a solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0438.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is said to be superior over a solution set ![upper B](images/c02-i0439.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if more than half the solutions in ![upper B](images/c02-i0440.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are dominated by at least half the solutions in ![upper A](images/c02-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. Then, the solution sets are assigned to different levels.

In the second step, the superiority between each two solution sets in terms of sparsity is determined by the following formula:

(2.32)![s p a r s i t y left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis greater-than-or-equal-to s p a r s i t y left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis plus StartFraction 1 Over upper D EndFraction comma](images/c02-math-0032.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![s p a r s i t y left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0442.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![s p a r s i t y left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0443.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> indicate the sparsity of solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and solution set ![upper B](images/c02-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, respectively. The solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is said to be superior over solution set ![upper B](images/c02-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if and only if the sparsity of solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is larger than ![upper B](images/c02-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, besides, the sparsity difference between the two solution sets is not smaller than ![1 slash upper D](images/c02-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>D</mi></math>. The sparsity of a solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is calculated as:

(2.33)![s p a r s i t y left-parenthesis upper A right-parenthesis equals 1 minus StartFraction 1 Over StartAbsoluteValue upper A EndAbsoluteValue EndFraction StartFraction 1 Over upper D EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript bold x element-of upper A Endscripts double-vertical-bar bold x double-vertical-bar Subscript 0 Baseline comma](images/c02-math-0033.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></mfrac><munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![upper D](images/c02-i0452.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> denotes the total number of decision variables and ![double-vertical-bar bold x double-vertical-bar Subscript 0](images/c02-i0453.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math> denotes the number of nonzero variables in solution ![bold x](images/c02-i0454.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>.

As for the step of assessing the diversity of each solution set, a reference vector‐based diversity criterion is used. The value of each objective function is first normalized by the following formula:

(2.34)![f Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction f Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis minus z Subscript i Superscript asterisk Baseline Over z Subscript i Superscript n a d Baseline minus z Subscript i Superscript asterisk Baseline EndFraction comma i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma upper M comma](images/c02-math-0034.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![z Superscript asterisk](images/c02-i0455.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is the ideal point containing the minimum objective values in all the solution sets and ![z Superscript n a d](images/c02-i0456.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></math> is the nadir point containing the maximum objective values in all the solution sets. Then, a set of uniformly distributed reference vectors are generated in the objective space, and each reference vector is associated with the solution closest to it. Next, the number ![c Subscript bold x](images/c02-i0457.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub></math> of reference vectors associated with each solution ![bold x](images/c02-i0458.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> is counted:

where ![d i s left-parenthesis bold f left-parenthesis bold a right-parenthesis comma r right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0459.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denotes the distance between solution ![bold a](images/c02-i0460.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi></mrow></math> and reference vector ![bold r](images/c02-i0461.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi></mrow></math>. where ![c overbar](images/c02-i0464.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> is the mean value of all ![c Subscript bold x](images/c02-i0465.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub></math>.

In the step of calculating the CSD value of each solution set, the harmonic average of the levels of each solution set in terms of convergence and sparsity is first calculated by

where ![l e v e l Subscript upper A Superscript c](images/c02-i0466.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![l e v e l Subscript upper A Superscript s](images/c02-i0467.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> denote the level of solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0468.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> in terms of convergence and sparsity, respectively. Then, the ranking ![r a n k Subscript upper A](images/c02-i0469.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub></math> of each solution set ![upper A](images/c02-i0470.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is obtained by sorting all the solution sets according to their harmonic averages of levels. Finally, the CSD value of each solution set is calculated by

where ![max Underscript r a n k Subscript upper B Baseline equals i Endscripts d i v e r s i t y left-parenthesis upper B right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0471.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>max</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denotes the maximum diversity value among the solution sets with a ranking of ![i](images/c02-i0472.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>.

It is worth noting that, in the step of assessing the diversity of each solution set, the used reference vectors are parallel instead of starting from the origin. As illustrated in [Fig. 2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0006), for the seven solutions uniformly distributed on a convex curve, they are associated with 1, 0, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1 reference vectors starting from the origin but 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 parallel reference vectors. Clearly, the parallel reference vectors can better assess the diversity of solution sets lying on convex or concave surfaces.

## 2.6 Summary

In this chapter, a brief introduction to evolutionary large‐scale multi‐objective optimization is first given. Then, some primary concepts are introduced, followed by the introduction of some commonly used large‐scale multi‐objective optimization test problems. Next, three kinds of performance indicators are elaborated, namely, the indicators assessing only convergence, the indicators assessing only diversity, and the indicators assessing both convergence and diversity. Afterward, this chapter introduces the test problems that are tailored for sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. Finally, a dedicated performance indicator which assesses convergence, sparsity, and diversity simultaneously is introduced in detail.

In the following chapters, the MOEAs customized for LSMOPs and sparse LSMOPs are elaborated in [Chapters 3](#c03.xhtml) and [4](#c04.xhtml), respectively, followed by the introduction of MOEAs tailored for some representative applications, mainly including the fields of community detection, logistic scheduling, power systems, deep learning, and radiotherapy planning.
