# 3  
Evolutionary Algorithms for Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization

 

## 3.1 Introduction

The research of evolutionary computation in many areas focuses on the innovation of selection strategies, such as multi‐objective optimization [\[1\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0001), many‐objective optimization [\[2\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0002), and constrained optimization [\[3\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0003). This is because evolutionary algorithms can generate promising solutions for these problems but are unable to distinguish them to retain the better ones. Thus, novel selection strategies are developed to preserve the population diversity for multi‐objective optimization [\[4\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0004), alleviate the dominance resistance phenomenon for many‐objective optimization [\[5\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0005), and balance between objective optimization and constraint satisfaction for constrained optimization [\[6\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0006). These selection strategies are combined with the variation operators in genetic algorithms, differential evolution, particle swarm optimization, and other metaheuristics, which are effective enough for obtaining a set of well‐converged and diversified solutions.

However, evolutionary algorithms can hardly generate promising solutions in high‐dimensional decision spaces due to the curse of dimensionality [\[7\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0007). Even if many metaheuristics and mathematical programming methods have shown fast convergence speed on single‐objective optimization problems, they are inefficient to generate a set of diversified solutions for multi‐objective optimization [\[8\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0008). Therefore, the research of large‐scale multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) focuses on the innovation of variation operators rather than selection strategies, which should be able to generate high‐quality solutions approximating the Pareto fronts of large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems (LSMOPs) with good diversity.

 

### 3.1.1 Ideas of Searching in High‐Dimensional Spaces

For large‐scale single‐objective optimization, many metaheuristics have shown outstanding performance on benchmark problems and competitions, such as the advanced variants of differential evolution and particle swarm optimization [\[9\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0009). Intuitively, the variation operators suggested in these metaheuristics can be equipped with multi‐objective selection strategies for handling LSMOPs. However, the difficulties of single‐objective optimization and multi‐objective optimization are fundamentally different. First, the goal of single‐objective evolutionary algorithms is to approximate the only optimal solution of a problem, which cannot make all solutions in the population well‐converged when solving LSMOPs [\[10\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0010). Second, it is difficult to distinguish non‐dominated solutions quantitatively, which hinders the parameter adaptation in differential evolution \[[11](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0011), [12](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0012)\] and the learning strategies in particle swarm optimization \[[13](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0013), [14](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0014)\]. As a matter of fact, the popular variation operators for single‐objective optimization and multi‐objective optimization are different. For instance, genetic operators are effective for the diversity preservation in multi‐objective optimization, but they converge slower than many other operators on a single objective [\[15\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0015). Most variation operators in MOEAs (including those based on differential evolution and particle swarm optimization) are tailed by polynomial mutation for local exploitation \[[16](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0016), [17](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0017)\], while it is rarely used in single‐objective optimization.

First‐order gradient descent methods are particularly effective for the optimization problems with massive variables, such as the training of deep neural networks \[[18](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0018), [19](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0019)\]. Besides, the gradients of black‐box objectives can be well approximated by finite difference [\[20\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0020) and solved by gradient descent methods. However, an inescapable issue is the high computational complexity of gradient calculation, where ![upper D](images/c03-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> function evaluations are consumed to calculate the gradients of a solution with ![upper D](images/c03-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> decision variables. When solving LSMOPs, gradient descent methods turn out to be less efficient than evolutionary algorithms, since the update of one solution in gradient descent methods takes more function evaluations than the update of a whole population in evolutionary algorithms. This fact seems counterintuitive since all the partial derivatives of some objective functions can be calculated together (e.g., the backpropagation of deep neural networks), which reduces the number of consumed function evaluations from ![upper D](images/c03-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> to 1 [\[21\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0021). Nevertheless, it is assumed that all the partial derivatives cannot be calculated together for generic problems, and the number of consumed function evaluations remains ![upper D](images/c03-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> when using finite difference. In addition, gradient descent methods have to aggregate multiple objectives when solving LSMOPs, which can only obtain boundary solutions (i.e., only one objective is minimized) on non‐convex Pareto fronts regardless of the weights for objective aggregation [\[8\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0008).

In short, single‐objective optimizers cannot be directly used for solving LSMOPs. Besides, the convergence speed of evolutionary algorithms cannot be unlimitedly improved due to the curse of dimensionality, which is inevitable in high‐dimensional decision spaces. Considering that LSMOPs are generally NP‐hard problems whose global optimal solutions cannot be found in polynomial time, novel strategies have to be designed to pursue other goals alternatively, such as solving LSMOPs with particular characteristics and finding local optimal solutions.

 

### 3.1.2 Taxonomy of Large‐Scale MOEAs

Large‐scale MOEAs can be roughly divided into three categories, including decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs, decision space reduction‐based MOEAs, and novel search strategy‐based MOEAs [\[22\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0022). As plotted in [Fig. 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0001)(a), decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs aim to solve LSMOPs in a divide‐and‐conquer manner, where the large number of decision variables is divided into multiple groups and optimized alternately. Assuming that an LSMOP has ![upper D](images/c03-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> decision variables with each having ![k](images/c03-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> candidate values, the total number of candidate solutions can be reduced from ![k Superscript upper D](images/c03-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math> to ![upper G k Superscript StartFraction upper D Over upper G EndFraction](images/c03-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><msup><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup></math> if the decision variables are divided into ![upper G](images/c03-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> groups with equal size. That is, the number of candidate solutions is exponentially reduced with the increment of the number of groups ![upper G](images/c03-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>. Extremely, each variable is assigned to an independent group making ![upper G equals upper D](images/c03-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi></math>, and thus the number of candidate solutions is minimized to ![upper D k](images/c03-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>D</mi><mi>k</mi></math>. However, the arbitrary division of decision variables is questionable due to the presence of variable interactions, where the optimal value of a decision variable may depend on the values of other decision variables, and the alternate optimization of these decision variables gets stuck in local optimums.

Taking the following single‐objective optimization problem as an example:

In short, the decision variables in Eq. ([3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0001)) can be separately optimized while the decision variables in Eq. ([3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0002)) cannot. The difference mainly lies in the partial derivatives, where the ![StartFraction partial-differential f Over partial-differential x 1 EndFraction](images/c03-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></math> of Eq. ([3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0001)) is independent of ![x 2](images/c03-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> but the ![StartFraction partial-differential f Over partial-differential x 1 EndFraction](images/c03-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></math> of Eq. ([3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0002)) is not. In other words,

holds for Eq. ([3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0001)) and thus the global optimal solution can be found by alternately optimizing ![x 1](images/c03-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![x 2](images/c03-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, whereas it does not hold for Eq. ([3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0002)) and thus the global optimal solution cannot be found by alternately optimizing ![x 1](images/c03-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![x 2](images/c03-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>. The ![x 1](images/c03-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![x 2](images/c03-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> in Eq. ([3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0002)) are known as interacted decision variables, which can only be divided into the same group and optimized simultaneously. To address this dilemma, a variety of variable grouping methods have been developed for large‐scale optimization, such as random grouping [\[23\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0023), ordered grouping [\[24\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0024), and differential grouping [\[25\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0025). While these grouping methods were originally tailored for converging to the single optimum of single‐objective optimization problems, they can hardly find multiple solutions spreading over the whole Pareto fronts due to the lack of the consideration of diversity. Therefore, some large‐scale MOEAs divide the decision variables by considering their contributions to convergence and diversity \[[26](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0026)–[28](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0028)\], where the convergence‐related variables are further divided according to their interactions for converging to the Pareto front, and the diversity‐related variables are simultaneously optimized to enhance the population diversity. Obviously, decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs are only suitable for LSMOPs with separable decision variables. If all the decision variables are interacted with each other like Eq. ([3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0002)), decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs will degenerate into general MOEAs since all the decision variables have to be optimized together.

As plotted in [Fig. 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0001)(b), decision space reduction‐based MOEAs aim to reduce the number of decision variables of LSMOPs, and thus the total number of candidate solutions can be directly reduced from ![k Superscript upper D](images/c03-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math> to ![k Superscript upper D prime](images/c03-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msup></math>, where ![upper D prime](images/c03-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is the number of reduced decision variables. Considering the following single‐objective optimization problem:

(3.4)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column Minimize 2nd Column f left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis equals minus x 1 squared minus left-parenthesis x 1 minus x 2 right-parenthesis squared comma 2nd Row 1st Column normal s period normal t period 2nd Column x 1 comma x 2 element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket comma EndLayout](images/c03-math-0004.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mtext>Minimize</mtext></mtd><mtd><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mo>.</mo></mtd><mtd><mspace width="0.15em"/><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> 

where the global optimum of the problem is ![negative 1](images/c03-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> when ![left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. During the optimization procedure, the desirable setting ![x 2 equals x 1](images/c03-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> may be concluded from the non‐dominated solutions in the current population, and thus only ![x 1](images/c03-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> needs to be optimized. At each generation, dimensionality reduction methods are used to reduce the number of decision variables of parent solutions according to the current population. Then, offspring solutions are generated by the shortened parent solutions, and they are recovered by dimensionality reduction methods for function evaluation. To reduce the dimensionality of decision spaces, some large‐scale MOEAs develop heuristic methods (e.g., problem transformation [\[29\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0029) and problem reformulation [\[30\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0030)) or adopt machine learning methods (e.g., random embedding [\[31\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0031), principal component analysis [\[32\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0032), neural networks [\[33\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0033), and clustering [\[34\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0034)) to mine the interrelations between decision variables. The dimensionality reduction methods work in an unsupervised manner, which focus on the decision variables of solutions without considering their objective values. Thus, they do not need to consider the interactions between decision variables and are much more efficient than decision variable grouping methods. Nevertheless, the decision variables of many problems like Eqs. ([3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0001)) and ([3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0002)) are unrelated to each other, the elimination of any decision variable is likely to lose the global optimums. Apart from specific LSMOPs such as those with low intrinsic dimensions [\[31\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0031) or sparse optimal solutions [\[33\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0033), decision space reduction‐based MOEAs can quickly converge to the local optimums of LSMOPs, but can hardly approximate the global optimums of LSMOPs even if massive function evaluations are available.

As plotted in [Fig. 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0001)(c), there exist some large‐scale MOEAs suggesting novel search strategies to directly search in the high‐dimensional decision space. While decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs and decisions space reduction‐based MOEAs employ conventional variation operators (e.g., simulated binary crossover [\[35\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0035), polynomial mutation [\[36\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0036), and differential evolution [\[37\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0037)) to generate offspring solutions after dividing and reducing the dimensionality of decision spaces, respectively, novel search strategy‐based MOEAs aim to enhance the convergence speed by suggesting new methods for offspring generation, including new variation operators and probability models. The new variation operators include particle swarm optimization [\[38\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0038), competitive swarm optimizer [\[10\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0010), memetic evolution [\[39\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0039), and so on \[[40](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0040), [41](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0041)\], and the probability models include the Gaussian process [\[42\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0042), direct sampling [\[43\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0043), covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy [\[44\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0044), generative adversarial networks [\[45\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0045), and so on \[[46](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0046), [47](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0047)\]. In addition, since gradient descent methods converge quickly in high‐dimensional decision spaces, the ideas of gradient‐assisted [\[8\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0008) and pseudo‐gradient‐assisted [\[48\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0048) evolutionary computation are also adopted by MOEAs, where the gradient search is responsible for enhancing the population convergence and the evolutionary search is responsible for retaining the population diversity and escaping from local optimums. As a consequence, novel search strategy‐based MOEAs are very versatile since they make no assumption about the characteristics of LSMOPs and strike a balance between exploitation and exploration in high‐dimensional decision spaces as well as low‐dimensional decision spaces. Novel search strategy‐based MOEAs may not be as efficient as decision variable grouping‐based and decisions space reduction‐based MOEAs, but they are suitable for handling the LSMOPs whose decision variables cannot be divided or decision spaces cannot be reduced.

 

## 3.2 Random Grouping‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

The cooperative coevolution generalized differential evolution 3 (CCGDE3) is the first MOEA tailored for solving LSMOPs, which is a decision variable grouping‐based MOEA with a random grouping method [\[23\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0023). Although the random grouping method does not consider the interactions between decision variables, it is very simple and does not introduce additional function evaluations. Moreover, the randomness of the division of decision variables can maintain the interactions to some extent [\[49\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0049), which has inspired many subsequent MOEAs with more advanced grouping methods \[[50](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0050)–[52](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0052)\].

 

### 3.2.1 Random Grouping Method of CCGDE3

Before the optimization procedure, CCGDE3 randomly divides ![upper D](images/c03-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> decision variables into ![upper S](images/c03-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> groups with equal size and assigns one subpopulation to each variable group to be evolved independently. As described in Algorithm 3.1, the initialization operation begins with the random grouping of all the decision variables (Lines 1–5), where each variable group ![upper G r o u p Subscript i](images/c03-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> contains approximately ![upper D slash upper S](images/c03-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>S</mi></math> decision variables. Then, a population ![upper P o p](images/c03-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> with ![upper N](images/c03-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions is randomly initialized (Line 6), and the decision variables belonging to each group ![upper G r o u p Subscript i](images/c03-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> constitute a subpopulation ![upper P Subscript i](images/c03-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> (Line 8). CCGDE3 will evolve the ![upper S](images/c03-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> subpopulations separately, where only the decision variables in ![upper G r o u p Subscript i](images/c03-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> will be optimized for subpopulation ![upper P Subscript i](images/c03-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>.

It should be noted that a solution with partial decision variables cannot be evaluated on objective functions. Thus, the solutions in each subpopulation should be combined with the solutions in other subpopulations to form complete decision vectors. For this aim, CCGDE3 randomly pairs the solutions as described in Algorithm 3.2. For each solution ![bold x](images/c03-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> in subpopulation ![upper P Subscript i](images/c03-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>, a solution ![bold y](images/c03-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> is randomly selected from the non‐dominated solutions in all the subpopulations (Line 3), and the decision variables of ![bold x](images/c03-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> that do not belong to ![upper G r o u p Subscript i](images/c03-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> are set to those of ![bold y](images/c03-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> (Line 6). That is, the solutions in subpopulation ![upper P Subscript i](images/c03-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> actually have complete decision vectors, but only the decision variables in ![upper G r o u p Subscript i](images/c03-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> mate with each other to generate offspring solutions.

 

### 3.2.2 Optimization via GDE3

Except for the coevolution of multiple subpopulations focusing on different decision variables, CCGDE3 does not suggest new variation operators or selection strategies. To evolve each subpopulation, GDE3 [\[53\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0053) is adopted to generate offspring solutions and truncate populations. The environmental selection strategy of GDE3 is an enhancement of that of NSGA‐II, where the crowding distances are iteratively calculated to alleviate the limitation of one‐off selection [\[4\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0004). As described in Algorithm 3.3, for each offspring solution ![bold y](images/c03-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> and its main parent ![bold x](images/c03-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, ![bold y](images/c03-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> is used to replace ![bold x](images/c03-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> directly if ![bold y](images/c03-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> dominates ![bold x](images/c03-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> (Line 5). Otherwise, ![bold y](images/c03-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> is put into the subpopulation if it is not dominated by ![bold x](images/c03-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> (Line 7). After all the offspring solutions are checked, the enlarged population is sorted by non‐dominated sorting (Line 8), and all the solutions in the first ![k](images/c03-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> non‐dominated fronts are retained, where ![k](images/c03-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is the minimum value ensuring that the number of retained solutions is not smaller than the population size ![upper N](images/c03-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> (Line 13). To eliminate excessive solutions, the crowding distances of the solutions are calculated (Line 15) and the solution with the smallest crowding distance is eliminated from the ![k](images/c03-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>th non‐dominated front (Line 16). This operation repeats until the number of retained solutions is equal to ![upper N](images/c03-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> (Line 14), and the retained solutions constitute the subpopulation for next generation (Line 17).

 

### 3.2.3 Procedure of CCGDE3

With the random grouping method and the optimization procedure of GDE3, the procedure of CCGDE3 is described in Algorithm 3.4. First, the decision variables are divided into ![upper S](images/c03-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> groups and ![upper S](images/c03-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> subpopulations with ![upper N](images/c03-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions are initialized (Line 1). At each generation, each subpopulation is evolved one by one (Line 3), and each solution in the subpopulation is selected as the main parent (Line 5) to generate an offspring solution by using differential evolution and polynomial mutation (Line 7). Note that here only the decision variables corresponding to the subpopulation are changed in the offspring solution. To evaluate the newly generated offspring solutions, they are combined with the solutions in other subpopulations to form complete decision vectors (Line 9). To select ![upper N](images/c03-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions from the combination of the subpopulation and its offspring solutions, the environmental selection strategy of GDE3 is adopted (Line 10). Finally, a population is obtained as the output of the algorithm, which consists of ![upper N](images/c03-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions selected from all the subpopulations by using the environmental selection strategy of NSGA‐II (Line 11).

At each generation of CCGDE3, the time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper S upper N upper D right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for offspring generation and ![upper O left-parenthesis upper S upper M upper N squared log upper N right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>log</mi><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for environmental selection, where ![upper S](images/c03-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of groups, ![upper D](images/c03-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of decision variables, and ![upper M](images/c03-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of CCGDE3 is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper S upper N upper D plus upper S upper M upper N squared log upper N right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>S</mi><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>log</mi><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

 

## 3.3 Decision Variable Clustering‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

The alternate optimization of randomly divided variable groups is likely to get stuck in local optimums, and the population diversity cannot be explicitly maintained among multiple subpopulations. Thus, the large‐scale many‐objective evolutionary algorithm (LMEA) uses two decision variable grouping strategies, namely, differential grouping and decision variable clustering [\[27\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0027), to address the above two issues. At the expense of additional function evaluations, LMEA first divides the decision variables into convergence‐related ones and diversity‐related ones via decision variable clustering, and then divides the convergence‐related variables via differential grouping, thus maintaining population diversity and global optimums. Besides, LMEA updates partial decision variables of a single population at a time, which does not require the random combination of solutions that may generate unpromising decision vectors. The idea of decision variable clustering in LMEA is robust in handling complex relations between decision variables and population convergence/diversity, which has been leveraged by many advanced MOEAs \[[54](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0054)–[56](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0056)\].

 

### 3.3.1 Decision Variable Clustering Method of LMEA

The core contribution of LMEA is the decision variable clustering strategy, which aims to divide all the decision variables into convergence‐related ones and diversity‐related ones to be optimized via different strategies. Convergence‐related variables indicate those mainly affecting the population convergence, i.e., the change of such decision variables changes the distance of a solution to the Pareto front. By contrast, diversity‐related variables indicate those mainly affecting the population diversity, i.e., the change of such decision variables changes the position of a solution on the Pareto front.

Considering the above natures of convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables, the decision variable clustering strategy identifies them based on the perturbations of decision variables. As detailed in Algorithm 3.5, given ![n upper S e l](images/c03-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>l</mi></math> randomly selected solutions for perturbation (Line 2), each decision variable of each solution is randomly perturbed (i.e., assigning a random value within the decision space) for ![n upper P e r](images/c03-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></math> times (Line 4). Thus, there will be ![n upper S e l times upper D](images/c03-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math> solution sets with each having ![n upper P e r](images/c03-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></math> solutions as depicted in [Fig. 3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0002)(a), where ![upper D](images/c03-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> denotes the total number of decision variables. Then, a line is fitted for each solution set in the ![upper M](images/c03-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional objective space (Line 5) as depicted in [Fig. 3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0002)(b), where the mean square error of the line is calculated (Line 6) and the angle between the line and ![f 1 plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus f Subscript upper M Baseline equals 1](images/c03-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> is calculated (Line 7), as depicted in [Fig. 3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0002)(c). Obviously, a smaller angle indicates that the solutions generated by perturbing a decision variable have greater difference in terms of distances to the Pareto front, and thus the decision variable is more likely to be a convergence‐related variable. By contrast, a larger angle indicates that the solutions generated by perturbing a decision variable have greater difference in terms of positions on the Pareto front, and thus the decision variable is more likely to be a diversity‐related variable.

(b) Fit a line for the sample solutions generated by the perturbations on each variable of each solution. (c) Calculate the angles between each line and the vector left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis. (d) Grouping the decision variables according to the angles related to them.](images/c03f002.png)

[**Figure 3.2**](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-fig-0002) Illustration of the decision variable clustering method in LMEA. (a) Perturb each of ![x 1 comma x 2 comma x 3 comma x 4](images/c03-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></math> of two solutions and generate multiple sample solutions. (b) Fit a line for the sample solutions generated by the perturbations on each variable of each solution. (c) Calculate the angles between each line and the vector ![left-parenthesis 1 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. (d) Grouping the decision variables according to the angles related to them.

Therefore, to distinguish between convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables, the angles of the lines generated by the perturbations on each decision variable can be used as features for clustering. As depicted in [Fig. 3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0002)(d), ![k](images/c03-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐means is used to divide the decision variables into two groups according to the angles of lines (Line 8), where the group with decision variables corresponding to smaller angles are identified as convergence‐related variables, and the group with decision variables corresponding to larger angles are identified as diversity‐related variables (Lines 9–11).

 

### 3.3.2 Interaction Analysis of LMEA

While the population diversity can be enhanced by fine‐tuning diversity‐related variables, the population convergence has to be ensured by fully optimizing convergence‐related variables. That is, the optimal values of convergence‐related variables are likely to be unique but the optimal values of diversity‐related variables are not. Thus, LMEA further divides convergence‐related variables into multiple groups to optimize them in a divide‐and‐conquer manner, where the convergence‐related variables in different groups are not interacted with any others to ensure that the global optimums are not lost. For this aim, a differential grouping method [\[25\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0025) is adopted to detect variable interactions based on perturbations. More specifically, decision variable ![x Subscript i](images/c03-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> is interacted with decision variable ![x Subscript j](images/c03-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> if there exist a solution ![bold x](images/c03-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and four variable values ![a 1 comma a 2 comma b 1 comma b 2](images/c03-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> such that

In order to maintain the global optimums, all the interacted convergence‐related variables should be assigned to the same group. For example, if ![x 1](images/c03-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> is interacted with ![x 2](images/c03-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![x 2](images/c03-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> is interacted with ![x 3](images/c03-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math>, but ![x 3](images/c03-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math> is not interacted with ![x 1](images/c03-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, then the three variables should be assigned to the same group. Thus, the detection between ![x 1](images/c03-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![x 3](images/c03-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math> is unnecessary if ![x 1](images/c03-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> has been verified to have interacted with ![x 2](images/c03-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![x 2](images/c03-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> has been verified to have interacted with ![x 3](images/c03-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and many unnecessary function evaluations can be saved. As detailed in Algorithm 3.6, LMEA checks the interactions between each convergence‐related variable ![v](images/c03-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> and those in existing groups (Line 9), on the basis of ![n upper C o r](images/c03-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi></math> solutions randomly selected from the population (Line 8). Then, if ![v](images/c03-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> is not interacted with any variable in existing groups, it is assigned to a new group (Line 16). While if ![v](images/c03-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> is interacted with some variables in multiple groups, all these groups together with ![v](images/c03-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> constitute a new group (Lines 18–20). In this case, LMEA need not to detect the interactions between all pairs of convergence‐related variables, thus saving many function evaluations especially when many variables are interacted with each other.

 

### 3.3.3 Convergence Optimization and Diversity Optimization

After performing decision variable clustering and interaction analysis, some groups of convergence‐related variables and one group of diversity‐related variables are obtained. To fully optimize convergence‐related variables for good convergence and fine‐tune diversity‐related variables for good diversity, LMEA suggests two different optimization procedures carried out on convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables, respectively. The optimization of convergence‐related variables is elaborated in Algorithm 3.7, which begins with the non‐dominated sorting on the current population (Line 1) and the calculation of the distances between solutions in the current population to the origin in the objective space (Line 2). Thus, both the non‐dominated front number and the distance to the origin can measure the convergence degree of a solution, and the convergence‐related variables of a solution with better convergence degree are more likely to be optimized. For each group of convergence‐related variables, LMEA generates ![upper N](images/c03-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> new offspring solutions by changing only the variables in the group (Line 5), where ![upper N](images/c03-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is the population size. Based on the non‐dominated front numbers, some solutions are selected from the current population and put into the mating pool ![upper S](images/c03-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> (Line 9), and ![StartAbsoluteValue upper S EndAbsoluteValue](images/c03-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> offspring solutions are generated by simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation (Line 14) based on two solutions selected via binary tournament selection (Line 12). Then, each offspring solution ![bold o](images/c03-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math> is associated with a parent ![bold s](images/c03-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></mrow></math> in ![upper S](images/c03-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>, where all the decision variables outside the current group of ![bold o](images/c03-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math> are set to the same as those of ![bold s](images/c03-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></mrow></math> (Line 13). This way, only the decision variables in the current group are changed. After the generation of offspring solutions, each of them is used to replace its parent in the population if it has a smaller non‐dominated front number or distance to the origin (Line 20). Since LMEA focuses on improving the population convergence without considering the population diversity, the selection strategies consider the convergence degrees rather than the diversity degrees of solutions. In fact, since diversity‐related variables keep unchanged during the optimization procedure, the population diversity is also unchanged in most cases.

The optimization of diversity‐related variables is elaborated in Algorithm 3.8, which is similar to general MOEAs as both the population convergence and population diversity are taken into consideration. By generating ![upper N](images/c03-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> offspring solutions by simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation (Line 5) based on two solutions randomly selected from the current population, each offspring solution ![bold o](images/c03-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math> is associated with a unique parent ![bold s](images/c03-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></mrow></math> in the population. That is, all the convergence‐related variables of ![bold o](images/c03-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math> are set to the same as those of ![bold s](images/c03-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></mrow></math> (Line 4); in other words, only the diversity‐related variables are changed. After the generation of offspring solutions, they are combined with the current population and ![upper N](images/c03-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions are selected and survive to the next generation. Here, LMEA selects solutions with better non‐dominated front numbers (Line 13) and selects solutions from the last non‐dominated front one by one according to their angles to the solutions having been selected (Line 16). This selection strategy adopts the non‐dominated sorting of NSGA‐II [\[57\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0057) and the truncation strategy of SPEA2 [\[58\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0058), which inherits the merits of both the two MOEAs for retaining ![upper N](images/c03-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions with good convergence and diversity.

 

### 3.3.4 Procedure of LMEA

With the decision variable clustering, interaction analysis, convergence optimization, and diversity optimization, the procedure of LMEA is described in Algorithm 3.9. First, a population with ![upper N](images/c03-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions is randomly initialized (Line 1), which is then used to divide all the decision variables into convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables (Line 2), and divide the convergence‐related variables into some groups (Line 3). At each generation, the convergence‐related variables and diversity‐related variables are alternately optimized (Lines 5 and 6), where only a single population is evolved during the whole optimization procedure. Finally, the population is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 7).

At each generation of LMEA, the time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for both convergence optimization and diversity optimization, where ![upper M](images/c03-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of LMEA is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

 

## 3.4 Problem Reformulation‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

Different from decision variable grouping, the large‐scale multi‐objective framework (LSMOF) aims to directly reduce the dimensionality of decision spaces, so as to solve a small‐scale optimization problem rather than a large‐scale one. Instead of optimizing all the ![upper D](images/c03-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> decision variables of an LSMOP, LSMOF optimizes two weight variables for each of ![r](images/c03-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> solutions, where the combination of a weight variable and a solution leads to a new solution for approximating the Pareto set. Thus, the dimensionality of the decision space is reduced from ![upper D](images/c03-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> to ![2 r](images/c03-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></math>. By maximizing the HV [\[59\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0059) value of the ![2 r](images/c03-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></math> new solutions, LSMOF reformulates the LSMOP into a small‐scale single‐objective optimization problem. LSMOF can quickly converge to local optimums due to the dimensionality reduction of decision spaces, but can hardly approximate the global optimums due to the inexistence of the global optimums in the reduced decision spaces. Owing to the rapid convergence speed of LSMOF, the idea of problem reformulation has been carried forward in many other MOEAs for solving LSMOPs \[[60](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0060)–[62](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0062)\].

 

### 3.4.1 Problem Reformulation of LSMOF

The problem reformulation method of LSMOF converts an LSMOP into a small‐scale single‐objective optimization problem to be solved by differential evolution. For the reformulated problem, the decision variables are a number of weight variables generating new solutions based on the existing ones, and the objective is the HV value of all the new solutions. As described in Algorithm 3.10, the nadir point (i.e., a point containing the maximum values of all the objectives) of the current population ![upper P](images/c03-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is first obtained as the reference point for HV calculation (Line 1). Then, ![r](images/c03-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> reference solutions are selected from ![upper P](images/c03-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> via an environmental selection strategy (Line 2). It is worth noting that LSMOF is a framework compatible with many existing MOEAs, where NSGA‐II with non‐dominated sorting and crowding distance‐based selection strategy is adopted here. For each reference solution ![bold x Subscript i](images/c03-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>, two weight variables ![lamda Subscript i Baseline 1](images/c03-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![lamda Subscript i Baseline 2](images/c03-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> are introduced to generate two new solutions ![bold x Subscript i Superscript l Baseline left-parenthesis lamda Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![bold x Subscript i Superscript u Baseline left-parenthesis lamda Subscript i Baseline 2 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, that is,

Similarly, ![bold x Subscript i Superscript u](images/c03-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> locates on the line through ![bold t](images/c03-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold x](images/c03-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, where the distance between ![bold x Subscript i Superscript u](images/c03-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![bold x](images/c03-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> is determined by the weight variable ![lamda Subscript i Baseline 2](images/c03-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>. Thus, the intersections of the two lines and the Pareto set are Pareto optimal solutions, which can be found by finding the optimal values of ![lamda Subscript i Baseline 1](images/c03-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![lamda Subscript i Baseline 2](images/c03-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>. That is, the optimization of the ![upper D](images/c03-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> decision variables of an LSMOP is converted into the optimization of two weight variables.

![Figure 3.3 Illustration of the problem reformulation method in LSMOF.](images/c03f003.png)

[**Figure 3.3**](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-fig-0003) Illustration of the problem reformulation method in LSMOF.

Since the optimization of the weight variables of a reference solution cannot explicitly specify the location of the new solution on the Pareto front, LSMOF optimizes the weight variables of ![r](images/c03-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> reference solutions together to enhance both the population convergence and population diversity (Line 6). To evaluate the new solutions generated by weight variable optimization, LSMOF calculates the HV value of all the new solutions (Line 7), where a higher HV value indicates a better convergence and diversity of the new solutions. As a consequence, LSMOF reformulates an LSMOP into the following single‐objective optimization problem:

This way, the number of variables to be optimized is decreased from ![upper D](images/c03-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> to ![2 r](images/c03-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></math>, and the dimensionality of the decision space is considerably reduced. The problem reformulation significantly increases the convergence speed on LSMOPs, but it can hardly approximate the global optimums since the one‐dimensional lines may not intersect the ![left-parenthesis upper M minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>‐dimensional Pareto set in the ![upper D](images/c03-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional decision space, where the number of objectives ![upper M](images/c03-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> is much smaller than the number of decision variables ![upper D](images/c03-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.

 

### 3.4.2 Single‐Objective Optimization of LSMOF

To fully optimize the weight variables of ![r](images/c03-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> best solutions in the current population, LSMOF adopts differential evolution to maximize the reformulated problem ![f prime](images/c03-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, where the detailed procedure is presented in Algorithm 3.11. More specifically, ![upper N prime](images/c03-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> solutions are first generated as the initial population (Line 1), where each solution is a vector of ![bold-italic lamda equals left-parenthesis lamda 11 comma lamda 12 comma ellipsis comma lamda Subscript r Baseline 1 Baseline comma lamda Subscript r Baseline 2 Baseline right-parenthesis element-of left-bracket 0 comma 0.5 right-bracket Superscript 2 r](images/c03-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></math>. Then, the initial population is evaluated on ![f prime](images/c03-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> (Line 5) and optimized for ![g](images/c03-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> generations (Line 6). Note that here the evaluation of a solution consumes ![2 r](images/c03-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></math> function evaluations on the original LSMOP. To update each solution ![lamda](images/c03-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> at each generation, a new solution ![gamma](images/c03-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> is generated by differential evolution based on three solutions randomly selected from the current population (Lines 8 and 9), and ![gamma](images/c03-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> is used to replace ![lamda](images/c03-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> in the population if the former has a better objective value on ![f prime](images/c03-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> (Lines 12 and 13). During the optimization procedure, LSMOF saves all the newly generated solutions for the original LSMOP in an archive ![upper A](images/c03-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> (Lines 4 and 10), which is the output of the single‐objective optimization procedure (Line 14). The solutions in the archive will be combined with the current population, and then truncated by an environmental selection strategy for the next round of optimization.

 

### 3.4.3 Procedure of LSMOF

With the problem reformulation and single‐objective optimization, the procedure of LSMOF is described in Algorithm 3.12, which begins with the random initialization of a population with ![upper N](images/c03-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions (Line 1). At each generation, if the ratio of consumed function evaluations is less than a predefined threshold ![t r](images/c03-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></math>, LSMOF reformulates the LSMOP (Line 4) and optimizes the weight variables via single‐objective differential evolution algorithm (Line 5), where the solutions generated during the single‐objective optimization procedure are combined with the population and truncated by non‐dominated sorting and crowding distance‐based selection (Line 6). Otherwise, LSMOF optimizes the population by using the mating selection strategy, genetic operators, and environmental selection strategy of NSGA‐II until termination (Lines 8–10). Finally, the population is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 11).

At each generation of LSMOF, the time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for problem reformulation and ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N prime g r Superscript upper M Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mi>g</mi><msup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for single‐objective optimization, where ![upper M](images/c03-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of objectives, ![r](images/c03-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of reference solutions, ![upper N prime](images/c03-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> denotes the population size for single‐objective optimization, and ![g](images/c03-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of generations for single‐objective optimization. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of LSMOF is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N prime g r Superscript upper M Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mi>g</mi><msup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

 

## 3.5 Competitive Swarm Optimizer‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

In addition to dividing the decision variables or reducing the number of decision variables, the large‐scale multi‐objective competitive swarm optimizer (LMOCSO) suggests a new variation operator for optimizing all the decision variables of LSMOPs together. With no assumption of the relations between decision variables, LMOCSO searches in the original decision spaces and follows a similar optimization procedure as general MOEAs. Although LMOCSO is less effective than decision variable group‐based and decision space reduction‐based MOEAs on particular LSMOPs, it is flexible to handle complex LSMOPs with a robust performance and has also been used in subsequent algorithms \[[63](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0063), [64](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0064)\].

 

### 3.5.1 Enhanced Competitive Swarm Optimizer of LMOCSO

In comparison to genetic algorithms that are widely adopted in MOEAs, particle swarm optimization converges faster in high‐dimensional decision spaces due to the learning strategies between particles. However, particle swarm optimization is not popular for multi‐objective optimization due to the difficulty in selecting best particles and maintaining the population diversity. By contrast, competitive swarm optimizer (CSO) is more flexible, which generates solutions in a similar way as genetic operators and is compatible with the selection strategies of many existing MOEAs. At the ![t](images/c03-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>th generation of CSO, two particles are selected each time and the worse one (i.e., loser particle) is updated by

Algorithm 3.13 details the procedure of generating offspring solutions in LMOCSO. First, the fitness value of each particle is calculated to determine loser and winner particles (Line 1). where ![f Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold p right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denotes the ![i](images/c03-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th objective value of ![bold p](images/c03-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper M](images/c03-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of objectives. At each time, two solutions are randomly picked up from the current population (Line 4), where the one with a smaller fitness value is the loser particle and the one with a larger fitness value is the winner particle (Lines 6–11). Then, the loser particle is updated by Eq. ([3.14](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0014)), and both the winner particle and the updated loser particle are tuned by polynomial mutation (Lines 12 and 13). The two mutated particles are regarded as offspring solutions (Line 14), and the algorithm repeatedly generates offspring solutions until all the particles in the current population have been picked up (Line 3).

 

### 3.5.2 Procedure of LMOCSO

With the enhanced CSO operator, the procedure of LMOCSO is described in Algorithm 3.14, which begins with the random initialization of a population with ![upper N](images/c03-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> particles (Line 1) and the generation of ![upper N](images/c03-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> uniformly distributed reference vectors (Line 2). At each generation, LMOCSO generates offspring solutions by using the proposed CSO operator (Line 4), which are further combined with the current population and truncated by the environmental selection strategy of RVEA [\[66\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0066) (Line 5). Finally, the population is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 6).

At each generation of LMOCSO, the time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N upper D right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for offspring generation and ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for environmental selection, where ![upper D](images/c03-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of decision variables and ![upper M](images/c03-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of LMOCSO is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N upper D plus upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c03-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

 

## 3.6 Experimental Comparisons

To investigate the performance of CCGDE3, LMEA, LSMOF, and LMOCSO, they are compared with two representative MOEAs on benchmark LSMOPs. The compared MOEAs include NSGA‐II [\[57\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0057) and GDE3 [\[53\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0053), which are based on genetic algorithms and differential evolution, respectively. The tested benchmark LSMOPs include DTLZ1–DTLZ4 [\[67\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0067) and LSMOP1–LSMOP4 [\[68\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0068), where the number of objectives is set to 2 and the number of decision variables ![upper D](images/c03-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is set to 100, 200, and 500. The population size is set to 100 and the number of function evaluations is set to ![10 comma 000 times upper D](images/c03-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math>; besides, the number of function evaluations for LSMOF is set to 100,000. The populations obtained by the compared algorithms are assessed by IGD [\[69\]](#c03.xhtml#c03-bib-0069).

[Table 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-tbl-0001) presents the experimental results averaged over 30 runs, where the best results are shown in bold and the statistically similar ones are highlighted. It can be found that the three algorithms LMEA, LSMOF, and LMOCSO exhibit the best overall performance and obtain the best results on all the test instances, which verify the effectiveness of their search strategies (i.e., decision variable grouping, decision space reduction, and novel variation operator) for solving LSMOPs. By contrast, CCGDE3 is not effective due to the simple random grouping strategy. For the problems DTLZ1–DTLZ4 without variable interaction, LMEA and LSMOF obtain the best performance by using the decision variable clustering‐based divide‐and‐conquer search and the problem reformulation‐based decision space reduction method, respectively. For the problems LSMOP1–LSMOP4 with complex variable interactions, LMOCSO obtains the best performance by using an enhanced CSO operator.

![Table 3.1  IGD Values Obtained by Six MOEAs on Eight Benchmark LSMOPs.](images/c03-i0255.png)

[**Table 3.1**](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-tbl-0001)  IGD Values Obtained by Six MOEAs on Eight Benchmark LSMOPs.

Moreover, [Fig. 3.5](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0005) depicts the convergence profiles of IGD values obtained by the compared MOEAs on DTLZ1 and LSMOP1 with 100 decision variables. For CCGDE3, it converges more slowly than the other MOEAs, which indicates the ineffectiveness of the random grouping method for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. For LMEA, it converges slowly at the beginning since many function evaluations are consumed for the sake of decision variable clustering, but it can obtain promising populations at last by using the divide‐and‐conquer search. For LSMOF, it converges much more quickly than the other MOEAs, but it is likely to get stuck in local optimums, especially on LSMOP1 with complex variable interactions. As for LMOCSO, it converges fast on LSMOP1 with complex variable interactions, but it gets stuck in local optimums on DTLZ1 due to the ineffectiveness of particle swarm optimization in handling multimodal landscapes.

![Figure 3.5 Solutions obtained by six MOEAs on DTLZ1 and LSMOP1 with 100 decision variables.](images/c03f005.png)

[**Figure 3.5**](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-fig-0005) Solutions obtained by six MOEAs on DTLZ1 and LSMOP1 with 100 decision variables.

 

## 3.7 Summary

This chapter introduces four representative MOEAs for solving LSMOPs. The most significant feature of these MOEAs is that they suggest different ideas to handle the high‐dimensional decision spaces, such as the decision variable grouping methods in CCGDE3 and LMEA, the decision space reduction method in LSMOF, and the novel variation operator in LMOCSO. According to the discussions and experimental results, different types of large‐scale MOEAs are effective for different types of LSMOPs, while no MOEA can obtain the best performance on all types of LSMOPs. For example, decision variable grouping‐based MOEAs are good at solving LSMOPs with few variable interactions, decision space reduction‐based MOEAs can quickly converge to local optimums of LSMOPs with simple Pareto sets, and novel search strategy‐based MOEAs are more robust in solving complex LSMOPs. Besides, most large‐scale MOEAs are ineffective for solving small‐scale problems. After all, if large‐scale MOEAs dominate general MOEAs on small‐scale problems, the latter will become meaningless and the research of large‐scale multi‐objective optimization will not be separated from the research of multi‐objective optimization.
