# 4  
Evolutionary Algorithms for Sparse Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization

 

## 4.1 Introduction

The “curse of dimensionality” encountered by evolutionary algorithms in huge decision spaces is inevitable, as they iteratively search for better solutions in a black‐box manner. In addition to developing multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) for solving general LSMOPs, it is reasonable to improve the convergence speed by involving problem‐specific information in offspring generation, such as the gradients used in mathematical programming methods [\[1\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0001). While it is costly to customize an evolutionary algorithm for every single LSMOP through human expertise, developing effective search strategies for specific types of LSMOPs turns out to be desirable.

 

### 4.1.1 Characteristics of Sparse Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization Problems

In real‐world applications, there exist many optimization problems having sparse optimal solutions, in which the optimal values of most decision variables are zero. For the neural network training task in supervised learning [\[2\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0002), the goal is to find the optimal weights between layers, where many weights are expected to be zero for alleviating overfitting. Hence, the optimal solutions for neural network training are sparse when real encoding is used, where each decision variable denotes a weight. For the frequent pattern mining task in data mining [\[3\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0003), the goal is to find the most frequent and complete pattern (e.g., a set of items) from a transaction dataset (e.g., a set of historical shopping lists having many candidate items), where only a small proportion of all the candidate items is preferred. Hence, the optimal solutions for frequent pattern mining are sparse when binary encoding is used, where each decision variable denotes whether an item is selected or not.

The above tasks are collectively known as sparse optimization problems, which are likely to contain a large number of decision variables. For the aforementioned examples, a neural network should have enough weights for learning complex mappings between features and labels [\[4\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0004), and a transaction dataset usually consists of abundant candidate items for recommending the most complete patterns to customers [\[5\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0005). Furthermore, sparse optimization problems generally have multiple conflicting objectives to be optimized. For some sparse LSMOPs like neural network training, the sparsity of optimal solutions is explicitly defined as an objective to be optimized (e.g., the network complexity). While for some other sparse LSMOPs like the frequent pattern mining, the sparsity of optimal solutions is implicitly determined by all the objectives (e.g., in Eq. (2.28), the selected items ![bold x](images/c04-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> should occupy a small proportion of all the items in a transaction dataset ![tau](images/c04-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math>, otherwise ![tau Subscript bold x](images/c04-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub></math> will be empty).

 

### 4.1.2 Ideas of Finding Sparse Solutions

It is possible to solve sparse LSMOPs using general large‐scale MOEAs, but their efficiency cannot meet the requirement in real‐world scenarios due to the relatively expensive objective functions. For example, evaluating a solution for neural network training needs to calculate the output of all the training samples, and evaluating a solution for frequent pattern mining should traverse the whole transaction dataset. Fortunately, the sparse nature of the optimal solutions of sparse LSMOPs is known in advance, making it possible to optimize only the nonzero variables. Since the nonzero variables are much fewer than the zero variables of sparse LSMOPs, the problems can be considerably eased and many function evaluations can be saved. In comparison to optimizing all the decision variables of general LSMOPs, there are two tasks in solving sparse LSMOPs, including finding the nonzero variables and optimizing the nonzero variables. Furthermore, for the sparse LSMOPs with binary encoding (e.g., frequent pattern mining), the task of optimizing the nonzero variables can be omitted.

Since large‐scale MOEAs focus on continuous optimization, they are suitable for optimizing the nonzero variables but unsuitable for finding the nonzero variables of sparse LSMOPs, where the latter is essentially a binary optimization problem. On the other hand, binary‐coded MOEAs (e.g., NSGA‐II with uniform crossover and bitwise mutation [\[6\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0006)) are also inefficient for finding nonzero variables since they are not tailored for finding sparse solutions. Taking the random initialization strategy as an example, the expectation of the number of zero variables ![upper E Subscript z e r o](images/c04-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> equals the expectation of the number of nonzero variables ![upper E Subscript n o n z e r o](images/c04-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> in the initial solutions. However, since ![upper E Subscript n o n z e r o Baseline much-less-than upper E Subscript z e r o](images/c04-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8810;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> in the optimal solutions of sparse LSMOPs, the initial solutions are far away from the optimal solutions and many function evaluations should be consumed for the sake of convergence. To address the difficulties encountered by large‐scale MOEAs and binary‐coded MOEAs in finding the nonzero variables of sparse LSMOPs, several sparse MOEAs have been proposed in recent years, each of which develops novel strategies to find nonzero variables and adopts existing operators to optimize nonzero variables. In the following sections, three representative sparse MOEAs are introduced and empirically compared.

 

## 4.2 Bi‐Level Encoding‐Based Evolutionary Algorithm

The sparse evolutionary algorithm (SparseEA) is the first generic evolutionary algorithm for solving sparse LSMOPs [\[7\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0007). The main contribution of SparseEA is to represent each solution by using a bi‐level encoding, which differentiates the search of nonzero variables and the optimization of nonzero variables. Moreover, a population initialization strategy, a crossover operator, and a mutation operator are customized to address the shortcomings of those in binary‐coded MOEAs, thus facilitating the search of nonzero variables.

stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi></math>, where the decision variables are calculated as

(4.4)![x Subscript i Baseline equals x b Subscript i Baseline times x r Subscript i Baseline comma i equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma upper D period](images/c04-math-0004.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

That is, SparseEA stores ![bold x bold b](images/c04-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></math> and ![bold x bold r](images/c04-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi></math> instead of ![bold x](images/c04-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> during the optimization. For instance, a binary vector ![bold x bold b equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 comma 0 comma 1 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and a real vector ![bold xr equals left-parenthesis 0.2 comma 0.4 comma 0.6 comma 0.8 comma 1.0 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xr</mtext><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> correspond to a solution ![bold x equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 0.4 comma 0 comma 0.8 comma 0 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In this way, the optimization of the binary vector is responsible for the search of nonzero variables, and the optimization of the real vector is responsible for the optimization of nonzero variables. It is worth noting that although the introduction of binary vector ![bold xb](images/c04-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext></mrow></math> doubles the number of variables to be optimized, all the ![bold xb](images/c04-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext></mrow></math> form a binary search space that is much smaller than the continuous decision space, and all the real variables ![x r Subscript i](images/c04-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> corresponding to ![x b Subscript i Baseline equals 0](images/c04-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> need not be optimized anymore. In other words, the search space is highly reduced by optimizing many variables in ![bold xb](images/c04-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext></mrow></math> to zero. Besides, the bi‐level encoding parallelizes the search and optimization of nonzero variables, which achieves high efficiency in searching for sparse optimal solutions.

As a matter of fact, the effectiveness of such a bi‐level encoding has been verified on specific applications such as neural network training [\[8\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0008) and portfolio optimization [\[9\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0009), while SparseEA adopts it as a generic strategy for solving various sparse LSMOPs. In SparseEA, the optimization of real vectors is implemented by general strategies used in real‐coded MOEAs, while the optimization of binary vectors is implemented by customized strategies for ensuring the sparsity of generated solutions. These customized strategies include a population initialization strategy, a crossover operator, and a mutation operator.

 

### 4.2.2 Population Initialization Strategy of SparseEA

In comparison to random initialization where the sparsity (i.e., the ratio of nonzero variables) of the generated solutions is approximately 0.5, the population initialization strategy of SparseEA aims to generate a set of solutions with different sparsity, thereby better approximating the optimal solutions whose sparsity is unknown. Moreover, SparseEA estimates the probability that each dimension of the binary vector should be zero, which can benefit the search of nonzero variables.

The pseudocode of the population initialization strategy of SparseEA is presented in Algorithm 4.1. To begin with, a solution set ![upper S](images/c04-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> with ![upper D](images/c04-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> solutions is generated for calculating the scores (Line 1). For the binary vector of the ![i](images/c04-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th solution in ![upper S](images/c04-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>, all of its binary variables ![x b](images/c04-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mi>b</mi></math> are set to zero (Line 3), except for the ![i](images/c04-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th binary variable being one (Line 4). For the real vector of the ![i](images/c04-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th solution in ![upper S](images/c04-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>, it is randomly sampled in the decision space for continuous sparse LSMOPs (Line 6) and set to a vector of ones for binary sparse LSMOPs (Line 8). That is, the real variables of all the solutions are fixed to one when solving binary sparse LSMOPs, while only the binary variables need to be optimized. Then, as illustrated in [Fig. 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0001), the quality of all the solutions in ![upper S](images/c04-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> are measured by non‐dominated sorting, where the non‐dominated front numbers of all the solutions constitute a vector ![bold score](images/c04-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">score</mtext></mrow></math> (Line 10). Obviously, a smaller non‐dominated front number ![s c o r e Subscript i](images/c04-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><msub><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> indicates a better quality of the solution whose ![i](images/c04-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th decision variable is nonzero, which implies a lower probability that the ![i](images/c04-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th dimension of the binary vector should be zero. Therefore, it is reasonable to use the vector ![bold score](images/c04-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">score</mtext></mrow></math> to guide the generation of the binary vectors of solutions, where a binary variable with a lower ![s c o r e](images/c04-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> value is more likely to be set to one, and vice versa. In the population initialization, crossover operator, and mutation operator of SparseEA, the binary variables to be flipped are selected by binary tournament selection according to the vector ![bold score](images/c04-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">score</mtext></mrow></math>.

![Figure 4.1 The strategy for calculating vector bold score in SparseEA.](images/c04f001.png)

[**Figure 4.1**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0001) The strategy for calculating vector ![bold score](images/c04-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">score</mtext></mrow></math> in SparseEA.

Afterward, a population ![upper P](images/c04-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> with ![upper N](images/c04-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions is initialized by generating the solutions one by one (Line 12). The generation of a new solution begins with setting its binary vector to a vector of zeros (Line 13). Then, two dimensions are randomly selected (Line 15) and the one corresponding to a lower ![s c o r e](images/c04-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> value is flipped to one (Lines 16–19). This operation repeats for ![left ceiling r a n d times upper D right ceiling](images/c04-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8968;</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8969;</mo></math> times to diversify the sparsity of the generated solutions (Line 14), where ![r a n d](images/c04-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> denotes a uniformly distributed random number within ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. As for the real vector of the new solution, it is randomly sampled in the decision space for continuous sparse LSMOPs (Line 21) and set to a vector of ones for binary sparse LSMOPs (Line 23). Lastly, both the initial population ![upper P](images/c04-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and the vector ![bold score](images/c04-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">score</mtext></mrow></math> are returned (Line 25).

 

### 4.2.3 Crossover and Mutation Operators of SparseEA

In SparseEA, the real vectors of offspring solutions are generated through simulated binary crossover [\[10\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0010) and polynomial mutation [\[11\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0011), which are the same as most multi‐objective genetic algorithms. On the contrary, the binary vectors of offspring solutions are generated through new crossover and mutation operators, which are designed on the basis of uniform crossover and bitwise mutation, respectively. Similar to the population initialization strategy of SparseEA, the vector ![bold score](images/c04-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">score</mtext></mrow></math> is additionally involved in the new crossover and mutation operators to ensure the sparsity of offspring. The pseudocode of the crossover and mutation operators of SparseEA is presented in Algorithm 4.2, where the binary vectors ![bold xb comma bold yb](images/c04-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yb</mtext></math> of two parents are used to generate the binary vector ![bold ob](images/c04-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">ob</mtext></mrow></math> of one offspring solution each time, and the real vectors ![bold xr comma bold yr](images/c04-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yr</mtext></math> of the same parents are used to generate the real vector ![bold or](images/c04-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">or</mtext></mrow></math> of the same offspring solution (Line 3).

First, the binary vector ![bold ob](images/c04-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">ob</mtext></mrow></math> of the offspring solution is set to the same as the first parent (Line 5), and one of the following two operations is performed with the same probability: randomly selecting two dimensions from the nonzero elements in ![bold xb intersection ModifyingAbove bold yb With bar](images/c04-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext><mo>&#8745;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">yb</mtext></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> (Line 7), and flipping the binary variable corresponding to a higher ![s c o r e](images/c04-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> value to zero (Lines 8–11); or randomly selecting two dimensions from the nonzero elements in ![ModifyingAbove bold xb With bar intersection bold yb](images/c04-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8745;</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yb</mtext></math> (Line 13), and flipping the binary variable corresponding to a lower ![s c o r e](images/c04-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> value to one (Lines 14–17). In short, the new crossover operator flips a zero variable or a nonzero variable with the same probability, hence, the ![upper E Subscript n o n z e r o](images/c04-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper E Subscript z e r o](images/c04-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> of each solution keep unchanged, and the sparsity of offspring solutions can be ensured.

Second, the binary vector ![bold ob](images/c04-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">ob</mtext></mrow></math> of the offspring solution is then mutated by one of the following two operations with the same probability: randomly selecting two dimensions from the nonzero elements in ![bold ob](images/c04-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">ob</mtext></mrow></math> (Line 19), and flipping the binary variable corresponding to a higher ![s c o r e](images/c04-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> value to zero (Lines 20–23); or randomly selecting two dimensions from the nonzero elements in ![ModifyingAbove bold ob With bar](images/c04-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">ob</mtext></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></math> (Line 25), and flipping the binary variable corresponding to a lower ![s c o r e](images/c04-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> value to one (Lines 26–29). Obviously, the new mutation operator can also ensure the sparsity since it flips a zero variable or a nonzero variable of each offspring solution with the same probability.

Third, when solving continuous sparse LSMOPs, the real vector ![bold or](images/c04-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">or</mtext></mrow></math> of the offspring solution is generated by performing simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation on ![bold xr](images/c04-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">xr</mtext></mrow></math> and ![bold yr](images/c04-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">yr</mtext></mrow></math> (Line 31). When solving binary sparse LSMOPs, the real vector ![bold or](images/c04-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">or</mtext></mrow></math> is always set to a vector of ones without performing crossover or mutation (Line 33). Lastly, the offspring population is returned (Line 35).

 

### 4.2.4 Procedure of SparseEA

With the new population initialization strategy, crossover operator, and mutation operator for generating sparse solutions, the procedure of SparseEA is detailed in Algorithm 4.3. First of all, a population ![upper P](images/c04-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> with ![upper N](images/c04-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions is initialized and the vector ![bold score](images/c04-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">score</mtext></mrow></math> is calculated by the new population initialization strategy (Line 1). Then, the non‐dominated front number and crowding distance of each solution in ![upper P](images/c04-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> are determined (Lines 2 and 3). At each generation, the mating pool ![upper P prime](images/c04-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is constructed by selecting ![2 upper N](images/c04-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi></math> parents from the population ![upper P](images/c04-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> via binary tournament selection according to the non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances of solutions (Line 5). After that, ![upper N](images/c04-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> offspring solutions are generated by the new crossover and mutation operators (Line 6). To select ![upper N](images/c04-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions from the combination of ![upper P](images/c04-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper O](images/c04-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>, SparseEA adopts the environmental selection strategy of NSGA‐II [\[6\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0006) for simplicity, where ![upper N](images/c04-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions with better non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances survive to the next generation (Line 7). Finally, the population ![upper P](images/c04-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 8).

It can be concluded from Algorithm 4.1 that the calculation of ![bold score](images/c04-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">score</mtext></mrow></math> is relatively time‐consuming for large‐scale optimization due to the use of non‐dominated sorting, which holds a time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper D squared right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for solving a problem with ![upper M](images/c04-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> objectives and ![upper D](images/c04-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> decision variables [\[12\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0012). Nevertheless, this operation is not in the main loop of the algorithm. At each generation of SparseEA, the time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for mating pool selection, ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N upper D right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for offspring generation, and ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for environmental selection. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of SparseEA is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared plus upper N upper D right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which is the same as many other MOEAs.

 

## 4.3 Machine Learning‐Assisted Evolutionary Algorithm

The multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm based on Pareto optimal subspace learning (MOEA/PSL) inherits the bi‐level encoding of SparseEA, where unsupervised neural networks are adopted to learn the Pareto optimal subspace according to the current population [\[13\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0013). More specifically, a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) is used to learn a sparse distribution from the binary vectors, and a denoising auto‐encoder (DAE) is used to learn a compact representation from the real vectors. By generating offspring solutions in the Pareto optimal subspace rather than in the original decision space, the search space is highly reduced and the optimization of the binary vectors and real vectors can be considerably eased.

 

### 4.3.1 Restricted Boltzmann Machine and Auto‐Encoder

As the building block of deep belief network, RBM is a two‐layer neural network for the dimensionality reduction of inputs with binary encoding [\[14\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0014). Assuming that the weights between the input layer and hidden layer are stored in a matrix ![bold w element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper D times k](images/c04-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></math>, the probability that the hidden layer ![bold h element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 1 times k](images/c04-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></math> being one can be calculated based on an input vector ![bold x element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 1 times upper D](images/c04-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math>:

(4.5)![p left-parenthesis bold h equals bold 1 vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis equals sigma left-parenthesis bold a plus bold x bold w right-parenthesis comma](images/c04-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold a element-of double-struck upper R Superscript 1 times k](images/c04-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></math> denotes the weights of the bias and ![sigma left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over 1 plus e Superscript negative x Baseline EndFraction](images/c04-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> denotes the sigmoid function. After calculating the probability, the value of each element ![h Subscript i](images/c04-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> can be sampled by comparing ![p left-parenthesis h Subscript i Baseline equals 1 vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a uniformly distributed random number within ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>:

As for the reconstruction operation, the probability that the input layer ![bold x prime element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet Superscript 1 times upper D](images/c04-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math> being one can be calculated based on ![bold h](images/c04-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math>:

where ![bold a prime element-of double-struck upper R Superscript 1 times upper D](images/c04-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math> denotes the weights of the bias. Similarly, the value of each element ![x prime Subscript i](images/c04-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> can be sampled by comparing ![p left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline equals 1 vertical-bar bold h right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> with a uniformly distributed random number within ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>:

(4.8)![x prime Subscript i Baseline equals p left-parenthesis x prime Subscript i Baseline equals 1 vertical-bar bold h right-parenthesis greater-than r a n d comma i equals 1 comma ellipsis comma upper D period](images/c04-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>.</mo></math> 

Given a set of training samples as input vectors, an RBM can be trained by using the contrastive divergence algorithm [\[15\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0015) for minimizing the difference between each pair of ![bold x](images/c04-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold x prime](images/c04-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> in an unsupervised manner. Thus, the hidden layer ![bold h](images/c04-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math> can be used as a reduced representation of ![bold x](images/c04-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> for ![k less-than upper D](images/c04-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>D</mi></math>.

Auto‐encoder serves as the building block of stacked auto‐encoder, which is a three‐layer neural network for the dimensionality of inputs with real encoding [\[16\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0016). In fact, the output layer of auto‐encoder is the same as the input layer, and thus the propagation from the hidden layer to the output layer is similar to the reconstruction operation of RBM. Assuming that the weights between the input layer and hidden layer are stored in a matrix ![bold w element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper D times k](images/c04-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></math> and the weights between the hidden layer and output layer are stored in a matrix ![bold w prime element-of double-struck upper R Superscript k times upper D](images/c04-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math>, the hidden layer ![bold h element-of double-struck upper R Superscript 1 times k](images/c04-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></math> can be calculated based on an input vector ![bold x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript 1 times upper D](images/c04-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math>:

(4.9)![bold h equals sigma left-parenthesis bold a plus bold x bold w right-parenthesis comma](images/c04-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold a element-of double-struck upper R Superscript 1 times k](images/c04-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></math> denotes the weights of the bias. Then, the output layer ![bold y element-of double-struck upper R Superscript 1 times upper D](images/c04-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math> can be calculated based on ![bold h](images/c04-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math>:

(4.10)![bold y equals sigma left-parenthesis bold a prime plus bold h bold w Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis comma](images/c04-math-0010.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold a prime element-of double-struck upper R Superscript 1 times upper D](images/c04-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></math> denotes the weights of the bias. Given a set of training samples as input vectors, an auto‐encoder can be trained by using gradient descent [\[17\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0017) for minimizing the difference between each pair of ![bold x](images/c04-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold y](images/c04-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> in an unsupervised manner. Thus, the hidden layer ![bold h](images/c04-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math> can be used as a reduced representation of ![bold x](images/c04-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> for ![k less-than upper D](images/c04-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>D</mi></math>. In MOEA/PSL, the DAE rather than the original auto‐encoder is used, which is a popular variant that randomly sets the elements in each input vector to zero [\[18\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0018).

 

### 4.3.2 Pareto Optimal Subspace Learning in MOEA/PSL

As illustrated in [Fig. 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0002), since RBM can learn the probability distribution of the input obeying a binomial distribution, it is desirable to learn a sparse distribution from the binary vectors used in bi‐level encoding. Analogously, since DAE can learn a compact representation of the input in a continuous space, it is desirable to reduce the dimensionality of the real vectors used in bi‐level encoding. By using the promising solutions found so far as training samples, the reduced binary vectors and real vectors form a promising approximation of the Pareto optimal subspace. Therefore, the efficiency of finding sparse optimal solutions can be improved by evolving a population in the learnt subspace, even if the search strategies in general MOEAs are employed.

![Figure 4.2 The unsupervised neural network‐based dimensionality reduction strategy in MOEA/PSL.](images/c04f002.png)

[**Figure 4.2**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0002) The unsupervised neural network‐based dimensionality reduction strategy in MOEA/PSL.

In comparison to other dimensionality reduction methods such as principal component analysis, the advantages of RBM and DAE lie in the fact that they can learn nonlinear interactions between real variables and interactions between binary variables. More importantly, the reduced binary vectors and real vectors can be easily recovered as shown in [Fig. 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0002), which is necessary for the function evaluation of decision vectors.

The pseudocode of the Pareto optimal subspace learning‐based offspring generation is presented in Algorithm 4.4. First of all, the binary vectors of the non‐dominated solutions in the current population are used to train an RBM (Lines 1 and 2), and the real vectors of the non‐dominated solutions in the current population are used to train a DAE (Lines 4 and 5). Note that the training of DAE can be omitted when solving binary sparse LSMOPs. Afterwards, the binary vectors ![bold xb comma bold yb](images/c04-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yb</mtext></math> of two parents are used to generate the binary vectors ![bold pb comma bold qb](images/c04-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">pb</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">qb</mtext></math> of two offspring solutions each time, and the real vectors ![bold xr comma bold yr](images/c04-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yr</mtext></math> of the same parents are used to generate the real vectors ![bold pr comma bold qr](images/c04-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">pr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">qr</mtext></math> of the same offspring solutions (Line 8). The generation of binary vectors is implemented by uniform crossover and bitwise mutation, and the generation of real vectors is implemented by simulated binary crossover [\[10\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0010) and polynomial mutation [\[11\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0011). Besides, the probability of generating offspring in the learnt subspace is controlled by a parameter ![rho](images/c04-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math>.

When generating two offspring solutions, if ![rho greater-than r a n d](images/c04-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math>, the two ![1 times upper D](images/c04-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math> binary vectors ![bold xb comma bold yb](images/c04-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yb</mtext></math> are first reduced to two ![1 times k](images/c04-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></math> binary vectors ![bold xb prime comma bold yb prime](images/c04-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">yb</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> via RBM (Line 11), then two ![1 times k](images/c04-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></math> binary vectors ![bold pb prime comma bold qb prime](images/c04-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">pb</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">qb</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> are generated by uniform crossover and bitwise mutation (Line 12), and they are further recovered via RBM to obtain two ![1 times upper D](images/c04-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math> binary vectors ![bold pb comma bold qb](images/c04-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">pb</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">qb</mtext></math> (Line 13). Also, when solving continuous sparse LSMOPs, the two ![1 times upper D](images/c04-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math> real vectors ![bold xr comma bold yr](images/c04-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yr</mtext></math> are first reduced to two ![1 times k](images/c04-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></math> real vectors ![bold xr prime comma bold yr prime](images/c04-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">xr</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">yr</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> via DAE (Line 15), then two ![1 times k](images/c04-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>k</mi></math> real vectors ![bold pr prime comma bold qr prime](images/c04-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">pr</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">qr</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> are generated by simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation (Line 16), and they are further recovered via DAE to obtain two ![1 times upper D](images/c04-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math> real vectors ![bold pr comma bold qr](images/c04-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">pr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">qr</mtext></math> (Line 17). When solving binary sparse LSMOPs, the real vectors ![bold pr comma bold qr](images/c04-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">pr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">qr</mtext></math> of offspring solutions are directly set to ![1 times upper D](images/c04-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math> vectors of ones (Line 19). By contrast, if ![rho greater-than r a n d](images/c04-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math>, the binary vectors ![bold xb comma bold yb](images/c04-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yb</mtext></math> are directly used to generate ![bold pb comma bold qb](images/c04-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">pb</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">qb</mtext></math> (Line 21), and the real vectors ![bold xr comma bold yr](images/c04-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yr</mtext></math> are directly used to generate ![bold pr comma bold qr](images/c04-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">pr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">qr</mtext></math> (Line 23) when solving continuous sparse LSMOPs.

 

### 4.3.3 Parameter Adaptation in MOEA/PSL

As can be observed from the above procedure, the probability of generating offspring in the learnt subspace ![rho](images/c04-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> and the hidden layer size ![k](images/c04-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> of the neural networks are given in advance. Intuitively, a larger ![rho](images/c04-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> generates more offspring solutions in the learnt subspace, but also leads to poorer population diversity. A smaller ![k](images/c04-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> learns a smaller subspace for higher convergence speed, but also increases the possibility of trapping into local optimums. In order to strike a good balance between greed and randomness, the two parameters should be carefully set. Instead of predefining the parameters by users, MOEA/PSL suggests a parameter adaptation strategy to dynamically estimate the values of ![rho](images/c04-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> and ![k](images/c04-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> according to the current population.

The pseudocode of the parameter adaptation in MOEA/PSL is described in Algorithm 4.5. At the end of each generation, the number of offspring solutions generated in the learnt subspace that successfully survives to the next generation ![s 1](images/c04-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and the number of offspring solutions generated in the original decision space that successfully survives to the next generation ![s 2](images/c04-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> are determined (Lines 1 and 2), and the parameter ![rho element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c04-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> is updated (Line 3):

(4.11)![rho equals 0.5 times rho plus 0.5 times StartFraction s 1 Over s 1 plus s 2 EndFraction comma](images/c04-math-0011.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the initial value of ![rho](images/c04-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> is set to 0.5. Obviously, a larger ![s 1](images/c04-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> indicates higher performance of generating offspring in the learnt subspace, hence ![rho](images/c04-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> is increased to generate more offspring solutions in the learnt subspace at the next generation. By contrast, a larger ![s 2](images/c04-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> indicates higher performance of generating offspring in the original decision space, hence ![rho](images/c04-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> is decreased to generate more offspring solutions in the original decision space at the next generation. Then, the non‐dominated solution set ![upper N upper P](images/c04-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></math> in the current population is identified (Line 4), and the probability that the decision vector ![bold dec](images/c04-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">dec</mtext></mrow></math> being one can be estimated based on ![upper N upper P](images/c04-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></math> (Line 5):

### 4.3.4 Procedure of MOEA/PSL

With the Pareto optimal subspace learning strategy and parameter adaptation strategy, the procedure of MOEA/PSL is described in Algorithm 4.6. Firstly, a population ![upper P](images/c04-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> with ![upper N](images/c04-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions is randomly initialized (Line 1), and the non‐dominated front number and crowding distance of each solution in ![upper P](images/c04-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> are determined (Lines 2 and 3). Then, the parameters ![rho](images/c04-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> and ![k](images/c04-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> are initialized (Lines 4 and 5). At each generation, the mating pool ![upper P prime](images/c04-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is constructed by selecting ![upper N](images/c04-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> parents from the population ![upper P](images/c04-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> via binary tournament selection according to the non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances of solutions (Line 7). After that, ![upper N](images/c04-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> offspring solutions are generated by the unsupervised neural network‐based Pareto optimal subspace learning strategy (Line 8). To select ![upper N](images/c04-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions from the combination of ![upper P](images/c04-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper O](images/c04-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>, MOEA/PSL adopts the same environmental selection strategy as SparseEA, where ![upper N](images/c04-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions with better non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances survive to the next generation (Line 9). Furthermore, the parameters ![rho](images/c04-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> and ![k](images/c04-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> are updated by the parameter adaptation strategy (Line 10). Finally, the population ![upper P](images/c04-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 11).

At each generation of MOEA/PSL, the time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N upper E upper D k right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for neural network training, ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N upper D k right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for offspring generation, ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for environmental selection, and ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N upper D right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for parameter adaptation, where ![upper E](images/c04-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of epochs for training, ![upper D](images/c04-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of decision variables, and ![upper M](images/c04-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of MOEA/PSL is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared plus upper N upper E upper D k right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

 

## 4.4 Data Mining‐Assisted Evolutionary Algorithm

The pattern mining‐based multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm (PM‐MOEA) also focuses on the dimensionality reduction of the decision spaces of sparse LSMOPs [\[19\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0019). In contrast to MOEA/PSL using unsupervised neural networks, PM‐MOEA suggests a novel evolutionary frequent pattern mining method to mine the sparse distribution from the binary vectors, which is quite different and more flexible than machine learning methods. Furthermore, PM‐MOEA suggests a binary crossover operator and a binary mutation operator for ensuring the sparsity of offspring solutions. In comparison to the binary operators of SparseEA flipping a single variable, the expectation of the number of flipped variables is controllable in PM‐MOEA and thus is more flexible to be used.

 

### 4.4.1 Evolutionary Frequent Pattern Mining

As introduced in [Section 4.1.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0002), frequent pattern mining aims to find the optimal patterns from a transaction dataset [\[3\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0003). In addition to considering it as a sparse LSMOP, it is also an effective tool for dimensionality reduction. In particular for solving sparse LSMOPs, the current population can be regarded as a transaction dataset with each decision vector being a transaction, and the set of nonzero variables is the optimal pattern to be mined. This way, the set of nonzero variables can be estimated through frequent pattern mining techniques to guide the offspring generation in later generations, and the dimensionality of the binary search space is naturally reduced.

According to Eq. (2.28), the optimal patterns are the most frequent and complete item sets of the transaction dataset. For solving sparse LSMOPs, the optimal patterns are the minimum estimations of the nonzero variable set, in which each binary variable is probably set to one. In addition, PM‐MOEA also aims to obtain the maximum estimations of the nonzero variable set, in which each binary variable is possibly set to one. More specifically, when generating offspring solutions, the binary variables out of the maximum estimation are always set to zero, the binary variables in the maximum estimation are determined by parents, and the binary variables in the minimum estimation are always set to one. For this aim, PM‐MOEA suggests two objectives for mining the maximum estimations:
