It can be found that the objectives ![f 3](images/c04-i0227.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![f 4](images/c04-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></math> are the same as ![f 1](images/c04-i0229.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![f 2](images/c04-i0230.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> in Eq. (2.28), where ![f 3](images/c04-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math> aims to find a minimum candidate set being an intersection set of the nonzero variables in all the binary vectors, and ![f 4](images/c04-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></math> makes the minimum candidate set as large as possible. On the other hand, the objectives ![f 1](images/c04-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> are ![f 2](images/c04-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> are novel, where ![f 1](images/c04-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> aims to find a maximum candidate set being a union set of the nonzero variables in all the binary vectors, and ![f 2](images/c04-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> makes the maximum candidate set as small as possible. At the beginning of the optimization procedure, the maximum candidate set is likely to contain most variables and the minimum candidate set is likely to contain few variables. With the evolution of the population, the maximum candidate set will be shortened and the minimum candidate set will be enlarged, and the nonzero variable set can be exactly found when the maximum candidate set equals the minimum candidate set. In comparison to machine learning‐based dimensionality reduction methods, frequent pattern mining has three main advantages: first, it mines the maximum and minimum candidate sets of nonzero variables rather than an exact estimation of nonzero variables, where the former are less greedy and can better tackle the inaccuracy of the binary vectors in the current population (since the current population is not optimal). Second, it provides multiple maximum candidate sets and minimum candidate sets, which can make diverse trade‐offs between ![f 1](images/c04-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![f 2](images/c04-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> or ![f 3](images/c04-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![f 4](images/c04-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></math>, thus preserving the population diversity in the decision space. Third, it does not contain any hyperparameter that needs to be tuned (e.g., the hidden layer size of RBM and DAE), which is flexible to be used since the ratio of nonzero variables in the optimal solutions is unknown.

It is obvious that the mining of maximum candidate sets and the mining of minimum candidate sets are also sparse LSMOPs, which have the same number of binary variables as the original sparse LSMOP. Nevertheless, the former are computationally cheap since they are pursued based on the binary vectors of the current population, regardless of the objectives or dataset of the original sparse LSMOP. While many practical frequent pattern mining methods have been proposed \[[3](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0003), [5](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0005), [20](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0020)\], they are inefficient for finding diverse patterns. Thus, PM‐MOEA suggests a fast evolutionary frequent pattern mining method to mine the maximum and minimum candidate sets of nonzero variables, which is actually the same as PM‐MOEA itself. Although the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method is adopted twice at each generation, it does not consume many computational resources since it uses a few function evaluations to evolve the population in an incremental manner, i.e., the final population in the previous mining operation is used as the initial population in the next mining operation.

 

### 4.4.2 Mining Candidate Sets in PM‐MOEA

As illustrated in [Fig. 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0003), the whole binary vector is divided into four parts. First, the variables being zero in all the binary vectors are directly fixed to zero and ignored in the mining operation. After obtaining the maximum and minimum candidate sets, the variables out of the maximum candidate set are also fixed to zero, the variables in the maximum candidate set may be one or zero, and the variables in the minimum candidate set are fixed to one. When generating an offspring solution, the variables in the maximum candidate set but out of the minimum candidate set are determined by its two parents.

![Figure 4.3 The evolutionary frequent pattern mining method in PM‐MOEA.](images/c04f003.png)

[**Figure 4.3**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0003) The evolutionary frequent pattern mining method in PM‐MOEA.

The pseudocode of mining maximum candidate sets is presented in Algorithm 4.7, where the maximum candidate sets ![upper Q Subscript m a x](images/c04-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></math> are initialized to those obtained in the previous mining operation. First of all, the binary vectors of the non‐dominated solutions in the current population are stored in ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> (Line 1), and the dimensions that are zero in all the binary vectors in ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> are eliminated from ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> (Lines 2 and 3) and ![upper Q Subscript m a x](images/c04-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></math> (Lines 4 and 5). To initialize ![upper N prime](images/c04-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> more maximum candidate sets according to the current ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math>, half the binary vectors are selected from ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> (Line 7) each time, and the dimensions that are nonzero in at least one of the selected binary vectors constitute a new initial maximum candidate set (Lines 8 and 9). After evaluating all the maximum candidate sets by Eq. ([4.15](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0015)) based on ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> (Line 10), the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method iteratively evolves them by using the selection strategies of NSGA‐II (Lines 13 and 16) and the binary genetic operators suggested in PM‐MOEA (Line 14). For the sake of efficiency, the number of candidate sets ![upper N prime](images/c04-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is set to 20 and the number of iterations is set to 10.

The pseudocode of mining minimum candidate sets is presented in Algorithm 4.8, which is very similar to the pseudocode of mining maximum candidate sets. First of all, the binary vectors of the non‐dominated solutions in the current population are stored in ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> (Line 1), and the dimensions that are zero in all the binary vectors in ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> are eliminated from ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> (Lines 2 and 3) and ![upper Q Subscript m i n](images/c04-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> (Lines 4 and 5). To initialize ![upper N prime](images/c04-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> more minimum candidate sets according to the current ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math>, half the binary vectors are selected from ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> (Line 7) each time, and the dimensions that are nonzero in all the selected binary vectors constitute a new initial minimum candidate set (Lines 8 and 9). After evaluating all the minimum candidate sets by Eq. ([4.16](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0016)) based on ![upper N upper B](images/c04-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi></math> (Line 10), the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method iteratively evolves them by using the selection strategies of NSGA‐II (Lines 13 and 16) and the binary genetic operators suggested in PM‐MOEA (Line 14).

 

### 4.4.3 Binary Genetic Operators of PM‐MOEA

After obtaining the maximum and minimum candidate sets by the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method, PM‐MOEA can generate the binary vectors of offspring solutions in the reduced binary search spaces. Different from MOEA/PSL that generates parts of the offspring solutions in the original decision space for alleviating prematurity, PM‐MOEA generates all the offspring solutions within the dimensions determined by the maximum candidate sets, since the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method provides multiple maximum and minimum candidate sets with good diversity, and one maximum candidate set and one minimum candidate set are randomly selected each time.

The pseudocode of offspring generation in PM‐MOEA is described in Algorithm 4.9, where two parents are used to generate one offspring solution each time. Before offspring generation, a maximum candidate set ![bold p](images/c04-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow></math> is randomly selected from ![upper Q Subscript m a x](images/c04-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></math> (Line 9) and a minimum candidate set ![bold q](images/c04-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math> is randomly selected from ![upper Q Subscript m i n](images/c04-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> (Line 11), where ![bold q](images/c04-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math> should be a subset of ![bold p](images/c04-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow></math> (Line 10). While if there does not exist any ![bold q element-of upper Q Subscript m i n](images/c04-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> being a subset of any ![bold p element-of upper Q Subscript m a x](images/c04-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></math> (Line 3), ![bold p](images/c04-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow></math> is randomly selected (Line 4) while ![bold q](images/c04-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math> is set to empty (Line 5). Then, the binary vectors ![bold xb comma bold yb](images/c04-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xb</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yb</mtext></math> of two parents are used to generate the binary vector ![bold ob](images/c04-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">ob</mtext></mrow></math> of one offspring solution, and the real vectors ![bold xr comma bold yr](images/c04-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="bold">xr</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold">yr</mtext></math> of two parents are used to generate the real vector ![bold or](images/c04-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">or</mtext></mrow></math> of one offspring solution (Line 12). The generation of binary vectors is implemented by the binary genetic operators suggested in PM‐MOEA (Line 15), and the generation of real vectors is implemented by simulated binary crossover [\[10\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0010) and polynomial mutation [\[11\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0011) (Line 18). Besides, the binary variables out of ![bold p](images/c04-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow></math> are fixed to zero (Line 14) and the binary variables in ![bold q](images/c04-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math> are fixed to one (Line 16).

The binary genetic operators of PM‐MOEA aim to **(a)** equate the expectation of the number of flipped nonzero variables with the expectation of the number of flipped zero variables, and **(b)** keep the expectation of the total number of flipped variables unchanged. By doing so, the generated binary vectors are not expected to have the same number of zeros and ones, and the sparsity of offspring solutions can be ensured. Assuming that a binary vector having ![d](images/c04-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> nonzero variables and ![left-parenthesis upper D minus d right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> zero variables is flipped with a probability of ![p](images/c04-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> on each dimension, then ![p 1 n equals p 0 left-parenthesis upper D minus n right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> holds for condition **(a)** and ![p 1 n plus p 0 left-parenthesis upper D minus n right-parenthesis equals p upper D](images/c04-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>D</mi></math> holds for condition **(b)**, where ![p 1](images/c04-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> denotes the probability of flipping each nonzero variable and ![p 0](images/c04-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math> denotes the probability of flipping each zero variable. Thus,

[(4.17)](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-disp-0017)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column p 1 2nd Column equals StartFraction p upper D Over 2 n EndFraction comma 2nd Row 1st Column p 0 2nd Column equals StartFraction p upper D Over 2 left-parenthesis upper D minus n right-parenthesis EndFraction period EndLayout](images/c04-math-0017.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable columnalign="right left" class="aligned"><mtr><mtd><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

Besides, ![p](images/c04-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> is set to ![2 n slash upper D](images/c04-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>D</mi></math> if it is larger than this value, otherwise ![p 1](images/c04-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> will be larger than 1. The pseudocode of the binary genetic operators is described in Algorithm 4.10. For the crossover operator, the offspring ![bold o](images/c04-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math> is first set to the same as one parent ![bold x](images/c04-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> (Line 5), and the dimensions that are different in two parents ![bold x comma bold y](images/c04-i0287.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></math> are stored in ![d i f f](images/c04-i0288.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi></math> (Line 6). Then, the probability of flipping each variable in dimensions ![d i f f](images/c04-i0289.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi></math> is calculated by Eq. ([4.17](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0017)) (Line 7), and the binary variables in dimensions ![d i f f](images/c04-i0290.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi></math> of ![bold o](images/c04-i0291.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math> are flipped accordingly (Line 8). Here, the number of variables ![upper D](images/c04-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> in Eq. ([4.17](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0017)) equals ![StartAbsoluteValue d i f f EndAbsoluteValue](images/c04-i0293.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>, ![n](images/c04-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> counts the number of nonzero variables in dimensions ![d i f f](images/c04-i0295.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi></math> of ![bold o](images/c04-i0296.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math>, and ![p](images/c04-i0297.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> is set to 0.5. For the mutation operator, the probability of flipping each variable is also calculated by Eq. ([4.17](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0017)) (Line 9), and the binary variables of ![bold o](images/c04-i0298.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math> are flipped accordingly (Line 10). Here, the number of variables ![upper D](images/c04-i0299.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> in Eq. ([4.17](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0017)) equals the total number of binary variables, ![n](images/c04-i0300.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> counts the total number of nonzero variables of ![bold o](images/c04-i0301.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow></math>, and ![p](images/c04-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> is usually set to ![1 slash upper D](images/c04-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>D</mi></math>.

 

### 4.4.4 Procedure of PM‐MOEA

With the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method and the binary genetic operators, the procedure of PM‐MOEA is presented in Algorithm 4.11. First, a population ![upper P](images/c04-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> with ![upper N](images/c04-i0305.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions is randomly initialized (Line 1), and the maximum candidate sets ![upper Q Subscript m a x](images/c04-i0306.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></math> and minimum candidate sets ![upper Q Subscript m i n](images/c04-i0307.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> are initialized to empty (Lines 3 and 4). At each generation, ![upper Q Subscript m a x](images/c04-i0308.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper Q Subscript m i n](images/c04-i0309.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> are updated through the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method based on the current population (Lines 6 and 7), and the mating pool ![upper P prime](images/c04-i0310.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is constructed by selecting ![2 upper N](images/c04-i0311.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi></math> parents from the population ![upper P](images/c04-i0312.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> via binary tournament selection according to the non‐dominated front numbers (Line 8). After that, ![upper N](images/c04-i0313.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> offspring solutions are generated with the assistance of ![upper Q Subscript m a x](images/c04-i0314.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></math>, ![upper Q Subscript m i n](images/c04-i0315.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math>, and the new binary genetic operators (Line 9). To select ![upper N](images/c04-i0316.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions from the combination of ![upper P](images/c04-i0317.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper O](images/c04-i0318.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow></math>, PM‐MOEA adopts the same environmental selection strategy as SparseEA and MOEA/PSL, where ![upper N](images/c04-i0319.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions with better non‐dominated front numbers and crowding distances survive to the next generation (Line 10). Finally, the population ![upper P](images/c04-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 11).

At each generation of PM‐MOEA, the time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper G prime left-parenthesis upper N prime squared plus upper N prime upper D right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for frequent pattern mining, ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N upper D right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for offspring generation, and ![upper O left-parenthesis upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for environmental selection, where ![upper G prime](images/c04-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> denotes the number of iterations for frequent pattern mining, ![upper N prime](images/c04-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> denotes the maximum number of maximum and minimum candidate sets, ![upper D](images/c04-i0326.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of decision variables, and ![upper M](images/c04-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of objectives. Therefore, the time complexity of one generation of PM‐MOEA is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper G prime left-parenthesis upper N prime squared plus upper N prime upper D right-parenthesis plus upper N upper D plus upper M upper N squared right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi><msup><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

 

## 4.5 Experimental Comparisons

To investigate the performance of SparseEA, MOEA/PSL, and PM‐MOEA, they are compared with several representative MOEAs on benchmark and real‐world sparse LSMOPs. The compared MOEAs include a classical evolutionary algorithm NSGA‐II [\[6\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0006), two decision variable grouping‐based evolutionary algorithms MOEA/DVA [\[21\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0021) and LMEA [\[22\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0022), two decision space reduction‐based evolutionary algorithms WOF‐SMPSO [\[23\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0023) and LSMOF‐NSGA‐II [\[24\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0024), and a novel search strategy‐based evolutionary algorithm LMOCSO [\[25\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0025). The tested sparse LSMOPs include the benchmark problems SMOP1–SMOP8 [\[7\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0007), the neural network training problem (including four test instances NN1–NN4 with different datasets) introduced in Eq. (2.23), and the frequent pattern mining problem (including four test instances PM1–PM4 with different datasets) introduced in Eq. (2.28). The population size is set to 100 and the number of function evaluations is set to ![100 times upper D](images/c04-i0517.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>100</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math>, where ![upper D](images/c04-i0518.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is the number of decision variables ranging from 100 to 6241. The populations obtained on benchmark problems are assessed by IGD [\[26\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0026), and the populations obtained on real‐world problems are assessed by HV [\[27\]](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0027).

[Table 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-tbl-0002) lists the experimental results averaged over 30 runs, where the best results are shown in bold and the statistically similar ones are highlighted. It can be observed that the decision variable grouping‐based and novel search strategy‐based evolutionary algorithms (i.e., MOEA/DVA, LMEA, and LMOCSO) perform worse than the classical NSGA‐II, which indicates that these MOEAs are ineffective for solving sparse LSMOPs, though they are tailored for solving general LSMOPs. The decision space reduction‐based evolutionary algorithms (i.e., WOF‐SMPSO and LSMOF‐NSGA‐II) perform better, as they can converge to quasi‐optimal regions very quickly. The three sparse evolutionary algorithms (i.e., SparseEA, MOEA/PSL, and PM‐MOEA) exhibit the best performance, which verifies the effectiveness of the strategies for finding sparse Pareto optimal solutions. More specifically, MOEA/PSL has the best overall performance on real‐coded problems (i.e., SMOP1–SMOP8 and NN1–NN4) since it uses RBM and DAE to reduce the dimensionality of both the binary vectors and real vectors, while PM‐MOEA has the best overall performance on binary‐coded problems (i.e., PM1–PM4), since it uses an evolutionary frequent pattern mining method to reduce the dimensionality of the binary vectors.

![Table 4.2  IGD Values Obtained by Nine MOEAs on Eight Benchmark Sparse LSMOPs and HV Values Obtained by Nine MOEAs on Two Real‐World Sparse LSMOPs.](images/c04-i0329.png)

[**Table 4.2**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-tbl-0002)  IGD Values Obtained by Nine MOEAs on Eight Benchmark Sparse LSMOPs and HV Values Obtained by Nine MOEAs on Two Real‐World Sparse LSMOPs.

Moreover, [Fig. 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0004) plots the populations with the median HV values obtained by the nine MOEAs on a neural network training problem, where the left axis shows the network complexity and training loss and the right axis shows the network complexity and test loss. Obviously, the solutions obtained by SparseEA, MOEA/PSL, and PM‐MOEA have worse training loss but similar test loss to the solutions obtained by the other MOEAs, which indicates that the solutions obtained by the other MOEAs overfit the training samples due to their high complexities. As a consequence, it is reasonable to use sparse MOEAs to minimize both the network complexity and loss in training neural networks.

![Figure 4.4 Solutions obtained by nine MOEAs on a neural network training problem.](images/c04f004.png)

[**Figure 4.4**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0004) Solutions obtained by nine MOEAs on a neural network training problem.

 

## 4.6 Summary

This chapter presents the first three MOEAs for sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. The most significant feature of these MOEAs is that they search for the sparse Pareto optimal solutions of specific LSMOPs by customizing effective strategies, such as the population initialization strategy in SparseEA, the Pareto optimal subspace learning strategy in MOEA/PSL, and the evolutionary frequent pattern mining method in PM‐MOEA. Due to the wide application scenarios of sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, it appears as an emerging topic in evolutionary multi‐objective optimization, and an increasing number of new methods are being proposed \[[28](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0028)–[37](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0037)\].

In the following chapters, a number of large‐scale MOEAs tailored for the applications in several representative areas are presented, where each MOEA customizes novel strategies to tackle the difficulties of a specific application.

# 5  
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization for Community Detection in Complex Networks

 

## 5.1 Introduction

The complex network is composed of a set of nodes and edges, where a node represents an item and an edge indicates that there is a relationship between the nodes connected by it. [Fig. 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001) gives an illustrative example of complex network. In the real world, there is a wide variety of complex systems that can be modeled as complex networks, such as social platforms, power systems, and World Wide Web. The community detection is to divide the nodes in a complex network into different groups, so that the nodes densely connect to the nodes in the same group (called community or cluster), but sparsely connect to the nodes in the other groups. In [Fig. 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001), the complex network can be divided into two communities. One is made up of nodes ![StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 EndSet](images/c05-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> and the other is made up of nodes ![StartSet 6 comma 7 comma 8 comma 9 EndSet](images/c05-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. The community detection is a vital analysis technique for revealing useful information hidden in complex networks. For example, in social networks, the communities are helpful to find a group of people with similar interests [\[1\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0001). In protein–protein interaction networks, the communities can be used to identify the functional modules \[[2](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0002), [3](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0003)\]. In recent years, a large number of community detection algorithms have been proposed based on different ideas \[[4](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0004)–[6](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0006)\]. Generally, the existing algorithms tailored for community detection can be divided into three groups [\[7\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0007). The first group adopts traditional methods in data clustering to merge densely connected nodes, such as hierarchical clustering [\[8\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0008) and spectral clustering [\[9\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0009). The second group removes the edges that connect different communities to partition networks [\[10\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0010). As for the third group, it resorts to optimization algorithms including mathematical programming [\[11\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0011) and heuristics [\[12\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0012), where the communities are determined by optimizing the metrics for the quality of communities.

![Figure 5.1 An example of complex network, where the network is divided into two communities. One consists of nodes StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 EndSet and the other contains nodes StartSet 6 comma 7 comma 8 comma 9 EndSet.](images/c05f001.png)

[**Figure 5.1**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0001) An example of complex network, where the network is divided into two communities. One consists of nodes ![StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 EndSet](images/c05-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> and the other contains nodes ![StartSet 6 comma 7 comma 8 comma 9 EndSet](images/c05-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>.

As a meta‐heuristic algorithm, evolutionary algorithms have been successfully applied for community detection in complex networks, which can be divided into two categories according to the number of objectives to be optimized. In the first category, the communities are obtained by evolutionary algorithms to optimize a single objective, such as the modularity and edge betweenness. In the second category, the evolutionary algorithms simultaneously optimize multiple conflicting objectives to divide the nodes into different communities. Compared to single‐objective evolutionary algorithms, multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) have attracted more attention in complex networks for community detection. The main reasons are twofold. On the one hand, there exist some potential disadvantages in community detection by optimizing a single objective, such as the limited resolution of modularity. As pointed out in \[[13](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0013), [14](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0014)\], only optimizing the modularity might overlook the communities with small size, and empirical results indicate that multi‐objective optimization is an effective way to tackle this issue. On the other hand, different from single‐objective optimization, the MOEAs can find a set of Pareto optimal solutions rather than a single optimal solution in one run. Since each solution in the Pareto optimal set represents a trade‐off between the multiple objectives, the MOEA‐based community detection methods can provide a set of network partitions with different hierarchical levels, which means that this kind of methods is a rich framework for finding the hierarchical community structure of complex networks \[[15](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0015), [16](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0016)\].

Despite the promising performance achieved by MOEAs on community detection, most of the existing algorithms suffer from the scalability issue due to the curse of dimensionality. As analyzed in \[[17](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0017), [18](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0018)\], the search space of MOEAs increases exponentially with the increase of network size in community detection. This fact can naturally lead to most of the existing MOEA‐based algorithms being only suitable for networks having a relatively small number of nodes. To enhance the scalability of MOEAs in large‐scale complex networks, a number of ideas and/or strategies have been proposed for MOEA‐based community detection algorithms in recent years. In the following sections, two representative ideas tailored for MOEAs to detect communities in large‐scale complex networks will be presented, namely, the network reduction for multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (RMOEAs) and the parallel framework for multi‐objective evolutionary algorithms (PMOEAs).

 

## 5.2 Network Reduction‐Based Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Community Detection

As discussed above, the main bottleneck of MOEAs for community detection in large‐scale complex networks lies in the curse of dimensionality. An intuitive idea is whether we can reduce the tremendous search space of MOEAs by utilizing the problem‐specific knowledge and information, i.e., those related to community detection and complex networks. Inspired by this idea, the network reduction‐based multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm (RMOEA) was first suggested in [\[19\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0019), where two kinds of strategies are proposed to reduce the size of complex networks, namely, prereduction and reduction in evolution. These two strategies are based on the following observation. For a given complex network, there usually exist some nodes in the network that can easily be checked for belonging to the same community. The prereduction reduces the size of complex networks by simply checking the local topology structures, and the reduction in evolution achieves further reduction of networks by finding the local communities found during the evolution of MOEAs. The proposed RMOEA considers the local communities obtained by prereduction and reduction in evolution as a whole in later evolution of the algorithm. By doing so, the size of complex networks being handled is reduced; hence, the scalability of RMOEA to large‐scale complex networks can be considerately enhanced.

 

### 5.2.1 Formulation of Multi‐Objective Community Detection Problem

In the proposed RMOEA, the community detection is formulated as the following bi‐objective optimization problem by minimizing two common metrics, the kernel k‐means (![bold KKM](images/c05-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">KKM</mtext></mrow></math>) [\[14\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0014) and the ratio cut (![bold RC](images/c05-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">RC</mtext></mrow></math>) [\[20\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0020).

From Eq. ([5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0001)), it can be found that the ![bold KKM](images/c05-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">KKM</mtext></mrow></math> measures the link density of intracommunities and the ![bold RC](images/c05-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">RC</mtext></mrow></math> evaluates the link density of intercommunities. The ![bold KKM](images/c05-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">KKM</mtext></mrow></math> decreases with the number of communities and the ![bold RC](images/c05-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">RC</mtext></mrow></math> owns an opposite trend. This means that the ![bold KKM](images/c05-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">KKM</mtext></mrow></math> and ![bold RC](images/c05-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">RC</mtext></mrow></math> are two conflicting objectives, and simultaneously minimizing them can ensure that the nodes belonging to the same community are densely connected and the nodes belonging to different communities are sparely connected, which is coincidence with the requirements of community detection.

 

### 5.2.2 Prereduction Based on Local Network Topology Structure

As discussed above, some local communities can be easily identified by only checking the local topology structure of networks. Hence, the proposed RMOEA first reduces the size of complex networks according to the local topology structure of networks, before the evolution of population starts. The pseudocode of prereduction in RMOEA is given in Algorithm 5.1. To be specific, the prereduction is performed as follows.

First, the RMOEA randomly selects a node ![s](images/c05-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> from the complex network ![upper G](images/c05-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>, and determines a subgraph ![upper G Superscript upper L upper S](images/c05-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup></math> of ![s](images/c05-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> (Lines 4–7). The subgraph ![upper G Superscript upper L upper S](images/c05-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup></math> consists of the nodes ![s](images/c05-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, ![s Superscript c](images/c05-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></math> (a neighboring node of ![s](images/c05-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> which has the largest degree), ![s Superscript c c](images/c05-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></math> (a neighboring node of ![s Superscript c](images/c05-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></math> which shares the largest number of neighbors with ![s Superscript c](images/c05-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></math>), and all common neighbors of ![s Superscript c](images/c05-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></math> and ![s Superscript c c](images/c05-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></math>. Then, the RMOEA extends the subgraph ![upper G Superscript upper L upper S](images/c05-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup></math> by adding some neighbors of ![upper G Superscript upper L upper S](images/c05-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup></math> (Lines 8–15). To ensure that these nodes belong to the same community, the RMOEA only adds each of the neighbors of ![upper G Superscript upper L upper S](images/c05-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup></math> whose number of links with ![upper G Superscript upper L upper S](images/c05-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup></math> is larger than one half of its degree. After that, the local communities of ![s](images/c05-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> is determined, and the RMOEA merges all nodes in ![upper G Superscript upper L upper S](images/c05-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup></math> into one node to reduce the size of network being handled (Lines 16 and 17). The RMOEA will repeat to find the other local communities for the remaining nodes in the network and this process stops until all nodes of the network have been assigned to local communities.

[Fig. 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002) gives an illustrative example of prereduction developed in the RMOEA, where a network with seven nodes is considered, and we assume that the node 1 is selected to identify the corresponding local community. First, the subgraph {1,2,3,5} plotted in [Fig. 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002) (b) is obtained by the RMOEA, given that the node 3 is the neighbor of node 1 that owns the largest degree, and nodes 2 and 5 share the largest number of neighbors with node 3. Second, as depicted in [Fig. 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002), since all the links of node 4 are connected to subgraph {1, 2, 3, 5}, whereas for nodes 6 and 7 only half of links are connected to subgraph {1, 2, 3, 5}, the node 4 is added to the local community. Third, the RMOEA merges the local community {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} into one node, so that the network to be handled is reduced to a network with only three nodes.

![Figure 5.2 An illustrative example of the prereduction. (a) The complex network consisting of seven nodes. (b) Subgraph of node 1, which contains four nodes, namely, nodes 1, 2, 3, and 5. (c) The local community of node 1 by adding node 4 to the subgraph. (d) The reduction network based on the found local community of StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 EndSet.](images/c05f002.png)

[**Figure 5.2**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0002) An illustrative example of the prereduction. (a) The complex network consisting of seven nodes. (b) Subgraph of node 1, which contains four nodes, namely, nodes 1, 2, 3, and 5. (c) The local community of node 1 by adding node 4 to the subgraph. (d) The reduction network based on the found local community of ![StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 5 EndSet](images/c05-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>.

 

### 5.2.3 Network Reduction in Evolution Based on Elite Individuals

In addition to the local topology structure, some local communities can also be obtained in evolution by using the elite individuals searched by MOEAs. In the proposed RMOEA, two metrics are employed to determine the elite individuals in population. One is the widely used metric for measuring the quality of found communities, namely, modularity ![upper Q](images/c05-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>. The larger the modularity ![upper Q](images/c05-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is, the better quality the found communities have. The other is the number of communities ![upper C Subscript n u m](images/c05-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></math>. Considering that the a large ![upper C Subscript n u m](images/c05-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></math> implies that the size of each found community is small, it is helpful to reduce the probability of incorrectly identified local communities. The procedure of elite individual selection is presented in Algorithm 5.2. For a population ![upper P](images/c05-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>, the modularity ![upper Q](images/c05-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> and the number of communities ![upper C Subscript n u m](images/c05-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></math> corresponding to each individual are first calculated, and the non‐dominated individuals are selected as the elite individuals for network reduction.

The pseudocode of network reduction based on elite individuals is presented in Algorithm 5.3. First, the elite individuals ![upper P prime](images/c05-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> are selected from current population ![upper P](images/c05-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> by using Algorithm 5.2. Then, the individual ![i n d](images/c05-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> with the largest number of communities is selected from ![upper P prime](images/c05-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. Third, the individual ![i n d](images/c05-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> is used to identify the local communities based on whether all the nodes in a community of ![i n d](images/c05-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> belong to the same community in the remaining elite individuals. Specifically, for a community ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> in ![i n d](images/c05-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math>, if all nodes in ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> are identified as in one community by the remaining elite individuals, then ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> is considered as a local community. Otherwise, the maximal subset of ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> which are identified in one community by the remaining elite individuals is considered as a local community. The above operations repeat until all communities in ![i n d](images/c05-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> are checked. Lastly, a reduced network ![upper G Subscript upper R](images/c05-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub></math> is obtained by merging all nodes in each local community into one node in ![upper G](images/c05-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>, and the population ![upper P Subscript upper R](images/c05-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub></math> for the reduced network is obtained by merging the genes of nodes of each local community into one gene for all individuals in ![upper P](images/c05-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>. For each individual, an index of the local community is assigned to the merged gene, and the community information on the rest genes in the individual keeps unchanged.

[Fig. 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003) plots an illustrative example of elite individual‐based network reduction. [Fig. 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)(a) displays the original complex network with seven nodes. In [Fig. 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)(b), it is assumed that the two elite individuals ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math> have been selected from population ![upper P](images/c05-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> for determining the local communities. Here, the individuals are represented by the locus‐based representation scheme, where each gene of the individual represents the index of a node that belongs to the same community. The partitions corresponding to ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math> are shown in [Fig. 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)(c), where ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math> has four communities including {1, 2, 3, 4}, {5}, {6}, and {7}, and the partition of ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math> is {1, 2, 3}, {4}, {5}, {6}, and {7}. Since the number of communities in ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math> is larger than that in ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math>, the ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math> is used to obtain the local communities. For community {1, 2, 3}, it is identified as a local community since all of its nodes are identified as in one community by individual ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math>. For community {4}, it is also considered as a local community due to the fact that only one node is contained in the community. This is also the case for communities {5}, {6}, and {7}. In this way, five local communities {1, 2, 3}, {4}, {5}, {6}, and {7} are obtained from the elite individuals ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math>, and the original complex network is reduced to a network with five nodes {![1 prime](images/c05-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, 4, 5, 6, 7} as displayed in [Fig. 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)(d). Here, the local community {1, 2, 3} is merged into one node ![1 prime](images/c05-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. Accordingly, the ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math> are changed to {![1 prime](images/c05-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, ![1 prime](images/c05-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, 5, 6, 7} and {![1 prime](images/c05-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, 4, 5, 6, 7} as shown in [Fig. 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)(d), where ![1 prime](images/c05-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is assigned to the merged gene and the information on the rest genes keeps unchanged.
