### 5.2.4 Procedure of RMOEA

The procedure of RMOEA is described in Algorithm 5.4, where the framework of MOEA/D [\[22\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0022) is adopted to evolve the population. First, the RMOEA conducts the prereduction for complex network ![upper G](images/c05-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> by using the local topology structure of network (Algorithm 5.1). Second, based on the network ![upper G Subscript upper R](images/c05-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub></math> obtained by the pre‐reduction, the RMOEA initializes a population ![upper P](images/c05-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and a reference point ![z Superscript asterisk](images/c05-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. Here, the locus‐based adjacency encoding schema is used to generate the population ![upper P](images/c05-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>, where each gene of individuals is first randomly assigned to an index of a neighbor of the node corresponding to this gene or index of the node itself, and then the genes in the individuals are iteratively replaced by the index shared by most of its neighbors, until the genes keep unchanged. For reference point ![z Superscript asterisk](images/c05-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, it is initialized as the best values of ![bold KKM](images/c05-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">KKM</mtext></mrow></math> and ![bold RC](images/c05-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">RC</mtext></mrow></math> in the population. Third, the RMOEA assigns ![n s](images/c05-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></math> individuals to each weight vector according to the Euclidean distance between the individuals and weight vectors. Fourth, the RMOEA further reduces the size of network by using elite individuals based on the network reduction in evolution. Specifically, for each generation ![i](images/c05-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> satisfying ![i percent-sign left-parenthesis left ceiling left-parenthesis m a x g e n plus 1 right-parenthesis slash left-parenthesis upper T plus 1 right-parenthesis right ceiling right-parenthesis equals equals 0](images/c05-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>%</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8968;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8969;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, the reduced network ![upper G Subscript upper R](images/c05-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub></math> is reduced by using elite individuals found during evolution (Algorithm 5.3). Here, ![percent-sign](images/c05-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> is the modular operation and ![upper T](images/c05-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is a parameter controlling the number of reductions during evolution. Moreover, for each individual ![j](images/c05-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>, the RMOEA randomly selects an individual from ![upper N Subscript j](images/c05-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> (a set of ![n s](images/c05-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></math> individuals assigned to the ![j](images/c05-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> weight vector) to generate an offspring by crossover and mutation operators in each generation. The ![upper N Subscript j](images/c05-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> and reference point ![z Superscript asterisk](images/c05-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> are updated according to the Tchebycheff value of the offspring. The details of crossover and mutation operations are given in [Fig. 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0004). The RMOEA will repeat to evolve the population until the maximum number of generations is reached.

![Figure 5.4 An illustrative example of crossover and mutation operators. (a) Complex network upper G and two individuals i n d Baseline 1 and i n d Baseline 2 with crossover positions p o s i t i o n Baseline 1 and p o s i t i o n Baseline 2 that are generated randomly. In crossover process, a randomly number r a n d is generated from {1, 2, 3}, which means that the parts before p o s i t i o n Baseline 1, between p o s i t i o n Baseline 1 and p o s i t i o n Baseline 2, and after p o s i t i o n Baseline 2 of i n d Baseline 1 and i n d Baseline 2 are mutually exchanged, respectively. (b) Two generated offspring i n d 1 prime and i n d 2 prime under crossover operator with r a n d equals 3. (c) Two mutation vectors for i n d 1 prime and i n d 2 prime, where the value of each node is randomly generated from \[0, 1\]. If the value of the node in mutation vector is smaller than mutation probability, the corresponding gene of the node will be changed to an index in its neighboring nodes. (d) Two offspring i n d 1 double-prime and i n d 2 double-prime, which are generated by mutation operation with the mutation probability set as 0.1.](images/c05f004.png)

[**Figure 5.4**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0004) An illustrative example of crossover and mutation operators. (a) Complex network ![upper G](images/c05-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and two individuals ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math> with crossover positions ![p o s i t i o n Baseline 1](images/c05-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![p o s i t i o n Baseline 2](images/c05-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></math> that are generated randomly. In crossover process, a randomly number ![r a n d](images/c05-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> is generated from {1, 2, 3}, which means that the parts before ![p o s i t i o n Baseline 1](images/c05-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></math>, between ![p o s i t i o n Baseline 1](images/c05-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![p o s i t i o n Baseline 2](images/c05-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></math>, and after ![p o s i t i o n Baseline 2](images/c05-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></math> of ![i n d Baseline 1](images/c05-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![i n d Baseline 2](images/c05-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></math> are mutually exchanged, respectively. (b) Two generated offspring ![i n d 1 prime](images/c05-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![i n d 2 prime](images/c05-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> under crossover operator with ![r a n d equals 3](images/c05-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. (c) Two mutation vectors for ![i n d 1 prime](images/c05-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![i n d 2 prime](images/c05-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, where the value of each node is randomly generated from \[0, 1\]. If the value of the node in mutation vector is smaller than mutation probability, the corresponding gene of the node will be changed to an index in its neighboring nodes. (d) Two offspring ![i n d 1 double-prime](images/c05-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8243;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![i n d 2 double-prime](images/c05-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><msup><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8243;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, which are generated by mutation operation with the mutation probability set as 0.1.

It is worth noting that the network reduction method might find incorrect local communities, which means that the local communities identified by the reduction in evolution may contain some nodes belonging to different communities. Hence, the RMOEA integrates a local community repairing strategy to correct the misidentified nodes in the reduced network. The pseudocode of the local community repairing strategy is elaborated in Algorithm 5.5. First, the set of elite individuals ![upper P prime](images/c05-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> are selected from the population ![upper P](images/c05-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (Line 1). Second, for each elite individual ![p prime Subscript i](images/c05-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> in ![upper P prime](images/c05-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, the misidentified nodes are detected by checking whether the communities of ![p prime Subscript i](images/c05-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> contain some nodes belonging to different local communities. More specifically, a node is considered as misidentified one if a better modularity ![upper Q](images/c05-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> can be achieved by moving it to the communities of its neighbors. Last, the misidentified nodes are removed from the merged nodes of reduced network ![upper G Subscript upper R](images/c05-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub></math> as a separate node, and the genes of the misidentified nodes are also added to each individual in population ![upper P Subscript upper R](images/c05-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub></math>.

[Fig. 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0005) shows an illustrative example of the local community repairing strategy. As plotted in [Fig. 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0005)(a), a local community {3, 5, 6, 7, 8} is identified by the elite individuals in the population, and only node 3 has at least one neighbor that does not belong to the local community. Furthermore, the modularity ![upper Q](images/c05-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> increases from 0.2219 to 0.3517, when node 3 is removed from the local community {3, 5, 6, 7, 8}. Hence, the local community is repaired as {5, 6, 7, 8}, by which the quality of local communities found by elite individuals can be considerably improved.

![Figure 5.5 An illustrative example of local community repairing strategy. (a) The local community StartSet 3 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 comma 8 EndSet found according to elite individuals during evolution. (b) Repaired local community StartSet 5 comma 6 comma 7 comma 8 EndSet by moving node 3 to the community StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 4 EndSet.](images/c05f005.png)

[**Figure 5.5**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0005) An illustrative example of local community repairing strategy. (a) The local community ![StartSet 3 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 comma 8 EndSet](images/c05-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> found according to elite individuals during evolution. (b) Repaired local community ![StartSet 5 comma 6 comma 7 comma 8 EndSet](images/c05-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> by moving node 3 to the community ![StartSet 1 comma 2 comma 4 EndSet](images/c05-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>.

For a complex network with ![n](images/c05-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> nodes and ![m](images/c05-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> edges, the RMOEA has a time complexity of O![left-parenthesis m a x g e n asterisk p o p asterisk left-parenthesis m prime plus n prime right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![n prime](images/c05-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![m prime](images/c05-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> are the number of nodes and edges of the reduced network, respectively. As presented in Algorithm 5.4, the RMOEA contains four main steps, network reduction based on the local topology, population initialization, network reduction based on the elite individuals, and population evolution. For the network reduction based on local topology, it holds a time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis n asterisk upper D asterisk upper D right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> since in the worst case, it needs the time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis upper D asterisk upper D right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> to identify the local community for a given node. Here, ![upper D](images/c05-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is the maximum degree of nodes in the complex network. The population initialization takes the time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis p o p asterisk n asterisk upper D right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, due to the fact that for each gene of individuals in the population, the maximum number of checking neighbors is ![upper D](images/c05-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>. The time complexity of the network reduction based on elite individuals is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper T asterisk p o p asterisk m right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. It is because that the most time‐consuming operation in this step is the calculation of modularity, which holds the time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis m right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for each individual. As for the population evolution, its time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis m a x g e n asterisk p o p asterisk left-parenthesis n prime plus m prime right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, considering that in each generation, the RMOEA needs to calculate the values of the two objectives, ![bold KKM](images/c05-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">KKM</mtext></mrow></math> and ![bold RC](images/c05-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">RC</mtext></mrow></math>, which takes the time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis n prime plus m prime right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Since ![m a x g e n asterisk left-parenthesis n prime plus m prime right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is larger than ![upper T asterisk m plus upper D asterisk n](images/c05-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, the RMOEA holds a time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis m a x g e n asterisk p o p asterisk left-parenthesis m prime plus n prime right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

 

### 5.2.5 Experimental Comparisons

To verify the performance of RMOEA, it is compared with several representative community detection algorithms. The compared algorithms include five popular evolutionary algorithm‐based community detection algorithms, namely, CoCoMi [\[23\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0023), MOCD [\[13\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0013), MOGA‐net [\[16\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0016), MODTLBO/D [\[24\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0024), and MODPSO [\[14\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0014), where the CoCoMi is a single‐objective evolutionary algorithm, while the MOCD, MOGA‐net, MODTLBO/D, and MODPSO are MOEAs. Moreover, two non‐EA‐based community detection algorithms, namely, Louvain [\[25\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0025) and SSCF [\[9\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0009), are also employed as compared algorithms. The parameters of the compared algorithms are set to the values recommended in [\[14\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0014), which is also listed in [Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0001). For the RMOEA, the number of reductions in evolution ![upper T](images/c05-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is set to 2 in the experiments.

![Table 5.1  Parameter Setting of the Compared Algorithms, Where p o p is the Population Size, m a x g e n is the Maximum Generations of the Algorithm, p c is the Probability of Crossover, p m is the Probability of Mutation, and n s is the Neighborhood Size.](images/c05-i0184.png)

[**Table 5.1**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-tbl-0001)  Parameter Setting of the Compared Algorithms, Where ![p o p](images/c05-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> is the Population Size, ![m a x g e n](images/c05-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></math> is the Maximum Generations of the Algorithm, ![p c](images/c05-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>c</mi></math> is the Probability of Crossover, ![p m](images/c05-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>m</mi></math> is the Probability of Mutation, and ![n s](images/c05-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></math> is the Neighborhood Size.

The test datasets include synthetic benchmark networks and real‐world networks. The synthetic benchmark networks are LFR networks [\[26\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0026), which are widely used to verify the performance of community detection algorithms \[[6](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0006), [27](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0027)\]. The real‐world networks include ![n e t](images/c05-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math>‐![s c i e n c e](images/c05-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></math> and ![b l o g s](images/c05-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>s</mi></math> networks that are used in [\[28\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0028), and ![c a](images/c05-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi></math>‐![upper G r upper Q c](images/c05-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>c</mi></math>, ![c a](images/c05-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi></math>‐![upper G r upper Q c](images/c05-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>c</mi></math>, ![c a](images/c05-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi></math>‐![upper H e p t h](images/c05-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></math>, ![c a](images/c05-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi></math>‐![upper A s t r o upper P h](images/c05-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>h</mi></math> and ![c a](images/c05-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi></math>‐![upper C o n d upper M a t](images/c05-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></math> that are collected by the Stanford Network Analysis Project [\[29\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0029). The details of the seven real‐world networks are given in [Table 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0002).

![Table 5.2  Details of Seven Real‐World Networks Used in Experiments.](images/c05-i0202.png)

[**Table 5.2**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-tbl-0002)  Details of Seven Real‐World Networks Used in Experiments.

The evaluation metrics used to measure the quality of detected communities are normalized mutual information (![upper N upper M upper I](images/c05-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>I</mi></math>) [\[30\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0030) and modularity (![upper Q](images/c05-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>) [\[31\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0031), which can be calculated as follows:

[Table 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0003) lists the experimental results of the RMOEA and seven compared algorithms, averaged over 20 runs on LFR benchmark networks with the nodes ranging from 10,000 to 50,000. The Wilcoxon rank sum test results with a significance level of 0.05 are also given at the bottom of the table. From [Table 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0003), it can be found that the RMOEA owns better scalability than the other five evolutionary algorithm‐based algorithms. Compared to non‐EA‐based algorithms, although the efficiency of RMOEA is worse than Louvain, the detection performance of RMOEA is significantly better than that of Louvain. Despite that the SSCF shows a better detection performance than RMOEA on the LRF networks with 10,000 and 20,000 nodes, it cannot obtain results within 12 hours on the other networks. Different from the SSCF, the RMOEA can always obtain community results within reasonable runtime on all sizes of LFR networks, and achieve competitive detection performance.

![Table 5.3  The upper N upper M upper I Values and Runtime(s) of the Eight Algorithms Averaging Over 20 Runs on Larger LFR Benchmark Networks.](images/c05-i0216.png)

[**Table 5.3**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-tbl-0003)  The ![upper N upper M upper I](images/c05-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>I</mi></math> Values and Runtime(s) of the Eight Algorithms Averaging Over 20 Runs on Larger LFR Benchmark Networks.

[Table 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0004) gives the experimental results of the community detection algorithms averaged over 20 runs on seven real‐world networks. In [Table 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0004), the Louvain achieves the best computational efficiency on all seven real‐world networks. The RMOEA also holds a competitive efficiency, which is much better than the other five evolutionary algorithm‐based algorithms. In terms of detection performance, the RMOEA owns the best overall performance. It achieves the best ![upper Q](images/c05-i0297.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> on five of seven networks. Based on the above experimental comparison, it can be concluded that the RMOEA is a promising community detection algorithm for large‐scale networks, in terms of detection performance and runtime.

![Table 5.4  The upper Q Values and Runtime(s) of the Eight Algorithms Averaging Over 20 Runs on Seven Real‐World Networks.](images/c05-i0259.png)

## 5.3 Parallel Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Community Detection

Parallelization is a widely adopted technique to enhance the scalability of evolutionary algorithms in tackling large‐scale optimization problems. The idea of parallelization has also adopted for community detection in large‐scale complex networks. Based on this idea, a parallel multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm called PMOEA is reported in [\[27\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0027). In the PMOEA, several key nodes of a complex network are first identified, and then the communities associated with these key nodes are parallel detected by MOEAs. After that, a single‐objective evolutionary algorithm is employed to integrate the communities associated with the key nodes, by which the communities of the entire network are obtained. Since the communities associated with the key nodes are detected in parallel, the efficiency of PMOEA in handling large‐scale complex networks can be significantly improved. The framework of PMOEA is presented in [Fig. 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0006) and the pseudocode is given in Algorithm 5.6.

 

### 5.3.1 Key Node Identification

The pseudocode of identifying key nodes is given in Algorithm 5.7, which consists of the following steps. First, the average degree of all nodes in ![upper G](images/c05-i0298.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> is calculated. Next, the nodes that own degree larger than the average degree are determined and added into the set ![upper L s e t](images/c05-i0299.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math>. All nodes with the maximum degree are considered as key nodes in ![upper G](images/c05-i0300.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>. Then, the nodes with the maximum degree and all other nodes that have at least one edge with these nodes are removed from the ![upper L s e t](images/c05-i0301.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math>. Among the remaining nodes in ![upper L s e t](images/c05-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, those with the maximum degree are also considered as key nodes. This process is repeated until no node remains in set ![upper L s e t](images/c05-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math>. It is necessary to stress that the key nodes of a network can also be identified by other effective strategies.

 

### 5.3.2 Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Detecting the Communities Associated with a Key Node

After identifying key nodes of a network, the PMOEA will detect the communities associated with these key nodes in parallel. To this end, an MOEA is devised based on the decomposition‐based MOEA (MOEA/D) [\[22\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0022), which detects a community ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> of a key node by simultaneously minimizing the following two objectives.

If ![upper E left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline comma upper V right-parenthesis greater-than upper E left-parenthesis upper V minus upper C Subscript i Baseline comma upper V right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>&#8726;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the ![upper C o n d left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is determined by the ratio of number of edges leaving community ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> to that in ![upper V minus upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>V</mi><mo>&#8726;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>. The ![upper C o n d left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> has been widely used to detect local communities, and achieved promising results on detecting a single community near a seed point or set \[[32](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0032), [33](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0033)\]. The ![upper N u m left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is defined as the number of key nodes in community ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0326.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>, and minimizing it enables the algorithm to focus on detecting the community associated with a single key node.

The pseudocode of the MOEA developed for detecting community of a key node is presented in Algorithm 5.8. The procedure of MOEA is similar to most of existing MOEA/D variants. Here, the MOEA uses the following Tchebycheff approach to decompose the multi‐objective optimization problem into a number of single‐objective optimization problems.

Specifically, the procedure of Algorithm 5.8 for detecting communities associated with a key node consists of four main steps. The first step is the population initialization. overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> are the labels of nodes that belong to the same community of key node ![k v](images/c05-i0341.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mi>v</mi></math>. For initializing the population, ![p o p](images/c05-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> individuals are generated by using the labels of key node ![k v](images/c05-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mi>v</mi></math> and a subset of neighbors of ![k v](images/c05-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mi>v</mi></math>. The second step is the initialization of reference point ![z Superscript asterisk](images/c05-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and a set of well‐distributed weight vectors ![lamda 1 comma lamda 2 comma ellipsis comma lamda Subscript p o p Baseline](images/c05-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math>, where ![p o p](images/c05-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> is a predefined parameter. The reference point ![z Superscript asterisk](images/c05-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is initialized by the best values of ![upper C o n d](images/c05-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>C</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> and ![upper N u m](images/c05-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>m</mi></math> of individuals in the initial population, and the weight vectors ![lamda 1 comma lamda 2 comma ellipsis comma lamda Subscript p o p Baseline](images/c05-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math> are uniformly generated. The third step is the assignment of individuals to weight vectors. For each weight vectors ![lamda Subscript i](images/c05-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>, it is assigned ![upper T](images/c05-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> individuals, denoted by ![upper N Subscript i](images/c05-i0354.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> according to the Euclidean distance between individuals and ![lamda Subscript i](images/c05-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> in the objective space. The ![upper N Subscript i](images/c05-i0356.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> is called the neighborhood of ![lamda Subscript i](images/c05-i0357.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> and all individuals in ![upper N Subscript i](images/c05-i0358.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> are called neighbors. The fourth step is the evolution of population. For each weight vector ![lamda Subscript i](images/c05-i0359.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>, two individuals are randomly selected from its neighborhood ![upper N Subscript i](images/c05-i0360.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>, and an offspring ![o f f s](images/c05-i0361.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> is generated based on these two individuals by using the crossover and mutation operators described in [Sections 5.3.2.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0011) and [5.3.2.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0012). The offspring ![o f f s](images/c05-i0362.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> will replace each individual in ![upper N Subscript i](images/c05-i0363.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> if the ![o f f s](images/c05-i0364.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> owns better Tchebycheff value than the individual. Moreover, the reference point ![z Superscript asterisk](images/c05-i0365.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> also needs to be updated if ![o f f s](images/c05-i0366.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> has better one or two objective values than that in ![z Superscript asterisk](images/c05-i0367.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. The fourth step will be repeated until the maximum number of generations is reached.

Using the MOEA above, a set of communities associated with a given key node can be detected, and the detection of communities for different key nodes can be easily parallelized. Since the MOEA only detects the communities associated with a key node instead of all communities in the complex network, the dedicated crossover and mutation operators need to be devised to guide the evolution of population, which are described as follows.

 

#### 5.3.2.1 Crossover Operator

For any two individuals ![p 1 equals left pointing angle x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript i Baseline right pointing angle](images/c05-i0368.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> and ![p 2 equals left pointing angle y 1 comma y 2 comma ellipsis comma y Subscript j Baseline right pointing angle](images/c05-i0369.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> in the neighborhood of a weight vector, the labels of nodes in ![p 2](images/c05-i0370.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> but not in ![p 1](images/c05-i0371.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> are first found. Let us assume that ![y Subscript k 1 Baseline comma y Subscript k 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma y Subscript k Sub Subscript l Subscript Baseline](images/c05-i0372.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math> are these labels. Then, for each ![y Subscript k Sub Subscript s](images/c05-i0373.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to s less-than-or-equal-to l](images/c05-i0374.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>l</mi></math>, we calculate the interest of node ![y Subscript k Sub Subscript s](images/c05-i0375.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math> joining the community encoded by individual ![p 1](images/c05-i0376.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> as follows:

where the ![upper E Subscript i n](images/c05-i0377.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the number of edges between the community encoded by individual ![p 1](images/c05-i0378.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and node ![y Subscript k Sub Subscript s](images/c05-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, and the ![upper E Subscript o u t](images/c05-i0380.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></math> denotes the number of edges between nodes outside the community of individual ![p 1](images/c05-i0381.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and node ![y Subscript k Sub Subscript s](images/c05-i0382.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>. After calculating the interest of all found nodes, a number ![r a n d](images/c05-i0386.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> is randomly generated in the range of ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0387.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. If the values of ![upper J left-parenthesis y Subscript k Sub Subscript s Subscript Baseline comma p 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is larger than ![r a n d](images/c05-i0389.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math>, then the label of node ![y Subscript k Sub Subscript s](images/c05-i0390.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math> will be added to individual ![p 1](images/c05-i0391.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>. Otherwise, it will not be added. Assuming that the added labels are ![y Subscript k 1 Baseline comma y Subscript k 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma y Subscript k Sub Subscript m Subscript Baseline](images/c05-i0392.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, an offspring ![o f f s equals left pointing angle x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript k 1 Baseline comma y Subscript k 2 Baseline comma ellipsis comma y Subscript k Sub Subscript m Subscript Baseline right pointing angle](images/c05-i0393.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> can be generated from the crossover between individuals ![p 1](images/c05-i0394.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![p 2](images/c05-i0395.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>.

 

#### 5.3.2.2 Mutation Operator

For an offspring ![o f f s equals left pointing angle z 1 comma z 2 comma ellipsis comma z Subscript t Baseline right pointing angle](images/c05-i0396.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> generated by the crossover operator, the mutation is conducted as follows. First, a number is randomly generated from the range of ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0397.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> to decide whether to add or delete some nodes from ![o f f s](images/c05-i0398.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math>. If the random number is less than 0.5, then the removal operator is conducted. Otherwise, the addition operator is performed.

If the removal operator is selected, another random number is generated from the range of ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> for each label in ![o f f s](images/c05-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> and the label will be removed from ![o f f s](images/c05-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> if the random number is less than 0.5. For the addition operator, all the neighbors of the nodes in community of ![o f f s](images/c05-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> are first found, and then the interest of each node joining the community of ![o f f s](images/c05-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> is calculated according to Eq. ([5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0006)). The label of a neighbor will be added to ![o f f s](images/c05-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math> if a random number generated from the range of ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> is less than the corresponding value of interest. By using the removal and addition operators, a new individual can be generated by the mutation from offspring ![o f f s](images/c05-i0406.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></math>.

[Fig. 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007) plots an illustrative example of crossover and mutation operators. As shown in [Fig. 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007)(a), the complex network to be detected owns 10 nodes labeled as ![1 comma 2 comma 3 comma ellipsis comma 10](images/c05-i0407.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, and the node 1 is the key node. [Fig. 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007)(b) gives two individuals ![p Baseline 1](images/c05-i0408.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![p Baseline 2](images/c05-i0409.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></math> of a weight vector, which encode two communities associated with the key node 1 ![left pointing angle 1 comma 2 comma 4 right pointing angle](images/c05-i0410.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#9001;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> and ![left pointing angle 1 comma 4 comma 5 comma 6 comma 7 right pointing angle](images/c05-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#9001;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#9002;</mo></math>, respectively. From [Fig. 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007)(b), it can be found that the labels 5, 6, and 7 in ![p Baseline 2](images/c05-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></math> do not appear in ![p Baseline 1](images/c05-i0413.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></math>. According to Eq. ([5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0006)), the interest of nodes 5, 6, and 7 added to the community of ![p Baseline 1](images/c05-i0414.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></math> are 0.5, 2, and 0, respectively. Assume that the random numbers generated for nodes 5, 6, and 7 are 0.6, 0.8, and 0.2, respectively. This means that only the label of node 6 is added to the community of ![p Baseline 1](images/c05-i0415.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></math>, and thus an offspring ![p prime equals left pointing angle 1 comma 2 comma 4 comma 6 right pointing angle](images/c05-i0416.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>&#9001;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> is generated by the crossover operator as shown in [Fig. 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007)(c).

In [Fig. 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007)(d), the mutation operator is applied to ![p prime equals left pointing angle 1 comma 2 comma 4 comma 6 right pointing angle](images/c05-i0427.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>&#9001;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>&#9002;</mo></math>. Let us assume that the addition operator is conducted. In [Fig. 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007)(d), there are two neighbors of nodes in the community of ![p prime](images/c05-i0428.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, namely, nodes 3 and 5. The interests of them joining the community of ![p prime](images/c05-i0429.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> are 2 and 0.5, respectively. If the randomly number generated for nodes 3 and 5 are smaller than 2 and larger than 0.5, only the label of node 3 is added to ![p prime](images/c05-i0430.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, and, hence, a new individual ![p Subscript n e w Baseline equals left pointing angle 1 comma 2 comma 3 comma 4 comma 6 right pointing angle](images/c05-i0431.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#9001;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> is obtained by the mutation operator as displayed in [Fig. 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0007)(d).

 

### 5.3.3 Evolutionary Algorithm for Determining the Communities of the Entire Network

After detecting the communities associated with all key nodes, the PMOEA will obtain the communities of the entire network based on these detected communities. Due to the fact that the MOEA returns a set of communities for each key node, the PMOEA employs an evolutionary algorithm to select a suitable community from the set of communities detected for each key node and then constitutes the community partition of the entire network by using the selected communities. The pseudocode of evolutionary algorithm for determining the community partition of the entire network is presented in Algorithm 5.9.

Algorithm 5.9 consists of four main steps. First, a population ![upper P prime](images/c05-i0432.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is randomly generated, where the individual ![p prime](images/c05-i0433.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is encoded as ![left pointing angle x prime 1 comma x prime 2 comma ellipsis comma x prime Subscript t right pointing angle](images/c05-i0434.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#9001;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#9002;</mo></math>, ![x prime Subscript i Baseline element-of StartSet 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma StartAbsoluteValue script upper C Subscript i Baseline EndAbsoluteValue EndSet](images/c05-i0435.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> represents the community selected from the set of detected communities ![script upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0436.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> of ![i](images/c05-i0437.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th key node, and ![t](images/c05-i0438.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is the number of identified key nodes in network ![upper G](images/c05-i0439.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>. Second, two individuals are randomly selected from the population ![upper P prime](images/c05-i0440.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and then two offsprings are generated by using the one‐point crossover and mutation operators. The mutation operator is conducted by changing each ![x prime Subscript i](images/c05-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> in individual ![p prime](images/c05-i0442.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> with a probability ![m Subscript p Baseline comma i element-of StartSet 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma t EndSet](images/c05-i0443.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. Third, the offsprings will replace their parents if they have better modularity than their parents. The second and third steps will be repeated until the maximum number of generations is reached. Fourth, the community partition ![script upper C](images/c05-i0444.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow></math> of the entire network is improved by using the following strategy. If the similarity between two communities ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0445.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper C Subscript j](images/c05-i0446.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> in ![script upper C](images/c05-i0447.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow></math> is larger than a predefined threshold ![normal alef element-of left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c05-i0448.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#8501;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>, then they are merged into one community. The similarity can be calculated as follows:

where ![StartAbsoluteValue upper C Subscript i Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c05-i0449.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> represents the number of nodes in community ![upper C Subscript i](images/c05-i0450.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>. Moreover, considering that some nodes might not be assigned to any community, we also need to assign each of these nodes to a community to which most of its neighbors have been assigned.

 

### 5.3.4 Time Complexity of PMOEA

For a given complex network with ![n](images/c05-i0451.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> nodes and ![m](images/c05-i0452.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> edges, the PMOEA owns the time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis m a x g e n asterisk p o p asterisk m right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0453.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Specifically, the key node identification step of PMOEA has the time complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis n prime asterisk upper D right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0454.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![upper D](images/c05-i0455.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is the largest degree of nodes in the complex network and ![n prime](images/c05-i0456.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is the number of nodes that have larger degree than the average degree. The time complexity of detecting the communities associated with key nodes is ![upper O left-parenthesis m a x g e n 1 asterisk p o p 1 asterisk left-parenthesis n Subscript c Baseline asterisk upper D plus left-parenthesis n Subscript c Baseline plus m Subscript c Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals upper O left-parenthesis m a x g e n 1 asterisk p o p 1 asterisk n Subscript c Baseline asterisk upper D right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0457.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. It is because that the crossover and mutation operators check at most ![upper O left-parenthesis n Subscript c Baseline asterisk upper D right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0458.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> neighboring nodes for an individual which encodes a community with ![n Subscript c](images/c05-i0459.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></math> nodes and ![m Subscript c](images/c05-i0460.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></math> edges, and the complexity of evaluating such individual is ![upper O left-parenthesis n Subscript c Baseline plus m Subscript c Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0461.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Since the population has ![p o p 1](images/c05-i0462.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> individuals and the maximum number of generations is ![m a x g e n 1](images/c05-i0463.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, the time complexity of the second step is ![upper O left-parenthesis m a x g e n 1 asterisk p o p 1 asterisk left-parenthesis n Subscript c Baseline asterisk upper D plus left-parenthesis n Subscript c Baseline plus m Subscript c Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0464.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. As for the third step, the calculation of modularity for each individual consumes the most computational time, of which time complexity is ![upper O left-parenthesis m a x g e n 2 asterisk p o p 2 asterisk m right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0465.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for an evolutionary algorithm with ![m a x g e n 2](images/c05-i0466.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> generations and ![p o p 2](images/c05-i0467.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> individuals. Assuming that ![m a x g e n equals m a x left-parenthesis m a x g e n 1 comma m a x g e n 2 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0468.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![p o p equals m a x left-parenthesis p o p 1 comma p o p 2 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0469.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><msub><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the PMOEA holds a complexity of ![upper O left-parenthesis m a x g e n asterisk p o p asterisk m right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0470.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, given that ![m](images/c05-i0471.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is usually larger than ![n prime asterisk upper D](images/c05-i0472.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi></math> and ![n Subscript c Baseline asterisk upper D](images/c05-i0473.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>D</mi></math>.

 

### 5.3.5 Experimental Comparisons

To verify the performance of PMOEA, it is compared to eight algorithms tailored for community detection. For these compared algorithms, six of them are evolutionary algorithm‐based algorithms, namely, CoCoMi [\[23\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0023), MOCD [\[13\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0013), MOGA‐net [\[16\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0016), MODPSO [\[14\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0014), QDM‐PSO [\[34\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0034), and PaGeCoDe [\[35\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0035), and two of them are non‐EA‐based algorithms including LET [\[36\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0036) and FOCS [\[37\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0037). The parameters of these algorithms are set to the values recommended in the original references, which are also listed in [Table 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0005). It is worth noting that in the MOEA of PMOEA, the crossover and mutation probabilities are set to 0.9 and 0.6, respectively, and in the EA of PMOEA, the crossover and mutation probabilities are set to 0.6 and 0.01, respectively. Moreover, the parameter ![alpha](images/c05-i0484.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> in PMOEA for merging two communities is set to 0.4 in the experiments.

![Table 5.5  Parameter Setting of the Compared Algorithms, Where p o p is the Population Size, m a x g e n is the Maximum Generations of the Algorithm, c Subscript p is the Probability of Crossover, m Subscript p is the Probability of Mutation, and upper T is the Neighborhood Size.](images/c05-i0479.png)

[**Table 5.5**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-tbl-0005)  Parameter Setting of the Compared Algorithms, Where ![p o p](images/c05-i0474.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> is the Population Size, ![m a x g e n](images/c05-i0475.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></math> is the Maximum Generations of the Algorithm, ![c Subscript p](images/c05-i0476.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the Probability of Crossover, ![m Subscript p](images/c05-i0477.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the Probability of Mutation, and ![upper T](images/c05-i0478.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is the Neighborhood Size.

Two groups of complex networks are used to verify the detection performance of different algorithms. The first group is the synthetic networks which are generated by using the LFR model [\[26\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0026) with nodes ranging from 50,000 to 200,000. The second group is the real‐world networks, including five networks from the Stanford large network dataset [\[29\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0029), namely, *ca‐HepTh2*, *ca‐AstroPh*, *ca‐CondMat*, *loc‐Brightkite*, and *loc‐Gowalla*. The details of these networks are given in [Table 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0006). The evaluation metric used for synthetic networks is the ![upper N upper M upper I](images/c05-i0485.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>I</mi></math> since the ground truth of these networks is known, and the modularity (![upper Q](images/c05-i0486.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>) is adopted for real‐world networks due to the fact that most of them do not have a known ground truth.

[**Table 5.6**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-tbl-0006)  Details of Five Real‐World Networks Used in Experiments.

| Network || Node number || Link number || Average degree |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *ca‐Hepth* || 12,008 || 118,521 || 19.74 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *ca‐AstroPh* || 18,772 || 198,080 || 21.10 |
| *ca‐CondMat* || 23,133 || 93,468 || 8.08 |
| *loc‐Brightkite* || 58,228 || 214,078 || 7.35 |
| *loc‐Gowalla* || 196,591 || 950,327 || 9.67 |

[Table 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0007) presents the detection performance of the PMOEA and the eight compared algorithms on LFR benchmark networks with a size ranging from 50,000 to 200,000. The Wilcoxon rank‐sum test results with a significance level of 0.05 are also given at the bottom of the tables. From [Table 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0007), it can be found that the PMOEA achieves the best detection quality on all LFR networks. On the contrary, most of the evolutionary algorithm‐based compared algorithms cannot obtain results within 17 hours. Although the FOCS owns higher computational efficiency than PMOEA, the detection quality is much worse than PMOEA. [Table 5.8](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0008) lists the detection quality of different algorithms on five real‐world networks, where the PMOEA also holds the best value of ![upper Q](images/c05-i0487.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>. As for the other evolutionary algorithm‐based community detection algorithms, although some of them can complete within 17 hours, the ![upper Q](images/c05-i0488.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> value of their detection results is worse than that of PMOEA. The non‐EA‐based algorithm FOCS consumes less computational time than PMOEA, but its detection quality is inferior to that of the PMOEA. Hence, it can be concluded that the PMOEA owns a good scalability for large‐scale complex networks in terms of both efficiency and detection performance.

## 5.4 Summary

This chapter presents two ideas of enhancing the scalability of MOEAs in solving the community detection problems for large‐scale complex networks, and two MOEAs, namely, RMOEA and PMOEA, are developed based on the ideas. The RMOEA utilizes the local communities detected during the evolution to reduce the size of complex networks, so that the scalability of MOEA to large‐scale complex networks can be considerately enhanced. The PMOEA is based on the idea of parallelization to tackle large‐scale complex networks, where the community detection of the entire network is decomposed into detecting the communities associated with a number of key nodes performed in parallel. Although the reduction and parallelization are two widely used technologies for large‐scale optimization, there are many other technologies that can be used to deal with large‐scale optimization, such as decomposition [\[38\]](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0038) and search enhancement \[[39](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0039), [40](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0040)\]. In the following chapters, a number of MOEAs with different strategies to tackle the large‐scale optimization in other applications are presented.
