# 6  
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization in Logistics Scheduling

 

## 6.1 Introduction

Logistics has been known as an important foundation of worldwide economic development and thus widely exists in social life [\[1\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0001). A good logistics scheduling plan guarantees that the materials flow fluently in a logistics system and significantly contributes to economic growth [\[2\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0002). Hence, logistics scheduling remains a hot research field over decades, which involves a large variety of optimization problems: facility location, vehicle routing, and container loading, to name a few \[[3](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0003)–[5](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0005)\]. A large number of algorithms have been developed to address these optimization problems, which are roughly categorized into two groups: exact algorithms and heuristic ones. Exact algorithms often formulate logistics scheduling problems as mathematical programming models that can be iteratively computed, such as linear programming models or dynamic programming models [\[6\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0006). Heuristic algorithms iteratively seek optimal solutions in the search space of logistics scheduling problems in a flexible way [\[7\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0007). Exact algorithms are often able to obtain the optimal solution of a small‐scale single‐objective logistics scheduling problem at an acceptable computational cost. Nevertheless, they can barely obtain high‐quality solutions for a large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problem, which typically formulates a multi‐objective problem as a single‐objective optimization model by a weighted method and neglects a potential conflict between multiple objectives. Thereafter, heuristic algorithms are developed to solve multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems due to their capability of simultaneously optimizing multiple objectives, which, however, still have difficulty in addressing large‐scale multi‐objective problems. Due to the NP‐hard characteristic of many logistics scheduling problems, a large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problem generally has a huge solution search space, which hinders many existing heuristic algorithms from obtaining satisfying solutions at an acceptable computational cost.

Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are a type of popular metaheuristic algorithms and have exhibited good performance in addressing multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems \[[8](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0008), [9](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0009)\]. Due to the fact that EAs are population‐based searching methods, they are able to simultaneously optimize multiple objectives by searching in multiple directions in the decision space. Nevertheless, it is still difficult for EAs to handle large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems, since the performance of an EA considerably deteriorates with the rapid growth of problem size. This motivates many researchers to improve EAs for large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems, and this chapter presents two state‐of‐the‐art EAs for two typical large‐scale multi‐objective logistics scheduling problems: an evolutionary multi‐objective route grouping‐based heuristic algorithm (EMRG‐HA) for the vehicle routing problem (VRP) [\[10\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010) and a clustering‐based surrogate‐assisted multi‐objective EA with reference point adaptation (AR‐MOEA+SA) for the facility location problem (FLP) [\[4\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0004). The VRP presented in this chapter is the classic and basic capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), which serves as a reliable testbed for many VRP optimization algorithms. The FLP presented in this chapter is a real‐world application in emergency management: the uncertain shelter location problem (USLP).

 

## 6.2 Evolutionary Multi‐Objective Route Grouping‐Based Heuristic Algorithm for Large‐Scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems

The task of a typical CVRP is to plan the optimal traveling routes with the lowest traveling cost for a fleet of vehicles so as to serve a set of customers with known demands, where all the vehicles are assumed to be homogeneous and thus have the same capacity. The large‐scale capacitated vehicle routing problem (LSCVRP) refers to the CVRP with thousands of customers to be served, which is challenging and draws much attention from CVRP researchers \[[11](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0011)–[14](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0014)\]. Particularly, the idea of divide‐and‐conquer has been widely used in developing large‐scale optimization algorithms by decomposing a large‐scale optimization problem into some small sub‐components that can be easily and independently solved \[[15](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0015), [16](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0016)\]. In the field of large‐scale logistics scheduling, the idea of divide‐and‐conquer is mainly used in two ways: to geographically decompose customers into groups of customers \[[17](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0017), [18](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0018)\] or to decompose routes into groups of routes for service of different vehicles \[[19](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0019), [20](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0020)\]. Regardless of the studies that use divide‐and‐conquer for LSCVRPs, many of these studies fail to produce a good decomposition for either customers or routes \[[18](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0018), [21](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0021)\]. The customer‐decomposition strategies could easily result in that customers served by the same vehicles in the optimal routes cannot be divided into a group, since the customers are divided into groups based on their geographical locations. For the route‐decomposition strategies, they are often hard to achieve a good decomposition since the clustering of routes is more difficult than the clustering of customers, especially for the definition of intraclustering and interclustering distances for routes.

Thereafter, this section presents a divide‐and‐conquer‐based heuristic algorithm EMRG‐HA for solving LSCVRPs, which reports an evolutionary multi‐objective route grouping method to achieve promising decomposition for LSCVRPs [\[22\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0022). By exploiting the advantage of evolutionary multi‐objective optimization, the route grouping method mathematically formulates a typical CVRP as a tri‐objective model by simultaneously optimizing the intra‐group similarity, inter‐group similarity and inter‐group balance. The three objectives guide the optimization of LSCVRPs to find high‐quality route groupings with low inter‐group similarity, high intra‐group similarity and inter‐group balance. Because of the fact that route groupings have a great influence on the quality of routes, the high‐quality route groupings thus can lead to high‐quality routes in the optimization of LSCVRPs.

In the following, we first present the formal definition of CVRP, then the EMRG‐HA for solving LSCVRPs is elaborated. Finally, experimental comparisons between the EMRG‐HA and state‐of‐the‐art approaches for CVRPs are presented and discussed.

The sixth constraint is the capacity constraint of a vehicle that already serves a customer.

 

### 6.2.2 Evolutionary Multi‐Objective Route Grouping Method

To obtain promising route groupings, EMRG‐HA uses an evolutionary tri‐objective optimization‐based route grouping method, termed EMRG, in the optimization of LSCVRPs. The three optimization objectives, namely, the intra‐group similarity, the inter‐group similarity and inter‐group balance, are adopted to guarantee that the EMRG finds promising route groupings in the optimization of LSCVRPs. Specifically, minimizing the intra‐group similarity ensures that the routes in the same group are similar enough to be served by the same vehicle, while maximizing the inter‐group similarity enables that the routes in different groups are different enough from each other to be served by different vehicles. Minimizing the inter‐group balance makes sure that EMRG achieves balanced route groupings so as to adapt the use of vehicles. Formally, the three optimization objectives are defined as follows.

The third objective minimizes the inter‐group balance in size, i.e., the difference of number of customers between groups. The third objective guarantees that each group in grouping ![script í’ž](images/c06-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54430;</mi></mrow></math> holds a similar number of customers so as to achieve a balanced grouping. For optimization of the above three objectives, EMRG‐HA employs a classical multi‐objective EA NSGA‐II [\[24\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0024). The pseudocode of the EMRG is presented in Algorithm 6.1.

For a grouping of ![k](images/c06-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> routes, EMRG‐HA encodes it as a vector ![left pointing angle x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript k Baseline comma y 1 comma ellipsis comma y Subscript k Baseline right pointing angle](images/c06-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo></math>, where ![x Subscript i](images/c06-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> (![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to k](images/c06-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>) denotes a real number in ![left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![y Subscript i](images/c06-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> (![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to k](images/c06-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>) denotes a nonnegative integer that is not larger than ![k](images/c06-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>. There are two components in the encoding: the first component ![left pointing angle x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript k Baseline right pointing angle](images/c06-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> indicates the fitness value of each route in sorting and the second component ![left pointing angle y 1 comma ellipsis comma y Subscript k Baseline right pointing angle](images/c06-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#9001;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> represents the grouping of the ![k](images/c06-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> routes. The ![x Subscript i](images/c06-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> denotes the fitness value of the ![i](images/c06-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th route in sorting. The ![y Subscript i](images/c06-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> indicates that the routes whose fitness values ranked from the ![left-parenthesis y 1 plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus y Subscript i minus 1 Baseline plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>th to the ![left-parenthesis y 1 plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>th are allocated in one group ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to k](images/c06-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>.

[Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0001) takes the individual ![left pointing angle 0.51 comma 0.39 comma 0.71 comma 0.89 comma 0.10 comma 3 comma 1 comma 2 comma 4 comma 2 right pointing angle](images/c06-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#9001;</mo><mn>0.51</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.39</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.71</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.89</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#9002;</mo></math> as an example, where a grouping of five routes denoted as ![upper R 1 comma ellipsis comma upper R 5](images/c06-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></math> are encoded. Hence, the five routes are decomposed into three groups in this individual, i.e., the groups ![StartSet upper R 1 comma upper R 2 comma upper R 5 EndSet](images/c06-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, ![left-brace upper R 3 right-brace](images/c06-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, and ![left-brace upper R 4 right-brace](images/c06-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. The first group of routes ![StartSet upper R 1 comma upper R 2 comma upper R 5 EndSet](images/c06-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is produced since ![y 1 equals 3](images/c06-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, indicating that the three routes with the first, second, and third minimum fitness values (namely, ![upper R 1](images/c06-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![upper R 2](images/c06-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and ![upper R 5](images/c06-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></math>) are allocated in a group. The second group of routes ![left-brace upper R 3 right-brace](images/c06-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is obtained due to ![y 2 equals 1](images/c06-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, and the route ![upper R 3](images/c06-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math> with the fourth minimum fitness value is allocated to one group. The third group of routes ![left-brace upper R 4 right-brace](images/c06-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> is obtained because ![y 3 equals 2](images/c06-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, which means that the routes with the fifth and sixth minimum fitness values are allocated in a group. Since the number of routes is five, the route ![upper R 4](images/c06-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></math> with the fifth minimum fitness value is finally allocated in one group. The assignment of all five routes to the groups is then finished, and thus ![y 4 equals 4](images/c06-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math> and ![y 5 equals 2](images/c06-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> is not considered in the individual. The encoding scheme can hinder the produced offspring to be trapped in local optima due to the single‐point crossover adopted in the EMRG. Therefore, there is no need to adopt a mutation operator in EMRG.

![Figure 6.1 An illustrative example of the encoding scheme.](images/c06f001.png)

### 6.2.3 Framework of EMRG‐HA

[Figure 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0002) illustrates the overall procedure of EMRG‐HA that integrates the evolutionary multi‐objective route grouping into the search process for solving LSCVRPs. As can be observed from the figure, integrating the route grouping into the search process guarantees that the route groupings can be flexibly adapted and updated based on route quality, due to the fact that the intra‐group similarity, inter‐group similarity, and inter‐group balance are continuously optimized for subsequent promising groupings. Furthermore, the route quality is in return improved with the quality improvement of grouping during the optimization process. More detailed steps of EMRG‐HA are presented in Algorithm 6.3, which mainly consists of three steps.

overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. Second, EMRG‐HA performs the evolutionary multi‐objective optimization‐based route grouping method EMRG to produce a set of groupings for routes of solution ![p](images/c06-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. Third, EMRG‐HA conducts the tabu search based local search in the produced route groupings so as to improve the quality of solution ![p](images/c06-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. The same operations for the improved solution in the above two steps will repeat until the termination criterion of EMRG‐HA is satisfied. Otherwise, the obtained solution will be output as the final solution for the LSCVRP. With the improvement of solution quality during the evolution, the EMRG‐HA is able to dynamically adapt the ingredients of decomposed subcomponents in the search process via the route grouping.

For the route grouping in each solution, a tabu search‐based local search (TS‐LS) is employed to improve the route quality in the groups of the grouping, which is presented in Algorithm 6.2. First, the TS‐LS randomly selects ![left floor delta times StartAbsoluteValue upper R upper G upper S e t EndAbsoluteValue right floor](images/c06-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8970;</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8971;</mo></math> groupings from ![upper R upper G upper S e t](images/c06-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mi>G</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, where ![delta](images/c06-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></math> is used to control the number of groupings for reducing computational cost of TS‐LS. Second, for each of the randomly selected groupings, the TS‐LS selects one group via the roulette wheel method to apply local search to customers in the group. Third, TS‐LS applies the tabu search to improve the route quality for each of the selected groups, where three operators: single insertion, swap, and 2‐opt, are randomly selected for route quality improvement. The local search is performed for ![t](images/c06-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> times for one group of routes. Finally, the routes improved by tabu search replace those in the selected group and a new solution thus is obtained for each grouping.

 

### 6.2.4 Experimental Comparisons

This section verifies the competitiveness of EMRG‐HA by comparing it with five state‐of‐the‐art algorithms for addressing LSCVRPs in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

The comparisons utilize two commonly used benchmark test sets for LSCVRPs: a set of 20 LSCVRP benchmark instances suggested by Golden *et al*. in [\[25\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0025) ranging from 240 to 483 customers (denoted as G1 to G20), and a set of 12 benchmark instances suggested by Li *et al*. in [\[26\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0026) ranging from 560 to 1200 customers (denoted as L1 to L12). Five existing heuristic algorithms for solving LSCVRPs are used as compared algorithms of EMRG‐HA, namely, hybrid genetic search with adaptive diversity control (HGSADC) [\[27\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0027), cooperative parallel metaheuristic (CPM) [\[28\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0028), parallel random record‐to‐record (PRRTR) [\[29\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0029), fixed‐J quantum annealing (FJ‐QA) [\[30\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0030), and variable neighbourhood simulated annealing (VNSA) [\[31\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0031). All the parameters of each of the compared algorithms are set to the same values that are suggested in their original references. For EMRG‐HA, the maximum number of iterations is set to 30. For EMRG in EMRG‐HA, the population size is set to 50 and the maximum number of iterations is set to 100. [Table 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0002) presents the parameter settings in EMRG‐HA. For fair comparisons, all algorithms are programmed in Matlab and executed on the CPU Intel Core i5‐7500 with 3.4 GHz and 16 GB memory.

![Table 6.2  The Parameter Settings in the Proposed EMRG‐HA.](images/c06-i0139.png)

[**Table 6.2**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-tbl-0002)  The Parameter Settings in the Proposed EMRG‐HA.

Tables [6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0003) and [6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0004) present the best traveling cost achieved by EMRG‐HA and 5 compared algorithms on 20 test instances of Golden *et al*. and 12 test instances of Li *et al*. over 20 independent runs, in which the best values achieved by the compared algorithms refer to their original references. The best‐known traveling cost for each instance is given in Tables [6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0003) and [6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0004) and the result for each algorithm represents the gap between the result achieved by the algorithm and the best‐known result. Hence, the result 0 means that the algorithm achieves the best‐known result, and “+” (“![minus](images/c06-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>”) indicates that the value is worse (better) than the best‐known result.

![Table 6.3  The Best Serving Cost Obtained by the Proposed EMRG‐HA and Five Compared Algorithms on the 20 Test Instances of Golden et al. Benchmarks.](images/c06-i0147.png)

[**Table 6.3**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-tbl-0003)  The Best Serving Cost Obtained by the Proposed EMRG‐HA and Five Compared Algorithms on the 20 Test Instances of Golden *et al*. Benchmarks.

![Table 6.4  The Best Serving Cost Obtained by the Proposed EMRG‐HA and Five Compared Algorithms on the 12 Test Instances of Li et al. Benchmarks.](images/c06-i0170.png)

[**Table 6.4**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-tbl-0004)  The Best Serving Cost Obtained by the Proposed EMRG‐HA and Five Compared Algorithms on the 12 Test Instances of Li *et al*. Benchmarks.

It can be observed from Tables [6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0003) and [6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0004) that EMRG‐HA can achieve the best‐known traveling cost on most LSCVRP test instances. Specifically, EMRG‐HA achieves the best‐known traveling cost on 16 of 20 Golden test instances, and it achieves the best‐known traveling cost on 7 instances of 12 Li test instances. Furthermore, EMRG‐HA produces a new best result on some test instances in comparison with the current best‐known result, i.e., the instance (G10) in Golden *et al*. benchmarks and the instance (L12) in Li *et al*. benchmarks. Thereafter, it can be concluded that the performance of EMRG‐HA is overall superior over five compared algorithms on the 32 LSCVRP test instances. Both HGSADC and CPM also have a competitive performance, despite that they fail to find a low traveling cost in a few instances, such as instances L2 and L5. It can be also found in Tables [6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0003) and [6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0004) that EMRG‐HA is computationally efficient in addressing LSCVRPs. To this end, EMRG‐HA is competitive in solving LSCVRPs in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

 

## 6.3 Clustering‐Based Surrogate‐Assisted Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Shelter Location Problem Under Uncertainty of Road Networks

Over the years, the USLP has attracted many researchers from a variety of fields due to its importance in tackling the threat of natural disasters, such as earthquakes, hurricanes, and tsunamis \[[32](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0032), [33](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0033)\]. There are two tasks for a shelter location problem, namely, selecting sites for shelter construction and assigning evacuees to shelters \[[34](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0034), [35](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0035)\]. The two tasks are obviously in conflict with each other since it is expected that less construction cost can be used to achieve a smaller evacuation distance from residential communities to shelters. The large‐scale uncertain shelter location problem (LSUSLP) refers to the USLP that contains hundreds of residential communities to be assigned, which is difficult to solve because it is computationally expensive to evaluate a solution for a USLP. One solution evaluation needs to compute the average traveling cost over a set of simulated damage scenarios. Since EAs are population‐based optimization algorithms, it will cost much computational budget to evaluate solutions at each generation of an EA optimization. Regardless of the wide applications of EAs in solving FLPs, few studies have been reported for LSUSLPs by using EAs \[[36](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0036)–[38](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0038)\].

This section introduces a surrogate‐assisted EA, termed AR‐MOEA+SA, for efficiently addressing LSUSLPs by using a surrogate modeling strategy [\[39\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0039). The surrogate modeling strategy helps create computationally cheap function evaluation that well approximates the computationally expensive exact function evaluation, to replace the exact evaluation with the approximate one. In this case, the computational efficiency of solving LSUSLPs can be significantly improved to obtain high‐quality solutions for LSUSLPs at a low computational cost.

In this section, we first give the mathematical formulation of USLP, then the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method and framework of ARMOEA+SA are detailed. Finally, experimental comparisons between AR‐MOEA+SA and state‐of‐the‐art approaches for USLPs are presented and comparison results are discussed.

 

### 6.3.1 Problem Formulation

The task of USLP is to select a set of shelters from candidate shelters for construction, to achieve that the traveling distance between evacuees and selected shelters are shortest in both undamage and damage road network scenarios, and the shelter construction cost is as low as possible. It is assumed that there are ![upper L](images/c06-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> candidate shelters, ![upper M](images/c06-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> residential communities and a defined road network between ![upper L](images/c06-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> candidate shelters and ![upper M](images/c06-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> communities. Each road in the defined road network holds a probability to be broken, and the probability for each road is generally obtained based on properties of the road, such as the collapse resistance and quality of buildings along the road, etc. The notations used in the USLP formulation are presented in [Table 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0005), and the USLP is formulated as follows:

The three optimization objectives minimize the construction area for the selected shelters, the total evacuation distance in the undamage scenario, and that in the damage scenario, respectively. The objective ![f 3](images/c06-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math> is computationally expensive since the roads in the road network will be randomly damaged under their breaking probability in the damage scenario. Hence, a number of damage scenarios are necessary for estimating the evacuation distance in the damage scenario in one individual evaluation.

The first constraint ensures that the population assigned to each shelter does not exceed the capacity of the shelter, the second constraint guarantees that the traveling distance of each community is equal to or smaller than the maximum distance, and the third constraint represents that each community will be exactly assigned to one shelter.

 

### 6.3.2 Clustering‐Based Surrogate Modeling Method

The AR‐MOEA+SA utilizes a surrogate modeling method to conduct computationally cheap function evaluation which approximates the original computationally expensive exact one. Surrogates are a popular method to replace time‐consuming exact function evaluations in an EA optimization and thus leads to significant efficiency improvement of EA optimization. Nevertheless, it is difficult for most existing surrogate‐assisted EAs to accurately train a surrogate model with hundreds of dimensions, since training a high‐dimensional high‐accuracy surrogate model needs a very large amount of training data which are often hard to obtain in optimization process of EAs. Hence, AR‐MOEA+SA adopts a clustering‐based surrogate modeling method to transform the high‐dimensional LSUSLP decision variables into low‐dimensional ones before training a surrogate model, which effectively approximates original function evaluation and guarantees high efficiency in addressing LSUSLPs.

The procedure of the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method is shown in [Fig. 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0003). The surrogate modeling method first selects non‐dominated individuals from current population via non‐dominated sorting. Next, the surrogate modeling method uses a clustering‐based strategy on the non‐dominated individuals in order to convert them into data points of low dimensions. Then, the surrogate modeling method updates the training data using the converted data points and an RBF network model is built by training on data. Finally, the surrogate modeling method uses the built RBF network model to evaluate the offsprings reproduced from current parent population. Note that here the clustering‐based strategy is also used to convert the offsprings into individuals of low dimensions, which is presented in Algorithm 6.4. Much sample data are necessary for effective surrogate modeling, which may be not affordable since the USLP generally holds hundreds of decision variables. Hence, a clustering‐based strategy is suggested in AR‐MOEA+SA to build the surrogate model at a low computational budget via converting the modeling of high dimensions into the one of low dimensions for the USLP. Specifically, [Fig. 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0004) illustrates the process of building a surrogate model by clustering. The candidate shelters are clustered into multiple groups based on the geography locations of shelters. For each individual found in AR‐MOEA+SA optimization, the residential communities are covered by the groups according to the shelter coverage situation in the individual. This is because of the fact that the residential communities covered by one group are often assigned to another shelter in the same group if they cannot be evacuated to the original assigned shelter in a damage scenario. The assignment of communities in each group can thus be regarded as a whole that is represented by the total evacuation distance in this group.

![Figure 6.3 The main procedure of the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method.](images/c06f003.png)

[**Figure 6.3**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0003) The main procedure of the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method.

![Figure 6.4 Illustration of the clustering‐based strategy for building the surrogate model.](images/c06f004.png)

[**Figure 6.4**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0004) Illustration of the clustering‐based strategy for building the surrogate model.

The surrogate model built using the above method should be continuously updated, due to the fact that a fixed surrogate model often works only in the cases where the decision space has very low dimensions and the training data used in the surrogate modeling is quite sufficient. The surrogate update also refers to model management in surrogate‐assisted EAs, which needs to handle two issues: when is the surrogate updated and which individuals in current population are selected for updating the surrogate. Specifically, Algorithm 6.5 presents the pseudocode of model management in the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method.

 

### 6.3.3 Procedure of AR‐MOEA+SA

Based on the clustering‐based surrogate modeling method, AR‐MOEA+SA uses a state‐of‐the‐art multi‐objective EA, termed AR‐MOEA that is proposed in [\[40\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0040). The AR‐MOEA is an indicator‐based multi‐objective EA using a performance indicator of inverted generational distance with noncontributing solution detection IGD‐NS [\[40\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0040). Specifically, Algorithm 6.6 shows the procedure of AR‐MOEA+SA, which employs the radial basis function (RBF) as the surrogate model and adopts the Gaussian function as the basis function for RBF network. There are six main steps in the procedure of AR‐MOEA+SA.

First, AR‐MOEA+SA performs the initialization of population and surrogate model, which uses the clustering strategy to convert the initial population into initial training data for surrogate modeling. Based on the initial training data, a surrogate model is built and an archive is created to store all individuals under exact evaluations. Second, AR‐MOEA+SA performs the uniform crossover and mutation to produce offsprings from current parent population. Third, AR‐MOEA+SA uses the latest surrogate model to approximately evaluate each individual in the offspring population. Fourth, AR‐MOEA+SA utilizes the environmental selection in AR‐MOEA to select the parent population in next generation, which is based on the approximate evaluation results of individuals to be selected. Fifth, AR‐MOEA+SA updates the surrogate model according to the model management method presented in Algorithm 6.5, and the training data and the archive are also updated. The second to the fifth steps repeat until the termination criterion is satisfied. Finally, AR‐MOEA+SA averagely reevaluates the individuals from the archive on a set of 100 randomly generated damage scenarios so as to alleviate the influence of randomness. The non‐dominated individuals that are identified based on the reevaluations are obtained from the archive and regarded as the final result achieved by AR‐MOEA+SA.

 

### 6.3.4 Experimental Comparisons

In this section, we evaluate the performance of AR‐MOEA+SA in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency by comparing it with four state‐of‐the‐art algorithms for USLPs.

A set of four USLP test instances are used as test instances for all the compared algorithms, which consist of three simulated numerical instances and one real case. Particularly, three simulated test instances are created on the basis of the parameter settings in [Table 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0006), in which the community scale varies from small, medium to large. Four compared algorithms are utilized for comparisons with AR‐MOEA+SA, namely, a mathematical programming method BD [\[33\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0033), an EA MNSGA‐II [\[41\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0041), a surrogate‐based optimization algorithm SA‐COSO [\[42\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0042), and AR‐MOEA without the surrogate modeling method [\[40\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0040).

![Table 6.6  Parameter Setting of Instances A, B, C, and the Real Case.](images/c06-i0219.png)

[**Table 6.6**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-tbl-0006)  Parameter Setting of Instances A, B, C, and the Real Case.

The population size for AR‐MOEA+SA is set to 100, while the two sub‐populations in SA‐COSO/MNSGA‐II are set to hold 80 individuals and 20 ones, respectively. Each algorithm that uses uniform crossover and mutation operators holds a crossover probability of 0.8 and a mutation probability of ![1 slash d](images/c06-i0222.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>d</mi></math>, where ![d](images/c06-i0223.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is the number of decision variables. For RBF in AR‐MOEA+SA, the size of hidden nodes is set to 6, and the scale of training data is set to ![d Subscript x Baseline asterisk 12](images/c06-i0224.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, in which ![d Subscript x](images/c06-i0225.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></math> indicates the data dimension. The results for each of MNSGA‐II, SA‐COSO, and AR‐MOEA+SA are obtained after 20 independent runs of the corresponding algorithm. All the experiments are performed on a PC with a 3.40 GHz Intel Core i7 CPU 6700 and the Windows 7 SP1 64 bit operating system.

[Table 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0007) presents the evacuation distances obtained by five compared algorithms on the four instances, averaging over 20 independent runs. For highlighting the performance of AR‐MOEA+SA, three non‐surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms BD, AR‐MOEA, and MNSGA‐II are performed for 20,000 exact function evaluations, while two surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms AR‐MOEA+SA and SA‐COSO are performed for 2000 exact function evaluations.

It can be observed from [Table 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0007) that AR‐MOEA+SA overall achieves the best performance in terms of the evacuation distances for both the undamage and damage scenarios on all test instances in comparison with four compared algorithms. Furthermore, AR‐MOEA+SA also uses the smallest shelter construction cost on all instances. Considering that the above results of AR‐MOEA+SA are obtained after only 2000 exact evaluations, AR‐MOEA+SA in fact achieves the best performance on all instances by using significantly less computational cost in comparison with non‐surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms BD, MNSGA‐II, and AR‐MOEA.

For a deeper insight into the computational efficiency of AR‐MOEA, [Table 6.8](#c06.xhtml#c06-tbl-0008) lists the runtime(s) of four compared algorithms and AR‐MOEA+SA on four instances, where three non‐surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms still are performed for 20,000 exact evaluations, and two surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms are performed for 2000 exact ones. It can be seen from the table that the two surrogate‐assisted compared algorithms AR‐MOEA+SA and SA‐COSO achieve the highest computational efficiency on all instances in comparison with the other three non‐surrogate‐assisted ones. This is because of the fact that the two surrogate‐assisted algorithms use a considerable number of computationally efficient approximate evaluations to replace computationally expensive ones during their evolution, which thus leads to high computational efficiency of the two algorithms.

| C || 3.87e+5 || 4.10e+5 || 4.27e+5 || 4.19e+4 || **3.91e+4** |
| Real case || 1.23e+6 || 1.52e+6 || 1.70e+6 || 1.58e+5 || **1.43e+5** |

Furthermore, [Fig. 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005) shows the number of exact function evaluations performed by AR‐MOEA, MNSGA‐II, SA‐COSO, and AR‐MOEA+SA on four instances with the growth of running generations. It can be observed from [Fig. 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005) that the two non‐surrogate‐assisted algorithms AR‐MOEA and MNSGA‐II perform much more exact evaluations than the two surrogate‐assisted algorithms SA‐COSO and AR‐MOEA+SA when they are in the same generations. This further validates that AR‐MOEA+SA is efficient in addressing computationally expensive LSUSLPs.

![Figure 6.5 (a–d) Number of exact function evaluations of AR‐MOEA, MNSGA‐II, SA‐COSO, and AR‐MOEA+SA on instances A, B, C, and the real case under different generations.](images/c06f005.png)

[**Figure 6.5**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0005) (a–d) Number of exact function evaluations of AR‐MOEA, MNSGA‐II, SA‐COSO, and AR‐MOEA+SA on instances A, B, C, and the real case under different generations.

It can also be seen from [Fig. 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005) that AR‐MOEA+SA performs more exact evaluations than the other surrogate‐assisted algorithm SA‐COSO when they are at the same generations. Nevertheless, AR‐MOEA+SA contrarily takes less runtime than SA‐COSO on all instances, which is exhibited in [Fig. 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0006). The reason lies in the fact that the surrogate model training of AR‐MOEA+SA consumes much less time than that of SA‐COSO during their evolution. The surrogate model training of SA‐COSO assists in creating approximate evaluations that have much cheaper computational cost than exact ones, which is, however, relatively more expensive than the model training of AR‐MOEA+SA. As a result, it is still necessary to develop surrogate‐assisted EAs that simultaneously hold high model precision and cheap training cost.

![Figure 6.6 (a–d) Computational time (s) of training of SA‐COSO and AR‐MOEA+SA on instances A, B, C, and the real case.](images/c06f006.png)

[**Figure 6.6**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0006) (a–d) Computational time (s) of training of SA‐COSO and AR‐MOEA+SA on instances A, B, C, and the real case.

In summary, it can be drawn from the comparison results that AR‐MOEA+SA is an effective and efficient optimization algorithm for solving LSUSLPs in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

 

## 6.4 Summary

This chapter presents a CVRP optimization algorithm and a USLP optimization algorithm for solving LSCVRPs and USLPs, respectively. Specifically, a divide‐and‐conquer‐based heuristic algorithm, EMRG‐HA is introduced for solving LSCVRPs, where an evolutionary multi‐objective route grouping method called EMRG is developed to perform the grouping of a set of given routes. The competitiveness of EMRG‐HA has also been empirically verified by comparing it with five existing heuristic algorithms for LSCVRPs in terms of both computational efficiency and solution quality.

A clustering‐based surrogate‐assisted multi‐objective EA, termed AR‐MOEA+SA, is detailed for addressing USLPs. To build an effective surrogate model for the LSUSLP, in the AR‐MOEA+SA, a clustering‐based strategy is developed to convert the surrogate modeling of high‐dimensional problem into one of low‐dimensional problem. Comparison with four state‐of‐the‐art facility location optimization algorithms demonstrates the superiority of AR‐MOEA+SA in effectively and efficiently addressing USLPs.

# 7  
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization in Power Systems

 

## 7.1 Introduction

Power systems are becoming increasingly complex due to rapid advancements in technology and the growing need for efficient, reliable, and sustainable energy management. This complexity is further intensified by the integration of renewable energy sources, distributed generation, and smart grid technologies. Managing and optimizing power systems necessitate addressing multiple objectives simultaneously, as various aspects of system performance, such as power generation, transmission, distribution, and consumption, are often interconnected and interdependent.

In order to effectively tackle these challenges, advanced optimization techniques are required that can capture the intricate relationships between multiple objectives and provide high‐quality solutions for the diverse array of problems encountered in power systems. Evolutionary algorithms are population‐based meta‐heuristics optimization algorithms, which are capable of obtaining a set of trade‐off solutions in a single run and less vulnerable to local optima. In the past few decades, evolutionary algorithms have demonstrated remarkable success in solving multi‐objective optimization problems across a wide range of domains. However, their performance usually deteriorates considerably when they are used to address large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems (LSMOPs), which is attributed to the curse of dimensionality. In fact, the curse of dimensionality is also widely present in power systems. After all, the optimization problems in power systems usually have tens of thousands of or even more decision variables to be optimized.

This chapter presents an in‐depth exploration of evolutionary algorithms applied to power systems, with a particular focus on a case study involving the ratio error estimation of voltage transformers (VTs). In the case study, first, we discuss the importance of ratio error estimation of VTs and the limitations of existing methods. Then, we introduce the time‐varying ratio error estimation (TREE) method as an innovative solution to address the shortcomings of existing methods. Next, we present a data‐driven approach for formulating the TREE problem as a LSMOP, detailing the process of extracting statistical and physical principles from power distribution systems. Finally, a problem knowledge‐driven coevolutionary algorithm is designed to solve the TREE problems, demonstrating the potential of evolutionary algorithms in addressing complex real‐world problems in power systems.

 

## 7.2 Ratio Error Estimation of Voltage Transformers

 

### 7.2.1 Problem Introduction

VTs are fundamental devices widely employed in industrial power delivery systems, particularly in substations, for measuring voltage values.

The ratio error (RE) of a VT can be mathematically expressed as [\[5\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0005)

In this substation, the RE can be calculated based on one of the primary voltage values, such as ![left-parenthesis upper A Subscript i Baseline minus upper A 0 right-parenthesis slash upper A 0](images/c07-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![left-parenthesis upper B Subscript i Baseline minus upper B 0 right-parenthesis slash upper B 0](images/c07-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math>, or ![left-parenthesis upper C Subscript i Baseline minus upper C 0 right-parenthesis slash upper C 0](images/c07-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math>.

[**Figure 7.1**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0001) The diagram of the VTs in a representative power delivery system, where ![upper A 0 comma upper B 0 comma upper C 0](images/c07-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![a 0 comma b 0 comma c 0](images/c07-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></math> are the true primary and secondary three‐phase voltage values, respectively. Note that, the primary side and the secondary side are connected by the power transformer.

To obtain the REs of VTs, there are primarily two types of methods: calibration methods and data‐driven estimation methods. Calibration is conducted by de‐energizing the power and manually comparing the uncalibrated VT with the standard one [\[6\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0006). Typical methods include off‐line and on‐site calibrations \[[7](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0007)–[9](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0009)\]. In contrast, data‐driven estimation methods construct specific models of the VTs and estimate the REs based on constraints derived from the electrical relationship and data collected from VTs, such as the adaptive detection method [\[10\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0010) and the line parameter estimation method [\[11\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0011). However, both calibration and data‐driven estimation methods suffer from practical deficiencies. While calibration methods provide accurate REs under standard working conditions, they are expensive in terms of time and cost and must be used periodically [\[6\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0006). For instance, most substations conduct calibration every four years or even longer, resulting in economic losses (e.g., over 0.3 million CNY) and taking a long time (e.g., more than one day) [\[12\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0012). As for data‐driven estimation methods, despite their lower cost, their accuracy and versatility are unsatisfactory due to the limitations of the VT‐specific models \[[13](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0013), [14](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0014)\].

To address the challenges associated with existing calibration and data‐driven methods, [Section 7.2.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0005) will introduce an innovative method that formulates the TREE problem as an LSMOP by taking into account the differences between the true voltage values and those measured by the VTs. Similar to calibration, the primary goal of the formulated problem is to estimate the true voltage values. The proposed method offers significant advantages over calibration and data‐driven error estimation methods, including reduced costs and enhanced versatility.

 

### 7.2.2 Data‐Driven Problem Formulation

 

#### 7.2.2.1 Overview of the Problem Formulation

In this section, we present the data‐driven problem formulation for six different TREE (TREE1 to TREE6) problems as LSMOPs with inequality constraints. These problems are categorized into three types based on the involved data: data with primary voltage values only (Type 1), data with both primary and secondary voltage values (Type 2), and data with both voltage and phase angle values (Type 3). [Figure 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0002) illustrates the primary/secondary voltage values or the phase angle values measured by the uncalibrated VTs for each problem.

![Figure 7.2 Primary/secondary voltage (PV and SV, respectively) values or phase angle values of TREE1 to TREE6 problems measured by real‐world uncalibrated VTs. Dimension number denotes the sample index of the measurement.](images/c07f002.png)

[**Figure 7.2**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0002) Primary/secondary voltage (PV and SV, respectively) values or phase angle values of TREE1 to TREE6 problems measured by real‐world uncalibrated VTs. Dimension number denotes the sample index of the measurement.

We use three symbols, ![upper K](images/c07-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, ![upper P](images/c07-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>, and ![upper T](images/c07-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, to formulate the TREE problems, with detailed settings provided in [Table 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-tbl-0001). ![upper K](images/c07-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> represents the total number of primary and/or secondary voltage phases, ![upper P](images/c07-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of VT sets involved in the problem, and ![upper T](images/c07-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is the length of the measured sequential data.

![Table 7.1  Settings of upper M, upper J, upper K, upper P, upper T, and the Type of Involved Data for Each TREE Problem, Where upper M and upper J Denote the Numbers of Objectives and Constraints, Respectively.](images/c07-i0038.png)

In the formulation of the TREE problems, the decision variables are defined as follows:

In [Sections 7.2.2.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0008) and [7.2.2.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0009), we present the details of the objective and constraint functions for the TREE problems.

 

#### 7.2.2.2 Objective Functions

The TREE problem involves three objective functions, which are formulated based on the relationship between the true voltage values and the measurements obtained from the VTs. A smaller objective value implies a better estimation accuracy for each objective function.

**(1) Total time‐varying REs**

The first objective is the total time‐varying relative errors (REs) of all uncalibrated VTs, which indicates the degree of matching between the true voltage values and the measured ones. The goal is to minimize the time‐varying REs over the VTs. The formulation for the first objective is:

(7.12)![f 1 left-parenthesis bold x comma bold e Superscript 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold e Superscript upper P Baseline right-parenthesis equals sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper T Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript upper K Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper P Endscripts e Subscript k comma j Superscript i Baseline comma](images/c07-math-0012.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></munderover><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></munderover><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold e Superscript i](images/c07-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msup></math> is given in Eq. ([7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0005)).

**(2) Sum of RE variation over time**

The second objective is the sum of the RE variation over time, which reflects the time‐varying relationship between the true voltage values and the measured ones. The variance of the RE variations for different VTs should be minimized. The formulation for the second objective is:

(7.13)![f 2 left-parenthesis bold x comma bold upper Delta bold e Superscript 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold upper Delta bold e Superscript upper P Baseline right-parenthesis equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper P Endscripts StartRoot s t d left-parenthesis normal upper Delta e Subscript 1 comma 1 Superscript i Baseline comma midline-horizontal-ellipsis comma normal upper Delta e Subscript upper L comma upper T Superscript i Baseline right-parenthesis EndRoot comma](images/c07-math-0013.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></munderover><msqrt><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mspace width="0.15em"/><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold upper Delta bold e Superscript i](images/c07-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msup></math> is given in Eq. ([7.7](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0007)), and ![upper L](images/c07-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> is ![upper K](images/c07-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> for TREE1 to TREE5 and ![left floor upper K slash 2 right floor](images/c07-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8970;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8971;</mo></math> for TREE6, respectively.

**(3) Phase angle relationship**

In contrast to the first two objectives, which only consider voltage values, the third objective focuses on the phase angle relationship among the true voltage values, the measured phase angle values, and the measured voltage values. The variance of the phase angle RE variations for different VTs should be minimized. The formulation for the third objective is:

(7.14)![f 3 left-parenthesis bold x comma bold upper Delta bold e Superscript 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold upper Delta bold e Superscript upper P Baseline right-parenthesis equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper P Endscripts StartRoot s t d left-parenthesis left-parenthesis normal upper Delta e Subscript left floor upper K slash 2 right floor comma 1 Superscript i Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal upper Delta e Subscript upper K comma upper T Superscript i Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis EndRoot period](images/c07-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></munderover><msqrt><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8970;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8971;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msqrt><mo>.</mo></math> 

Although the formulations for the second and third objectives are similar, they are not merged due to the presence of different types of data.

 

#### 7.2.2.3 Constraint Functions

In a power delivery system, VTs in the same substation are connected through conductors, and the measurement of voltage and phase angle values is a long‐term process. Therefore, three main constraints can be formulated to restrict the feasible area of the problem: topology constraint, time series constraint, and phase constraint.

**(1) Topology constraints**

Topology constraints are derived from the three‐phase balance principle, stating that the true three‐phase primary voltages should be kept in balance if the grid is under control [\[15\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0015). This balance is described by the voltage unbalance factor (VUF), which indicates the balance between three‐phase impedance. Since the three‐phase impedance is balanced and varies slowly (especially in the high‐voltage grid) [\[16\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0016), the VUF value and its fluctuation can be limited within a range as

(7.15)![sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper K Endscripts left-parenthesis tau Subscript i Baseline minus upper C 1 right-parenthesis less-than 0 period](images/c07-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></munderover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></math> 

Moreover, because the primary side voltage value is proportional to the secondary side voltage value, all proportions for three‐phase voltages should be the same. We can derive the second constraint from its fluctuation by



**(3) Phase constraint**

The VT is an inductive sensor in the power delivery system, and the primary voltage phasors will be lagged after being transformed to the secondary side. Besides, the phase angle difference between every two phasors mainly depends on the equivalent impedance of the power transformer and the load current through it. The basic assumption of the phase constraint is that the difference between three‐phase angles in a power transformer system is held constant. Therefore, the first phase constraint indicates the tolerance of phase angle imbalance, and its formulation is:

With the objective functions and constraints established, the TREE problems can be solved using evolutionary algorithms. The goal is to obtain the best estimation of the true voltage values and phase angles, while satisfying the constraints derived from the power delivery system's characteristics. This will lead to a more accurate and reliable operation of the power grid, ensuring that the VTs perform their crucial role in monitoring and controlling the system effectively.

 

### 7.2.3 Problem Analysis

From the elaborations on the proposed TREE problems, it can be found that these problems are scalable to have a very vast search space, causing the curse of dimensionality. Besides, the TREE problems have multiple complicated constraints, which reduce the size of feasible search space considerably. When the above characteristics of TREE problems are known, some other problem characteristics deserve to be explored, including the relationships among decision variables, objectives, and constraints. After all, an LSMOP can be easily solved by a divide‐and‐conquer method if its decision variables are fully separable. By contrast, when the decision variables have intricate interactions, the difficulty of the problem usually increases considerably.

In this section, we explore the relationships among decision variables, objectives, and constraints using three different methods, including the differential grouping method from [\[17\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0017), and the variable interaction analysis methods in multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm with decision variable analysis (MOEA/DVA) [\[18\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0018) and large‐scale multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm (LMEA) [\[19\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0019). For these analyses, ![upper T](images/c07-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is set to 200 for each problem, and the number of decision variables is 600, 600, 1200, 1200, 1200, and 2400 for TREE1 through TREE6, respectively.

[Table 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-tbl-0002) presents the numbers of interacting and independent decision variables associated with each objective/constraint for each TREE problem. It can be seen that the first objectives of TREE1 through TREE5 are fully separable, while the second ones can be partially divided into three equal‐sized groups without any separable variables. Additionally, all constraints of TREE1 through TREE5, except for TREE6, are fully nonseparable. In summary, the proposed test suite encompasses both separable and nonseparable components.

![Table 7.2  The Decision Variable Interaction in Association with Different Objective and Constraint Functions.](images/c07-i0061.png)

[**Table 7.2**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-tbl-0002)  The Decision Variable Interaction in Association with Different Objective and Constraint Functions.

[Table 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-tbl-0003) presents the numbers of different types of decision variables obtained by MOEA/DVA and LMEA. The analysis results indicate that almost all decision variables of TREE1 through TREE5 are position variables, and approximately half of the decision variables of TREE6 are distance variables concerning relationships between decision variables and objectives. However, significant differences arise when applying MOEA/DVA and LMEA methods to analyze relationships between decision variables and constraints. This discrepancy can be attributed to the fact that both methods were designed for analyzing relationships between decision variables and objectives and might not perform effectively when handling constraints.
