## 7.3 Problem Knowledge‐Driven Coevolutionary Algorithm for Time‐Varying Ratio Error Estimation

Based on the problem analysis as above, it can be noted that the TREE problems pose stiff challenges to the existing MOEAs tailored for general LSMOPs. However, this does not mean that evolutionary algorithms cannot effectively address the TREE problems. For this specific problem, as indicated in previous work, it may be very useful to utilize the information of the problem in designing effective MOEAs. For this reason, the following observation can be found. Despite that the TREE problems are characterized by the vast search space, complicated constraints, and intricate decision variable interactions, another important characteristic of TREE problems is that most VTs work under normal operating conditions, which means that there only exist a small proportion of VTs having relatively large errors. Therefore, it can be inferred that most decision variables in each TREE problem have similar values, which inspires us to exploit this problem knowledge to design a novel search strategy, thus improving the effectiveness and efficiency for solving the challenging TREE problems.

 

### 7.3.1 Problem Knowledge Utilization

When we exploit the problem knowledge (i.e., most decision variables in each TREE problem have similar values) to improve the search efficiency of evolutionary algorithms in solving TREE problems, the idea is to coevolve two populations, where one population consists of non‐sparse solutions and the other population is composed of sparse solutions. As shown in [Fig. 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0003), when a sparse solution and a non‐sparse solution are selected as parent solutions for offspring generation, most decision variables in the generated offspring solution have similar values, which enables the Pareto optimal solution sets of TREE problems to be handled effectively. Thus, in the case that many algorithms can be used to evolve the population that contains non‐sparse solutions, the main task of solving TREE problems changes to design a novel search strategy to evolve the population that contains sparse solutions.

![Figure 7.3 The offspring solution generated by a sparse parent solution and a non‐sparse parent solution. (a) Non‐sparse parent solution. (b) Sparse parent solution. (c) Offspring solution.](images/c07f003.png)

[**Figure 7.3**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0003) The offspring solution generated by a sparse parent solution and a non‐sparse parent solution. (a) Non‐sparse parent solution. (b) Sparse parent solution. (c) Offspring solution.

As introduced in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), in recent years, a lot of works have been reported for sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization. Considering that the search space of TREE problems is more complicated, in this section, we propose a new operator to improve the efficiency in generating sparse solutions. In the operator, decision variables are first divided into multiple groups. Then, a group of decision variables are selected randomly to perform grouped and linked polynomial mutation [\[20\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0020), which has been verified to be effective to generate sparse solutions in SparseEA2 [\[21\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0021). However, in the grouped and linked polynomial mutation, the direction of mutation is determined randomly, which is prone to mutate a decision variable from zero to nonzero, thus affecting the efficiency of generating sparse solutions. To address this issue, in the proposed operator, a unidirectional mutation operator is incorporated, which always mutates decision variables along the direction of coming close to zero. In this way, the effectiveness and efficiency of generating sparse solutions can be improved greatly. In [Fig. 7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0004), two illustrative examples are presented, which show that promising sparse solutions can be obtained by performing the proposed unidirectional mutation operator.

![Figure 7.4 Examples of the proposed unidirectional mutation operator. (a) Mutating selected decision variables along the direction of decreasing their values to zero. (b) Mutating selected decision variables along the direction of increasing their values to zero.](images/c07f004.png)

[**Figure 7.4**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0004) Examples of the proposed unidirectional mutation operator. (a) Mutating selected decision variables along the direction of decreasing their values to zero. (b) Mutating selected decision variables along the direction of increasing their values to zero.

To describe the proposed operator in more detail, its pseudocode is presented in Algorithm 7.1. To begin with, the mutation operator divides decision variables into ![k](images/c07-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> groups by the grouping method ![upper G upper M](images/c07-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mi>M</mi></math>. Then, a group of decision variables are selected randomly to perform mutation operator. Specifically, a rand number ![r 1](images/c07-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> is first generated and compared with 0.5. If ![r 1](images/c07-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> is smaller than 0.5, the unidirectional mutation is performed; otherwise, the bidirectional mutation (i.e., grouped and linked polynomial mutation) is performed. In the unidirectional mutation, the direction of mutation is determined in the following way. Decision variables in the selected decision variable group ![images](images/c07-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><?xmlltex?><mi>j</mi></math> are first sorted. Then, the decision variable with the median value is selected and termed as ![x Subscript f l a g](images/c07-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math>. If ![x Subscript f l a g](images/c07-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is larger than zero, which means that at least a half of decision variables in ![images](images/c07-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><?xmlltex?><mi>j</mi></math> have values larger than zero, all decision variables in ![images](images/c07-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><?xmlltex?><mi>j</mi></math> are mutated along the direction of decreasing their values to zero. Otherwise, there exist at least a half decision variables in ![images](images/c07-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><?xmlltex?><mi>j</mi></math> that their values are smaller than zero; thus, all decision variables in ![images](images/c07-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><?xmlltex?><mi>j</mi></math> are mutated along the direction of increasing their values to zero.

 

### 7.3.2 Framework of PKCEA

This section gives the framework of the proposed problem knowledge‐driven coevolutionary algorithm, namely, PKCEA. As shown in [Fig. 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0005), the proposed algorithm contains two optimization tasks, namely, the main optimization task and the auxiliary optimization task. The main optimization task is addressed by population ![upper P Baseline 1](images/c07-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></math>, which uses the conventional genetic operators (i.e., simulated binary crossover [\[22\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0022) and polynomial mutation [\[23\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0023)) to generate offspring solutions. The auxiliary optimization task is addressed by population ![upper P Baseline 2](images/c07-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></math>, which uses the improved grouped and linked polynomial mutation operator to generate offspring solutions. In fact, a lot of similar frameworks \[[24](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0024)–[27](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0027)\] have been reported in recent years, which demonstrate their effectiveness to solve multi‐objective optimization problems with constraints by introducing auxiliary optimization. However, the majority of existing algorithms devote their efforts to solving medium and small‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems, and the auxiliary optimization is designed by easing the difficulty brought by constraints [\[28\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0028), thus improving the effectiveness and efficiency of environmental selection. By contrast, the algorithm PKCEA is proposed to solve LSMOPs and the auxiliary optimization is designed by focusing on generating sparse solutions, which enables the generated solutions similar to the Pareto optimal solution sets as much as possible, thus improving the effectiveness and efficiency in solving TREE problems.

![Figure 7.5 Framework of the proposed problem knowledge‐driven coevolutionary algorithm PKCEA.](images/c07f005.png)

[**Figure 7.5**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0005) Framework of the proposed problem knowledge‐driven coevolutionary algorithm PKCEA.

Algorithm 7.2 gives the detailed procedure of PKCEA. To begin with, two initial populations ![upper P Baseline 1](images/c07-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![upper P Baseline 2](images/c07-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></math> are generated, where population ![upper P Baseline 1](images/c07-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></math> is generated by the random method and population ![upper P Baseline 2](images/c07-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></math> is generated by Algorithm 4.1. When solutions in the two populations are evaluated, the algorithm enters the loop. In the loop, first, two mating parent pools, namely, ![upper S Baseline 1](images/c07-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![upper S Baseline 2](images/c07-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></math>, are obtained by the binary tournament selection method, where the non‐dominated front number and crowding distance of solutions are used as the selection criteria. Then, two offspring populations are generated by genetic operators. Specially, the offspring in ![upper O Baseline 1](images/c07-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mn>1</mn></math> are generated by the simulated binary crossover and polynomial mutation operators, the offspring in ![upper O Baseline 2](images/c07-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mn>2</mn></math> are generated by the improved grouped and linked polynomial mutation operator. Next, the two offspring populations are combined with ![upper P Baseline 1](images/c07-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![upper P Baseline 2](images/c07-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></math> to obtain populations ![upper H Baseline 1](images/c07-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![upper H Baseline 2](images/c07-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></math>. Finally, when the solutions in ![upper H Baseline 1](images/c07-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![upper H Baseline 2](images/c07-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></math> are evaluated, the environmental selection strategy of non‐dominated sorting based genetic algorithm‐II (NSGA‐II) [\[29\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0029) is performed to update populations ![upper P Baseline 1](images/c07-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></math> and ![upper P Baseline 2](images/c07-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></math>. The loop iterates until the number of function evaluations ![upper F upper E](images/c07-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mi>E</mi></math> is not smaller than the maximum number of function evaluations ![upper M a x upper F upper E s](images/c07-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>s</mi></math>, and the algorithm terminates and outputs population ![upper P Baseline 1](images/c07-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></math>.

 

### 7.3.3 Experimental Comparisons

In this section, experimental comparisons between the proposed algorithm and several representative MOEAs are performed on the formulated TREE test problems, namely, TREE1–TREE5. For each test problem, the number of decision variables is set to 3000, 6000, 9000, 12,000, and 15,000; thus, there are totally 25 test instances used for performance assessment. The proposed algorithm is compared with five MOEAs, including NSGA‐II [\[29\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0029), large‐scale multi‐objective optimization framework (LSMOF) [\[30\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0030), large‐scale multi‐objective competitive swarm optimizer (LMOCSO) [\[31\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0031), constrained large‐scale reference vector guided evolutionary algorithm (CLS‐RVEA) [\[32\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0032), and FLEA [\[33\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0033).

In the experiments, the maximum number of function evaluations is adopted as the termination criterion, which is set to ![20 times upper D](images/c07-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>20</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math> for each algorithm on each test problem with ![upper D](images/c07-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> denoting the number of decision variables. For all algorithms, the population size is set to 100. For the proposed PKCEA, the ordered grouping method is used, and the number of decision variable groups is set to four. For the compared algorithms, their algorithm‐specific parameters are set to the values in their original papers. Considering that the Pareto fronts of the TREE problems are unknown, the hypervolume (HV) [\[34\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0034) indicator is used for performance assessment. It is worth noting that the experiments as mentioned above are performed on PlatEMO [\[35\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0035).

[Table 7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-tbl-0004) shows the HV results obtained by the six algorithms on the 25 test instances. From the table, it can be seen that the proposed algorithm PKCEA achieves the best overall performance, having obtained the best result on most test instances. LSMOF and FLEA show inferior overall performance than the proposed PKCEA, but they can always obtain a nonzero HV value on each test instance. By contrast, the HV values obtained by the other three algorithms on some test instances are zero, due to the fact that they fail to obtain any feasible solution. To be specific, NSGA‐II fails to obtain any feasible solution on the TREE3, TREE4, TREE5, high‐dimensional TREE1, and high‐dimensional TREE2 problems, LMOCSO cannot obtain any feasible solution on the TREE3 and TREE4 problems, and CLS‐RVEA does not obtain any feasible solution on TREE3.

![Table 7.4  The HV Results Obtained by NSGA‐II, LSMOF, LMOCSO, CLS‐RVEA, FLEA, and PKCEA on 25 TREE Test Instances. The Best Result in Each Row is Highlighted.](images/c07-i0102.png)

[**Table 7.4**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-tbl-0004)  The HV Results Obtained by NSGA‐II, LSMOF, LMOCSO, CLS‐RVEA, FLEA, and PKCEA on 25 TREE Test Instances. The Best Result in Each Row is Highlighted.

[Figure 7.6](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0006) plots the populations and convergence curves with median HV values obtained by the six algorithms on the TREE1, TREE3, and TREE5 problems with 3000 decision variables. It is worth noting that the populations and convergence curves of NSGA‐II, LMOCSO, and CLS‐RVEA on some problems are not provided since they fail to converge to feasible regions. From the figure, it can be seen that the proposed algorithm exhibits better performance.

![Figure 7.6 Populations and convergence curves with median HV values obtained by the six algorithms on the TREE1, TREE3, and TREE5 problems.](images/c07f006.png)

[**Figure 7.6**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0006) Populations and convergence curves with median HV values obtained by the six algorithms on the TREE1, TREE3, and TREE5 problems.

 

## 7.4 Summary

In this chapter, a data‐driven problem formulation method is proposed for ratio error estimation of VTs, which offers several advantages, including lower cost compared to on‐site/off‐line calibration, real‐time estimation for early warnings of potential faulty VTs, and versatility in handling different substation types and VT models. These advantages make the method practical and valuable for real‐world applications. Based on the data‐driven problem formulation method, a number of test problems are proposed. In the proposed TREE problems, a lot of challenges are associated, including the vast search space, the complex constraints, and the intricate interactions between decision variables.

To solve the challenging TREE problems, a problem knowledge‐driven coevolutionary algorithm is reported, which introduces a sparse large‐scale multi‐objective optimization as the auxiliary optimization. In the auxiliary optimization, a novel genetic operator is proposed to improve the efficiency of generating sparse solutions, thus enabling the Pareto optimal solution sets of TREE problems to be solved effectively. Experimental studies show that the proposed algorithm is superior over the compared MOEAs.

# 8  
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization in Radiotherapy Planning

 

## 8.1 Introduction

Since X‐ray was found by Röntgen in the 1890s, ionizing radiation has received increasing attention in the therapy of malignant tumors. With the invention of linear accelerators in the 1950s, computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging in the 1970s, and multileaf collimators (MLCs) in the 1980s, radiotherapy has become an important modality used in cancer treatment. Together with surgery and chemotherapy, nearly 70% cancer patients have received radiotherapy during their course of illness [\[1\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0001). To provide conformal dose distribution for different clinical cases, intensity‐modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) has served as an effective technique for radiotherapy, able to generate individual‐specific therapeutic fields by adjusting the angles, intensities, and shapes of radiation [\[2\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0002).

 

### 8.1.1 Challenges of IMRT Planning

As illustrated in [Fig. 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0001), the therapeutic fields are formed by the photons or protons transmitted through a MLC, where the photons or protons are emitted by radiation beams produced by a linear accelerator [\[3\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0003). The therapeutic fields form heterogeneous dose distribution, so as to meet the clinical requirements of a given cancer case, i.e., maximizing the tumor control probability while minimizing the normal tissue complication probability [\[4\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0004). Therefore, the core issue of IMRT planning is essentially an optimization problem, where the decision variables include the angles, intensities, and shapes of radiation, and the objectives include the satisfaction of the dose distribution in the planning tumor volume (PTV consisting of tumor cells) and the minimization of the dose distribution in the organ at risk (OAR consisting of healthy cells).

![Figure 8.1 The therapeutic fields generated in intensity‐modulated radiotherapy (IMRT).](images/c08f001.png)

[**Figure 8.1**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0001) The therapeutic fields generated in intensity‐modulated radiotherapy (IMRT).

IMRT planning introduces challenging optimization problems characterized by discrete variables, high‐dimensional decision spaces, many objectives, and computationally expensive functions. First, the therapeutic fields are partitioned into many small grids to ease the calculation of dose distribution; hence, their shapes are determined by integer variables rather than continuous variables. Second, since all the small grids can only have the same intensity at a time, many apertures with different shapes and intensities are required to form a therapeutic field with heterogeneous dose distribution, which leads to thousands of shape‐related variables. Third, a clinical case usually has multiple PTV and OAR regions and each region corresponds to multiple clinical requirements, which leads to dozens of conflicting objectives to be optimized simultaneously. Lastly, the calculation of dose distribution involves the multiplication of large matrices, where too many function evaluations are unaffordable in clinical practice. Due to these difficulties of IMRT planning, a variety of methods have been developed in the last three decades, and some of which are introduced in the following.

 

### 8.1.2 IMRT Planning Methods

Existing IMRT planning methods can be roughly grouped into two categories, including two‐step optimization methods and direct aperture optimization methods. The two‐step optimization methods aim to obtain the optimal dose distribution and then obtain the corresponding apertures, where the first step is known as fluence map optimization and the second step is known as MLC sequencing. The task of fluence map optimization is to obtain the optimal intensity for each small grid in the therapeutic fields, and thus the therapeutic fields can form heterogeneous dose distribution in the PTV and OAR regions. Fluence map optimization is a continuous optimization problem that has been handled by various advanced techniques, including analytical algorithms (e.g., Fourier transform [\[5\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0005) and Taylor series expansion [\[6\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0006)), mathematical programming (e.g., mixed integer programming [\[7\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0007) and quadratic programming [\[8\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0008)), machine learning (e.g., regression forests [\[9\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0009) and deep neural networks [\[10\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0010)), and metaheuristics (e.g., simulated annealing [\[11\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0011) and genetic algorithms [\[12\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0012)). While the small grids with different intensities cannot be implemented directly, the task of MLC sequencing is to obtain the optimal apertures, where the small grids in each aperture share the same intensity. Thus, MLC sequencing aims to minimize the difference between the fluence map and the superposition of all apertures, which is usually handled by column generation methods \[[13](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0013), [14](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0014)\].

The direct aperture optimization methods aim to obtain the optimal apertures directly, so as to eliminate the distortion of intensities caused by MLC sequencing. Obviously, direct aperture optimization is more challenging, since it is a combinatorial optimization problem. Some methods have been suggested for direct aperture optimization, such as enumeration [\[15\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0015), gradient descent [\[16\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0016), random search [\[17\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0017), local search [\[18\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0018), and genetic algorithms [\[19\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0019). Nevertheless, direct aperture optimization is so complex that it cannot be solved in a totally black‐box manner, where problem‐dependent search strategies are required to avoid invalid solutions brought by the physical limitations of MLC.

The difficulty encountered by the above methods mainly lies in the balance between many conflicting objectives (i.e., clinical requirements). Basically, larger intensities are more effective for killing tumor cells but also damage more healthy cells [\[20\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0020). Therefore, MOEAs have been suggested for IMRT planning in recent research \[[21](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0021), [22](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0022)\], which can provide many candidate solutions with diverse trade‐offs between objectives, thus highly reducing the human expertise required by medical physicists. Nevertheless, IMRT planning involves a large number of discrete variables, where MOEAs should be equipped with customized search strategies for high efficiency \[[23](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0023), [24](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0024)\].

 

## 8.2 Problem Formulation

IMRT planning is essentially a combinatorial LSMOP, which aims to find the optimal angles, intensities, and shapes of multiple apertures for meeting many clinical requirements of a given cancer case. The clinical requirements are related to the dose distribution determined by apertures, where the apertures are two‐dimensional regions partitioned into many small grids and the dose distribution corresponds to a three‐dimensional region partitioned into many voxels (i.e., small cubes). Here, the angles of apertures are fixed by experience while the intensities and shapes of apertures are optimized by optimizers, and thus the dose deposition coefficient of the ![v](images/c08-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math>th voxel in terms of the ![g](images/c08-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math>th small grid ![upper D Subscript g v](images/c08-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> can be calculated by Monte Carlo methods [\[25\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0025) in advance. Then, the dose of the ![v](images/c08-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math>th voxel ![d o s e Subscript v](images/c08-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> can be calculated by

Clinically, an IMRT planning task contains dozens of the above objectives for multiple regions of PTV and OAR, which constitute a many‐objective optimization problem that is difficult to distinguish between solutions by algorithms and decision‐makers. Considering that some objectives are not conflicting with each other, all the objectives are aggregated into five new objectives to be optimized simultaneously as suggested in [\[24\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0024). As a consequence, IMRT planning is formulated as the following LSMOP:

Although there have been many generic MOEAs tailored for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, they are ineffective for solving the problem defined in Eq. ([8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0006)) due to two main reasons. First, most generic MOEAs evolve populations in continuous decision spaces, where the search strategies (e.g., decision variable grouping and decision space reduction) cannot handle the discrete variables related to aperture shapes. Second, many solutions generated in a stochastic search paradigm are likely to be invalid due to the physical limitations of MLC; moreover, the repair of invalid solutions is highly disruptive to the evolution of populations. To address these issues, several MOEAs have been suggested for IMRT planning with customized search strategies in recent years \[[23](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0023), [24](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0024)\], where the first MOEA tailored for IMRT planning is introduced in [Section 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0005).

 

## 8.3 Bi‐Encoding Coevolutionary Algorithm for IMRT Planning

The multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm for intensity‐modulated radiotherapy planning (MOEA/IMRT) suggests a bi‐encoding coevolutionary framework for solving the problem defined in Eq. ([8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0006)) [\[24\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0024). More specifically, one population represented in fine encoding is evolved for the local exploitation of complex and irregular aperture shapes, and another population represented in rough encoding is evolved for the global exploration of simple and regular aperture shapes. The population represented in fine encoding serves as the final output, which provides diverse candidate treatment plans for medical physicists and doctors. On the other hand, the population represented in rough encoding forms a low‐dimensional decision space for the acceleration of the convergence of the population represented in fine encoding, where the transfer of useful genetic material has been verified to be effective in handling complex constraints [\[29\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0029). Furthermore, MOEA/IMRT customizes two local search strategies for repairing invalid solutions and accelerating the convergence, respectively.

 

### 8.3.1 Bi‐Encoding Scheme of MOEA/IMRT

While the intensities of apertures can be directly represented by real variables, the first issue that should be addressed is to represent the shapes of apertures by proper variables. Intuitively, as shown in [Fig. 8.2](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0002), a binary matrix can be associated with an aperture to indicate whether each small grid is shielded or not. However, most solutions represented by this encoding scheme will violate the physical limitations of MLC shown in [Fig. 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0001), as the unshielded small grids must be successive in each row. Therefore, the fine encoding scheme of MOEA/IMRT uses many integer variables to represent the positions of MLC leaves for each aperture, and the rough encoding scheme of MOEA/IMRT uses four integer variables to determine a rectangular region of unshielded small grids.

[Figure 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0003) illustrates the bi‐encoding scheme used in MOEA/IMRT. For an IMRT task with ![upper N Subscript upper B](images/c08-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></math> radiation beams and ![upper N Subscript upper A](images/c08-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub></math> apertures for each beam, a solution ![bold x equals left-parenthesis bold x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper N Sub Subscript upper B Subscript times upper N Sub Subscript upper A Subscript Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the concatenation of ![upper N Subscript upper B Baseline times upper N Subscript upper A](images/c08-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub></math> vectors, where vector ![bold x Subscript i](images/c08-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> encodes the intensity and shape of the ![i](images/c08-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th aperture. For an aperture ![bold x Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript i Baseline 5 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> represented in rough encoding, it consists of five decision variables, where the real number ![x Subscript i Baseline 5](images/c08-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></math> denotes the intensity of the aperture and the integers ![x Subscript i Baseline 1](images/c08-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![x Subscript i Baseline 2](images/c08-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![x Subscript i Baseline 3](images/c08-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and ![x Subscript i Baseline 4](images/c08-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></math> denote the horizontal position of the upper left corner, the vertical position of the upper left corner, the width, and the height of the rectangular region of unshielded small grids, respectively. In short, a solution represented in fine encoding contains ![upper N Subscript upper B Baseline times upper N Subscript upper A Baseline times left-parenthesis 2 upper K plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>K</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> variables forming a high‐dimensional decision space, and a solution represented in rough encoding contains ![upper N Subscript upper B Baseline times upper N Subscript upper A Baseline times 5](images/c08-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math> variables forming a low‐dimensional decision space.

![Figure 8.3 Illustration of the bi‐encoding scheme used in MOEA/IMRT.](images/c08f003.png)

[**Figure 8.3**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0003) Illustration of the bi‐encoding scheme used in MOEA/IMRT.

As can be observed from [Fig. 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0003), the solutions represented in fine encoding can search for irregular apertures to be used in clinical practice, while the solutions represented in rough encoding can only search for rectangular apertures to assist the optimization of the solutions represented in fine encoding. Thus, the exploitation and exploration can be balanced by the cooperation of the two encoding schemes. In order to transfer useful genetic material between the solutions represented in different encoding schemes, MOEA/IMRT suggests the conversion strategies presented in [Fig. 8.4](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0004). [**Figure 8.4**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0004) Illustration of the conversion between find encoding and rough encoding used in MOEA/IMRT.

Considering a population ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> represented in fine encoding and a population ![upper P 2](images/c08-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> represented in rough encoding, Algorithm 8.1 details the procedure of the conversion between the two populations. To begin with, ![upper L](images/c08-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> solutions are selected from each of ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper P 2](images/c08-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> by using the environmental selection strategy of MOEA/IMRT (Lines 1 and 2). The algorithm then exchanges the encoding schemes of the ![2 upper L](images/c08-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></math> solutions rather than all the solutions, since the transferred solutions need to be reevaluated and only the best solutions (i.e., useful genetic material) are expected to be transferred for the assistance of convergence. For each solution represented in fine encoding (Line 4), each of its apertures is converted into a new aperture by Eq. ([8.7](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0007)) (Lines 6–8), and all the new apertures constitute a new solution represented in rough encoding to be stored in ![upper P prime 2](images/c08-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> (Line 9). For each solution represented in rough encoding (Line 11), each of its apertures is converted into a new aperture by Eq. ([8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0008)) (Lines 13–15), and all the new apertures constitute a new solution represented in fine encoding to be stored in ![upper P prime 1](images/c08-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> (Line 16). Lastly, all the transferred solutions are returned (Line 17), where the encoding scheme of ![upper P prime 1](images/c08-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is transferred from rough encoding to fine encoding, and the encoding scheme of ![upper P prime 2](images/c08-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is transferred from fine encoding to rough encoding.

 

### 8.3.2 Local Search Strategies of MOEA/IMRT

The two encoding schemes consider the physical nature of MLC leaves, but they are still unable to prevent invalid apertures such as those with very small shapes or disconnected shapes. Besides, the co‐evolution of two populations with different encoding schemes is not efficient enough to converge in the high‐dimensional decision space. To handle these problems, MOEA/IMRT develops a local search strategy for repairing invalid solutions and a local search strategy for finding better solutions.

As illustrated in [Fig. 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0005), an aperture represented in fine encoding may be too small (i.e., the number of unshielded grids is less than a threshold) or disconnected (i.e., some of the unshielded grids are not connected), and an aperture represented in rough encoding may also be too small. To repair such apertures, a local search strategy is developed in MOEA/IMRT for ensuring clinical practicality. Specifically, given an aperture ![bold x Subscript i Baseline equals left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline 1 Baseline comma ellipsis comma x Subscript i left-parenthesis 2 upper K plus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>K</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> represented in fine encoding, it is repaired by the following formulas:

where ![upper S equals y Subscript i Baseline 3 Baseline times y Subscript i Baseline 4](images/c08-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></math> counts the number of unshielded grids in the aperture, and ![r a n d](images/c08-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></math> is a uniformly distributed random number within ![left-bracket 0 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c08-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. These formulas ensure that the aperture has at least ![upper S Subscript m i n](images/c08-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></math> unshielded grids, by means of expanding the aperture shape vertically or horizontally at random. Considering a population ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> represented in fine encoding and a population ![upper P 2](images/c08-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> represented in rough encoding, Algorithm 8.2 elaborates on the procedure of repairing invalid solutions in the two populations. For each solution represented in fine encoding (Line 1), each of its apertures is repaired by Eq. ([8.9](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0009)) (Lines 2 and 3). While for each solution represented in rough encoding (Line 4), each of its apertures is repaired by Eq. ([8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0010)) (Lines 5 and 6). Lastly, the repaired populations are directly returned (Line 7).

![Figure 8.5 Illustration of the local search strategy for repairing invalid solutions in MOEA/IMRT.](images/c08f005.png)

[**Figure 8.5**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0005) Illustration of the local search strategy for repairing invalid solutions in MOEA/IMRT.

The aforementioned bi‐encoding scheme and repair strategy of MOEA/IMRT focus on the optimization of aperture shapes. To further improve the convergence speed, the second local search strategy of MOEA/IMRT aims to enhance the optimization of aperture intensities, whose procedure is described in Algorithm 8.3. Given a population ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> represented in fine encoding, the non‐dominated solutions in ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> are firstly copied to a new set ![upper P Subscript upper N](images/c08-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></math> (Line 1), whose shape‐related variables are retained while intensity‐related variables are to be optimized. Then, a new population ![upper Q](images/c08-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> with ![upper N Subscript upper Q](images/c08-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></msub></math> solutions having only aperture intensities is randomly initialized (Line 2), i.e., each solution has only one real variable. To evaluate ![upper Q](images/c08-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> on the objectives of IMRT planning, each solution in ![upper Q](images/c08-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is associated with a solution randomly selected from ![upper P Subscript upper N](images/c08-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></math> (Line 3). In other words, the decision vector to be evaluated consists of the shape‐related variables of a solution from ![upper P Subscript upper N](images/c08-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></math> and the intensity‐related variable of each solution in ![upper Q](images/c08-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>, and thus the aperture shapes are retained in ![upper P Subscript upper N](images/c08-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></math> and the aperture intensities are optimized by evolving ![upper Q](images/c08-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>. The evolution of ![upper Q](images/c08-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is conducted for a predefined number of generations, by means of the mating selection strategy (Line 6), variation operators (Line 7), and environmental selection strategy (Line 9) of MOEA/IMRT, whose procedures are elaborated in [Section 8.3.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0008). It should be noted that the optimization of aperture intensities consumes additional function evaluations, hence it is just conducted with a population size ![upper N Subscript upper Q Baseline equals 20](images/c08-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math> and 100 generations after every 100 main generations of MOEA/IMRT. This way, the local search does not deteriorate the efficiency of the whole algorithm obviously.

 

### 8.3.3 Procedure of MOEA/IMRT

With the bi‐encoding scheme and two local search strategies, the procedure of MOEA/IMRT is described in Algorithm 8.4. First, a population ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> with ![upper N](images/c08-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions represented in fine encoding is randomly initialized (Line 1), and a population ![upper P 2](images/c08-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> with ![upper N](images/c08-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> solutions represented in rough encoding is randomly initialized (Line 2). Then, the solutions in the two populations are repaired by the repair strategy of MOEA/IMRT (Line 3), and the fitness values of all the solutions are calculated to be used in selection strategies (Lines 4 and 5). MOEA/IMRT adopts the fitness assignment strategy of SPEA2 with shift‐based density estimation [\[30\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0030) as described in Algorithm 8.5, which is the same as that of the original SPEA2 [\[31\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0031) except for a new method to measure the distances between solutions. When calculating the Euclidean distances to a solution ![bold x](images/c08-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> in the objective space, all the objective values of the other solutions are shifted to be not less than the objective values of ![bold x](images/c08-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> (Line 7 of Algorithm 8.5). Such a shift‐based density estimation can consider both the convergence and diversity of solutions in the Euclidean distances, which is particularly effective for many‐objective optimization problems including IMRT planning where general selection strategies suffer from the Pareto dominance resistance phenomenon [\[32\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0032).

 

At each generation, the mating pool ![upper P prime 1](images/c08-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is constructed by selecting ![upper N](images/c08-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> parents from the population ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> via binary tournament selection according to the fitness of solutions (Line 7). Then, ![upper N](images/c08-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> offspring solutions are generated by simulated binary crossover [\[33\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0033) and polynomial mutation [\[34\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0034) (Line 8), and the first ![2 upper K](images/c08-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>K</mi></math> decision variables of each offspring solution are rounded since these shape‐related variables can only be integers (Lines 9–12). Similarly, the mating pool ![upper P prime 2](images/c08-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is constructed by selecting ![upper N](images/c08-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> parents from the population ![upper P 2](images/c08-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> via binary tournament selection according to the fitness of solutions (Line 13). Then, ![upper N](images/c08-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> offspring solutions are generated (Line 14) and the first four decision variables of each offspring solution are rounded since these shape‐related variables can only be integers (Lines 15–18). Afterward, the offspring solutions represented in two encoding schemes are repaired by the repair strategy of MOEA/IMRT (Line 19) and transferred by the conversion strategy of MOEA/IMRT (Line 20). After combing each of ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper P 2](images/c08-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> with the offspring solutions represented in the same encoding scheme, ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper P 2](images/c08-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> are truncated by the environmental selection strategy of SPEA2 with shift‐based density estimation (Lines 21 and 22). As presented in Algorithm 8.6, the procedure of environmental selection is the same as that of the original SPEA2 except for the shift‐based density estimation‐based Euclidean distance calculation. Lastly, the local search strategy for intensity optimization is conducted periodically to further enhance the convergence of ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> (Lines 23–25), and ![upper P 1](images/c08-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> is returned as the output of the algorithm (Line 26).

## 8.4 Experimental Studies

To study the performance of MOEA/IMRT, it is compared with several representative IMRT methods and MOEAs on a number of clinical cases. The compared methods include Shepard's method [\[17\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0017), NSGA‐II [\[35\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0035), CCGDE3 [\[36\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0036), LSMOF‐NSGA‐II [\[37\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0037), LMOCSO [\[38\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0038), and MOEA/IMRT, where Shepard's method is the first direct aperture optimization method based on simulated annealing and mathematical programming, NSGA‐II is a classical MOEA, CCGDE3 is a decision variable grouping‐based MOEA, LSMOF‐NSGA‐II is a decision space reduction‐based MOEA, and LMOCSO is a novel search strategy‐based MOEA. The population size is set to 100, the number of function evaluations is set to 100,000, and the number of transferred solutions ![upper L](images/c08-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> in MOEA/IMRT is set to 10. For Shepard's method generating a single solution in one run, it is executed for 100 independent runs with 100 uniformly distributed weight vectors for aggregating all the objectives, and the number of function evaluations is also equally divided. For NSGA‐II, CCGDE3, LSMOF‐NSGA‐II, and LMOCSO, they represent solutions by using the fine encoding scheme given in [Fig. 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0003) and repair invalid solutions by using the local search strategy given in Algorithm 8.2. Five clinical cases are taken from the real world, whose statistics are listed in [Table 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0001). It can be found that the number of objectives varies from 9 to 25 and the number of decision variables varies from 1950 to 2715, which results in typical combinatorial LSMOPs. The populations obtained by the methods are assessed by HV [\[39\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0039) since the true Pareto fronts are unknown.

![Table 8.1  Statistics of Five Clinical Cases.](images/c08-i0150.png)

[**Table 8.1**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-tbl-0001)  Statistics of Five Clinical Cases.

[Table 8.2](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0002) lists the experimental results averaged over 30 runs, where the best results are shown in bold. It can be found from the table that Shepard's method obtains the worst performance since it generates only a single solution in one run and cannot maintain a good diversity for the solutions obtained in different runs. NSGA‐II obtains the second worst performance among the six compared methods, since it does not contain any strategy for searching in high‐dimensional decision spaces. By contrast, the three large‐scale MOEAs exhibit significantly better performance, and the LMOCSO based on a novel competitive swarm optimizer seems very suitable for IMRT planning tasks. Nevertheless, they are underperformed by the customized method MOEA/IMRT, which suggests a bi‐encoding scheme and two local search strategies leading to the best performance on all the cases.

![Table 8.2  HV Values Obtained by Six Methods on Six Clinical Cases of IMRT Planning.](images/c08-i0162.png)

[**Table 8.2**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-tbl-0002)  HV Values Obtained by Six Methods on Six Clinical Cases of IMRT Planning.

For a visual comparison, [Fig. 8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0006) plots the dose–volume histograms of the treatment plans obtained by six methods on the Sneezer case, which is a popular visualization method for physicists. A dose–volume histogram contains several curves representing the cumulative doses in each region, where a point ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> on a curve indicates that the proportion of voxels with doses larger than ![x](images/c08-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is ![y](images/c08-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>. [Figure 8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0006) plots the curves of three regions (i.e., PTV, OAR1, and OAR2) of the treatment plan having the minimum sum of all objectives in the population with the median HV value obtained by each method and also plots the vertical lines of maximum dose of PTV, minimum dose of PTV, maximum dose of OAR1, and maximum dose of OAR2. Ideally, the curves should decrease sharply, and the vertical parts of the curves should be to the left of the lines of maximum doses and to the right of the lines of minimum doses. As can be observed from the figure, the vertical parts of the curves of PTV obtained by Shepard's method, NSGA‐II, CCGDE3, and LSMOF‐NSGA‐II are mostly to the left of the line of minimum dose of PTV, which means that the obtained treatment plans are ineffective to kill tumor cells. By contrast, the vertical parts of the curves of PTV obtained by LMOCSO and MOEA/IMRT are mostly in between the lines of minimum dose and maximum dose of PTV, which means that the obtained treatment plans are obviously more effective. In particular, the curve of PTV obtained by MOEA/IMRT decreases more sharply than that obtained by LMOCSO, which further evidences the superiority of customized search strategies over generic large‐scale MOEAs for IMRT planning.

![Figure 8.6 Dose–volume histograms of the treatment plans obtained by six methods on the Sneezer case.](images/c08f006.png)

[**Figure 8.6**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0006) Dose–volume histograms of the treatment plans obtained by six methods on the Sneezer case.

 

## 8.5 Summary

This chapter introduces an emerging application of evolutionary large‐scale multi‐objective optimization, namely, IMRT planning. The challenges of this task lie in a large number of discrete variables and dozens of objectives, and the strict limitations of MLC also lead to many invalid solutions. Mathematical programming methods \[[7](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0007), [16](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0016)\], heuristics \[[6](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0006), [15](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0015)\], and deep learning methods \[[10](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0010), [40](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0040)\] are incapable of handling the conflicting objectives for providing diverse treatment plans, while general evolutionary algorithms \[[12](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0012), [22](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0022)\] are ineffective to optimize the large number of variables within a limited number of function evaluations. Therefore, several MOEAs have been developed for IMRT planning with customized search strategies \[[23](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0023), [24](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0024)\], such as the bi‐encoding scheme and local search strategies of MOEA/IMRT. We can conclude from the experimental results that large‐scale MOEAs are indeed more effective than conventional optimizers including general MOEAs for IMRT planning. However, the research of evolutionary multi‐objective optimization mostly focuses on continuous optimization, while MOEA/IMRT can further improve the performance on IMRT planning by developing customized search strategies for combinatorial optimization.

# 9  
Evolutionary Large‐Scale Multi‐Objective Optimization in Deep Learning

 

## 9.1 Introduction

Deep learning has made significant success in tackling various machine learning tasks, including image processing and computer vision [\[1\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0001), natural language processing [\[2\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0002), and object detection [\[3\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0003). To achieve desirable performance, it is widely recognized that the weights and architecture of deep neural networks (DNNs) are very crucial. Hence, optimizing the weights and designing the architectures of DNNs remain a hot research field in recent years.

Regarding optimizing weights of DNNs, a number of learning algorithms have been developed, including the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [\[4\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004), RMSProp [\[5\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0005), and Adam [\[6\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006), among several others, most of which are gradient‐based methods. The success of DNNs has proven that gradient‐based methods are efficient in training DNNs due to the rapid convergence speed provided by the gradient information. But, they also suffer from several limitations \[[7](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0007)–[11](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011)\]. First, they may easily get trapped into local optimums or saddle points due to their greedy nature \[[7](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0007), [8](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0008)\]. Second, a regularization term usually needs to be included to alleviate overfitting [\[12\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0012), which may not always lead to the desired training performance, since it is nontrivial to specify the hyperparameter for regularization. Finally, a number of other hyperparameters, such as the learning rate, momentum, and drop rate, must be carefully predefined [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011).

Regarding designing architectures of DNNs, early efforts are devoted to manually designing various neural architectures. Examples of this category include the ResNet [\[13\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0013), DenseNet [\[14\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0014), and GoogLeNet \[[15](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0015), [16](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0016)\]. Due to the requirements of human domain knowledge and expertise in handcrafted neural architectures, a hot research direction called neural architecture search (NAS) has arisen since it first appeared in [\[17\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0017). To solve the NAS task, a variety of optimization techniques have been adopted for NAS to yield high‐performance architectures, including reinforcement learning (RL) \[[18](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0018), [19](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0019)\], gradient optimization \[[20](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0020), [21](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0021)\], Bayesian optimization [\[22\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0022), and others [\[23\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0023).

As a class of population‐based meta‐heuristics, evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have been shown effective in solving the weight optimization of neural networks (NNs) (i.e., the training of NNs) and the architecture search of DNNs (i.e., NAS). Compared to gradient‐based approaches to training NNs and other optimization approaches to NAS, EAs are more insensitive to local optimums due to the attractive exploratory ability [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011) and perform better in handling multiple objectives without extra hyperparameters [\[24\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0024), which can provide a set of potential solutions for decision. Nevertheless, it is still difficult for EAs to solve large‐scale optimization problems for DNNs (e.g., training DNNs) [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011), since EAs suffer from poor scalability to the search dimension; besides, it is also challenging for EAs to solve the NAS task, because equipping EAs with an effective encoding scheme and genetic operators for NAS are not easily attainable, where the population characteristics of EAs further makes NAS need more computational resources. This motivates many researchers to improve EAs for large‐scale multi‐objective optimization problems in deep learning and this chapter presents two state‐of‐the‐art EAs for two typical multi‐objective optimization problems for deep learning: a gradient‐guided multi‐objective EA for training DNNs (termed GEMONN) and an action command‐based surrogate‐assisted multi‐objective EA for searching neural architectures of DNNs (termed ACEncoding).

 

## 9.2 Gradient‐Guided Multi‐Objective Evolutionary Algorithm for Training Deep Neural Networks

To obtain better weights for NNs, many EAs have been suggested for training NNs \[[10](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010), [11](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011),[25](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0025)–[31](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0031)\]. For instance, Whitley *et al*. [\[27\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0027) adopted a genetic algorithm to optimize the weights of NNs, where experimental results demonstrated its competitiveness on training NNs. Montana and Davis [\[26\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0026) trained a feedforward NNs with a total of 126 weights via a tailored genetic algorithm, which was shown to outperform gradient‐based approaches. Despite their superiority in training NNs, EAs are less efficient in solving the training of DNNs due to the curse of dimensionality [\[32\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0032). To address this issue, some attempts have been made to enhance the scalability of EAs in training large‐scale NNs, especially DNNs. For example, Gong *et al*. [\[31\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0031) suggested a bi‐objective EA to optimize the weights of sparse DNNs by only considering the biases instead of all weights, mainly because the biases are the main factor for controlling the sparsity of hidden layers; Liu *et al*. [\[10\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010) suggested an evolutionary layer‐wise structure learning approach for optimizing network weights, which reduces the large search space by limiting the weight value to 0 or 1 and making multiple weights in the same region share the same value; Sun *et al*. [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011) developed a single‐objective EA to optimize the weights of DNNs, where the weight optimization was converted into the optimization of orthogonal bias vector in weight space; instead of simplifying the optimization problem, Such *et al*. [\[33\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0033) used the parallel computing devices to enhance the search ability, aiming to improve the scalability of EAs in optimizing the weights of DNNs, by which millions of weights can be effectively optimized on a single modern desktop; Cui *et al*. [\[8\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0008) proposed an evolutionary approach to optimize the weights by combining the SGD and an EA, where the EA enhances the stability of the SGD and guarantees steady reduction of loss function. Most of these evolutionary approaches for training large‐scale NNs aim to address the curse of dimensionality by reducing the search space (i.e., number of weights to be optimized), which may miss the optimal search region and increase the probability of getting trapped in local optima [\[34\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0034).

To remedy this limitation, this section introduces a gradient‐guided evolutionary approach to training DNNs (called GEMONN), which can take advantages of the strength of both gradient descent (GD) and EAs. The presented crossover is a gradient‐guided simulated binary crossover operator [\[35\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0035), termed gSBX, for optimizing the weights of DNNs. The search direction of gSBX is defined to be the same as the gradient of the parent to strike a balance between exploitation and exploration in optimizing the weights of DNNs. gSBX is then embedded in an evolutionary multi‐objective algorithm to train DNNs, which minimizes the training loss and the network sparsity at the same time. To validate the performance of the proposed approach, GEMONN is adopted to train the weights of four types of NNs, namely, auto‐encoder (AE), stacked auto‐encoder (SAE), long short‐term memory (LSTM), and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Experimental results indicate that GEMONN is able to enhance the scalability of EAs in training large‐scale neural networks having up to millions of weights.

In the following, we first present the formal definition of neural network training, then the GEMONN for training the DNNs is elaborated. Finally, experimental comparisons between the GEMONN and state‐of‐the‐art approaches for network training are showcased and discussed.

 

### 9.2.1 Problem Formulation of Multi‐Objective Neural Network Training

Given a training set ![upper D](images/c09-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> and a network ![n e t](images/c09-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, EAs usually search for the optimal values of the weights and/or the optimal architecture \[[36](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0036)–[38](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0038)\] by minimizing the following bi‐objective optimization problem [\[9\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0009):

where ![bold x](images/c09-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> is the set of all the weights to be optimized, ![f 1 left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denotes the complexity of ![n e t](images/c09-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math> with the weights being ![bold x](images/c09-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, and ![f 2 left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denotes the training loss of ![n e t](images/c09-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></math> averaged over all the samples in ![upper D](images/c09-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>. In practice, the network complexity can be measured by the number of nonzero weights [\[39\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0039) or the sum of absolute weights [\[32\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0032), while the training loss can be classification error as [\[9\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0009) or reconstruction error [\[10\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010).

Since each solution contains two objective values, the quality of solutions is usually determined by the Pareto dominance relation. Specifically, a solution ![bold x 1](images/c09-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> is said to Pareto dominate solution ![bold x 2](images/c09-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, denoted as ![bold x 1 precedes bold x 2](images/c09-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8826;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, if and only if the following conditions hold:

(9.2)![StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column for-all i 2nd Column equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma m comma f Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold x 1 right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to f Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold x 2 right-parenthesis comma 2nd Row 1st Column there-exists j 2nd Column equals 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma m comma f Subscript j Baseline left-parenthesis bold x 1 right-parenthesis less-than f Subscript j Baseline left-parenthesis bold x 2 right-parenthesis comma EndLayout](images/c09-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>i</mi></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#8707;</mo><mi>j</mi></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![m](images/c09-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is the number of objectives and equals to two in this section. The goal of multi‐objective neural network training is to find a set of solutions approximating the Pareto front, presenting trade‐offs between the neural network complexity and training loss.

 

### 9.2.2 Gradient‐Guided Evolutionary Multi‐Objective Training of Deep Neural Networks

 

#### 9.2.2.1 Motivations

In spite of the promising performance of existing evolutionary approaches to training NNs, most of them encounter difficulties in optimizing a large number of weights in DNNs [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011). The limitation of these approaches can mainly be attributed to the dimension reduction strategies they employ, which typically can address the curse of dimensionality to some extent but is easily vulnerable to get trapped in local optima [\[34\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0034). Hence, these approaches have to reduce the number of optimized weights due to the limitation of the search ability of EAs for large‐scale optimization [\[32\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0032). Besides, there are some approaches \[[8](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0008), [31](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0031)\] directly combining EAs and the GD to conduct search in the original search space, where the weights are successively updated by a traditional genetic operator and GD. However, the poor scalability of EAs to large‐scale optimization problems is also not overcame. In other words, the EA in these approaches can only guarantee that the best fitness in the population does not degrade, while the GD is mainly responsible for finding better solutions in the original search space.

To better understanding the limitation of traditional genetic operators, [Fig. 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001) illustrates the difference between the search behaviors of genetic operators and GD in optimizing a multimodal function ![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. More specifically, the popular genetic operator simulated binary crossover (SBX) [\[35\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0035) is taken as an example in [Fig. 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001)(a), where the generated offspring solutions distribute on both sides of the parent ![bold x](images/c09-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, since SBX determines the search direction randomly and enables more unknown areas to be explored. In other words, SBX makes many unnecessary search efforts, which becomes even more serious in optimizing the weights of DNNs in a high‐dimensional search space. The GD method, by contrast, has shown better exploitation ability since the search direction is always opposite to the gradient of ![bold x](images/c09-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, as shown in [Fig. 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001)(b). However, an unsuitable step size (determined by the learning rate) is likely to drive ![bold x](images/c09-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> to a local optimum.

![Figure 9.1 Search behaviors of the simulated binary crossover (SBX) and the gradient descent on a minimization problem f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis. (a) The offspring solutions generated by the genetic operator (SBX). (b) The offspring solution generated by the gradient descent. (c) The offspring solutions generated by combining SBX with the gradient descent.](images/c09f001.png)

[**Figure 9.1**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0001) Search behaviors of the simulated binary crossover (SBX) and the gradient descent on a minimization problem ![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. (a) The offspring solutions generated by the genetic operator (SBX). (b) The offspring solution generated by the gradient descent. (c) The offspring solutions generated by combining SBX with the gradient descent.

As illustrated in [Fig. 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001)(c), the weakness of SBX, i.e., it generates offspring solutions only in the expected direction, can be remedied by the GD. Vice versa, the vulnerability of the gradient approach to local optimums can be alleviated by the genetic operator. To be more specific, the introduction of gradient information into the genetic operator can guide the search behavior toward promising directions, thereby significantly enhancing the search efficiency. Meanwhile, the generation of multiple offspring solutions can considerably reduce the probability of getting trapped into local optima and improve the exploration ability of the GD. In addition, this combination also eliminates the use of learning rate, which is difficult to be predefined or adapted.

Following the above basic idea, a gradient‐guided evolutionary search approach to training DNNs will be presented below. In contrast to existing approaches that are usually tailored for a specific type of DNN, the proposed generic approach is applicable to different types of DNNs.

 

#### 9.2.2.2 Simulated Binary Crossover

In recent years, many crossover operators have been proposed for real‐coded EAs, such as SBX, UNDX [\[40\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0040), and DE [\[41\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0041). Among these crossovers, SBX exhibits better performance on most test problems as demonstrated in [\[42\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0042). Therefore, we adopt SBX as the basic genetic operator, which is widely used for solving continuous optimization problems. Formally, given two parents ![bold x 1](images/c09-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold x 2](images/c09-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> with ![n](images/c09-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> decision variables, SBX generates two offspring solutions ![bold c 1](images/c09-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold c 2](images/c09-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> by
