For a visual observation of the search behavior of SBX, [Fig. 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0003)(a) depicts the probability distribution of the offspring solutions generated by SBX, based on two one‐dimensional parents ![x 1 equals 0.2](images/c09-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></math> and ![x 2 equals 0.7](images/c09-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></math>. It can be seen that the offspring solutions locate on the left and right sides of each parent with the same probability. By taking into account of the gradient information, as shown in [Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0003)b, the offspring solutions should only locate on the left side of the first parent ![x 1](images/c09-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and the right side of the second parent ![x 2](images/c09-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, where the gradient ![g 1](images/c09-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> of the first parent is assumed to be positive and the gradient ![g 2](images/c09-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> of the second parent is assumed to be negative. Next, we elaborate how the gradient information can be incorporated into SBX.

![Figure 9.3 Probability distribution of the offspring solutions generated based on two parents x 1 equals 0.2 and x 2 equals 0.7 by SBX and a modified SBX. (a) Offspring solutions generated by SBX. (b) Offspring solutions generated by a modified SBX.](images/c09f003.png)

[**Figure 9.3**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0003) Probability distribution of the offspring solutions generated based on two parents ![x 1 equals 0.2](images/c09-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></math> and ![x 2 equals 0.7](images/c09-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></math> by SBX and a modified SBX. (a) Offspring solutions generated by SBX. (b) Offspring solutions generated by a modified SBX.

By rewriting Eq. ([9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0003)), we have

Since the value of ![left-parenthesis bold x 1 Superscript i Baseline minus bold x 2 Superscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is given, the sign of ![bold-italic alpha 1 Superscript i](images/c09-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![bold-italic alpha 2 Superscript i](images/c09-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> can be changed as desired by tuning ![mu](images/c09-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> according to ([9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0004)) and ([9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0006)). #### 9.2.2.4 Uniform Crossover in gSBX

The idea of uniform crossover is also adopted in gSBX, which has been used in many existing genetic operators for improving the diversity [\[43\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0043). Specifically, the uniform crossover exchanges the decision variables in each dimension of the two offspring solutions ![bold c 1](images/c09-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold c 2](images/c09-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> at a probability of 0.5. According to ([9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0005)), we have

Additional attention should be paid when exchanging ![bold c 1 Superscript i](images/c09-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![bold c 2 Superscript i](images/c09-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>. For example, if gradient ![bold g 1 Superscript i Baseline greater-than 0](images/c09-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, it is unreasonable to change ![bold c 1 Superscript i](images/c09-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> to ![bold c 2 Superscript i](images/c09-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> when ![bold x 1 Superscript i Baseline less-than bold x 2 Superscript i](images/c09-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#60;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>, since ![bold x 1 Superscript i](images/c09-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> should be moved along the negative direction of ![bold g 1 Superscript i](images/c09-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math>. Therefore, some restrictions should be applied to limit the uniform crossover, where the uniform crossover can be performed only when ![bold g 1 Superscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold x 1 Superscript i Baseline minus bold x 2 Superscript i Baseline right-parenthesis greater-than 0](images/c09-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![bold g 2 Superscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold x 1 Superscript i Baseline minus bold x 2 Superscript i Baseline right-parenthesis less-than 0](images/c09-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. To sum up, the proposed gSBX sets ![alpha 1](images/c09-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![alpha 2](images/c09-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> as

#### 9.2.2.5 Sparsity in gSBX

To maintain the sparsity of the offspring solutions in gSBX, it is intuitive to make the offspring solutions have the same or a higher degree of sparsity than their parents. For this purpose, gSBX sets each decision variable of an offspring solution to zero if the variable of the corresponding parent is zero. Thus, the number of zero weights in the offspring solution is always equal to or larger than the number of zero weights in the parent. According to ([9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0005)), ![bold c 1 Superscript i Baseline equals bold x 1 Superscript i Baseline equals 0](images/c09-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> holds if we set ![alpha 1 equals 0](images/c09-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. As a result, the proposed gSBX further repairs ![alpha 1](images/c09-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![alpha 2](images/c09-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> by

#### 9.2.2.6 Procedure of gSBX

The main steps of gSBX are listed in Algorithm 9.1. It can be seen from the algorithm that two parents, ![bold x 1](images/c09-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold x 2](images/c09-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, are randomly selected from population ![upper P](images/c09-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>, which are used to generate two offspring solutions ![bold c 1](images/c09-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold c 2](images/c09-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>. For each dimension, ![mu 1](images/c09-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![mu 2](images/c09-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![beta 1](images/c09-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![beta 2](images/c09-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>, ![alpha 1](images/c09-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and ![alpha 2](images/c09-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> are determined in sequence, and the decision variables ![bold c 1 Superscript i](images/c09-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![bold c 2 Superscript i](images/c09-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> are calculated accordingly. All solutions in ![upper P](images/c09-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> go through this procedure, and all newly generated solutions form the offspring population.

A preliminary comparative study is performed to verify the advantage of the proposed gSBX over original SBX. In the comparison, both gSBX and SBX are implemented in a simple genetic algorithm to minimize the following function:

(9.15)![min Underscript bold x Endscripts bold f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript 40 Endscripts x Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline minus one half sigma-summation Underscript i equals 41 Overscript 60 Endscripts x Subscript i Baseline sine left-parenthesis StartRoot StartAbsoluteValue x Subscript i Baseline EndAbsoluteValue EndRoot right-parenthesis comma](images/c09-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>40</mn></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>41</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mi>sin</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![bold x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x 60 right-parenthesis element-of left-bracket negative 500 comma 500 right-bracket Superscript 60](images/c09-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>500</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>500</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></msup></math>. The population size is set to 100 and the number of generations is 100. Besides, the GD with a learning rate of 0.1 is also adopted to minimize the function for 10,000 epochs. The minimum objective values found by the steepest descent method, genetic algorithm with SBX, and genetic algorithm with the proposed gSBX are plotted in [Fig. 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0004). It can be found that the steepest descent method quickly gets stuck a local optimum, while SBX is able to find an acceptable solution, although it converges slower than the steepest descent method. The proposed gSBX has a similar convergence speed to the gradient method, and finds a similar objective value to SBX. From these results, we can conclude that gSBX can strike a balance between exploitation and exploration. Therefore, it is expected to be efficient in training DNNs with a large number of weights.

![Figure 9.4 Profiles of the minimum objective value found by the gradient method, a genetic algorithm with SBX, and a genetic algorithm with the proposed gSBX on an objective function with mixed landscape.](images/c09f004.png)

[**Figure 9.4**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0004) Profiles of the minimum objective value found by the gradient method, a genetic algorithm with SBX, and a genetic algorithm with the proposed gSBX on an objective function with mixed landscape.

Based on the proposed gSBX, a gradient‐guided evolutionary approach is proposed to train DNNs, the details of which are presented in the next subsection.

 

### 9.2.3 Framework of GEMONN

Algorithm 9.2 presents the procedure of the proposed GEMONN. To begin with, a population with predefined size is initialized, where the decision variables (i.e., weights) of each solution are set to a random value within ![left-bracket negative 1 comma 1 right-bracket](images/c09-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> or 0 with the same probability. Then, the objective values of each solution are evaluated and the gradient in terms of the training loss is calculated. In each generation of GEMONN, a number of solutions is selected from the population by the mating selection strategy of NSGA‐II [\[44\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0044) and used to generate the same number of offspring solutions by the proposed gSBX. Then, the offspring population is combined with the parent population, and half the solutions in the combined population are retained for the next generation by the environmental selection strategy of NSGA‐II. After the evolution terminates, a single solution should be picked up from the final population as the output. For this purpose, strategies for updating Pareto optimal solutions and for selecting a final solution are developed.

A flowchart of the proposed GEMONN is plotted in [Fig. 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0005). In the following, the details of the main components of GEMONN, including solution evaluation, Pareto optimal solution update, and final solution selection, are described separately.

![Figure 9.5 Overall flowchart of the proposed GEMONN.](images/c09f005.png)

[**Figure 9.5**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0005) Overall flowchart of the proposed GEMONN.

where ![bold y Subscript i Superscript j](images/c09-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> denotes the ![j](images/c09-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>th label of the ![i](images/c09-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th sample, ![bold s Subscript i Superscript j](images/c09-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> denotes the ![j](images/c09-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>th feature of the ![i](images/c09-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th sample, ![l](images/c09-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> is the total number of labels, and ![m](images/c09-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is the total number of features.

Since the network may overfit the training data if only the training loss is minimized, we consider the network complexity to alleviate overfitting. As shown in [\[9\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0009), the two objectives ![f 1](images/c09-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and ![f 2](images/c09-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math> are conflicting with each other since a network with lower training loss usually corresponds to a higher complexity. Owing to the delicate selection strategy provided by evolutionary multi‐objective optimization, however, a set of solutions striking a good trade‐off between the two objectives can be found, and a network with acceptable training loss without overfitting the training set is expected to be obtained.

 

#### 9.2.3.2 Update of Pareto Optimal Solutions

Once the evolutionary optimization process is completed, a strategy for updating Pareto optimal solutions is designed for the final exploitation. To be specific, the dominated solutions in the population are removed, and then each non‐dominated solution is fine‐tuned by SGD [\[46\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0046) with a learning rate of 0.1 for one epoch. It is worth noting that only the nonzero weights are updated here, while the zero weights are kept unchanged. Such the proposed trick can decrease the training loss while maintaining the network sparsity, and we call it sparse stochastic gradient descent (SSGD) hereafter.

 

#### 9.2.3.3 Final Solution Selection

Last but not the least, a single solution should be selected from the fine‐tuned population as the output. Intuitively, it is unreasonable to select the solution with the lowest training loss or complexity, as the former tends to overfit the training set and the latter is usually not well trained. Since the solutions in the knee area of the population have a better trade‐off between the two objectives [\[9\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0009), they are usually preferred in many scenarios \[[10](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010), [31](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0031)\]. Based on this idea, the proposed GEMONN selects a solution ![bold p](images/c09-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow></math> according to the following criteria:

The second criterion also aims to guarantee the training performance of the selected solution. The third criterion is used to find the final solution according to ![gamma left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which calculates the angle between the left and right neighbors of the solution [\[47\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0047).

 

#### 9.2.3.4 Time Complexity Analysis

 The time complexity of proposed GEMONN is mainly determined by two components, i.e., the calculation of gradients and the optimization process of NSGA‐II. According to [\[48\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0048), the time complexity for calculating the gradients is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N times m right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![upper N](images/c09-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> and ![m](images/c09-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are the size of a mini‐batch and feature dimensionality, respectively. The time complexity of one generation of NSGA‐II is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper P o p squared right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> [\[44\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0044), where ![upper P o p](images/c09-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> is the population size. Therefore, the overall time complexity of GEMONN is ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N times m times upper P o p times upper G e n right-parenthesis plus upper O left-parenthesis upper P o p squared times upper G e n right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><msup><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Since ![upper N times m much-greater-than upper P o p](images/c09-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8811;</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> in general, the time complexity of GEMONN can be regarded as ![upper O left-parenthesis upper N times m times upper P o p times upper G e n right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>G</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which is same as that of SGD [\[48\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0048).

 

### 9.2.4 Empirical Studies

 

#### 9.2.4.1 Neural Networks to be Trained

The performance of the proposed GEMONN is verified on four types of NNs, including AE, SAE [\[49\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0049), LSTM [\[50\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0050), and CNNs [\[18\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0018). A brief introduction to the training of the four types of NNs is given in the following.

1.  Auto‐encoder (AE). As a fully connected (FC) feedforward NN with a single hidden layer, AE is often used for dimensionality reduction, where the output is expected to be the same as the input and the hidden layer can be regarded as a meaningful and reduced representation of the training sample. As a result, AE can be trained in an unsupervised manner, and many existing EAs have been adopted to train it \[[10](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010), [11](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011), [31](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0031)\]. To train AE by the proposed GEMONN, the MSE is adopted as the second objective. Besides, the sigmoid activation function is applied in the hidden layer.
2.  Stacked auto‐encoder (SAE). By using AE as the building blocks, SAE can reduce the training sample layer by layer and perform classification at last. With the greedy layer‐wise training process, the dependency of weights in different layers can be properly handled, and the weights in each layer can be optimized separately. The training of SAE consists of two phases \[[11](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011), [51](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0051)\], i.e., pre‐training and fine‐tuning. The pre‐training phase trains a set of AEs with different numbers of hidden nodes by minimizing the reconstruction error. Then, these AEs are stacked together and tailed by an FC layer, and the fine‐tuning phase optimizes all the weights for minimizing the classification error. To train SAE by the proposed GEMONN, the MSE is adopted as the second objective in the pre‐training phase and the CE is adopted in the fine‐tuning phase.
3.  Long short‐term memory (LSTM). LSTM is currently one of the most popular recurrent NNs for many deep‐learning tasks, in which the connections between layers are much more complex than those in feedforward NNs. Since all the weights in LSTM should be optimized together, it is much more difficult than training SAE whose weights are optimized layer by layer, and none of the existing evolutionary approaches have been applied to it. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed genetic operator in training DNNs without dimensionality reduction, we also use the proposed GEMONN to train LSTM with its structure shown in [Fig. 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0006)(a), where the CE is adopted as the second objective.
4.  Convolutional neural networks (CNNs). CNNs are also powerful NNs for many deep learning tasks, especially computer vision. To investigate the ability of GEMONN in training CNNs, we consider the LeNet‐5 [\[52\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0052) and its variant (termed LeNet‐deeper) having more convolutional operations and more filters, as shown in [Fig. 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0006)(c), where a ReLu [\[53\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0053) activation function follows each convolutional operation. To investigate the results on deeper CNNs, a Vgg16 [\[54\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0054) variant with channel setting \[[8](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0008), [16](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0016), [32](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0032), [55](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0055)\] is employed, whose last two FC layers are set to 512 and 256. Besides, an effective cell‐based CNN [\[56\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0056) is also considered, termed Cell‐CNN, whose normal cell and reduction cell are set to the best architecture founded in [\[18\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0018), as plotted in [Fig. 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0006)(b) and (d). To facilitate the training of the Cell‐CNN, as suggested in [\[24\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0024), the neural network contains 6 cells, 16 filters in all the nodes, and an auxiliary head classifier with a loss weight of 0.4.

![Figure 9.6 The structure of used NNs, including LSTM, LeNet‐5 as well as its variant (deeper and more filters), and cell‐based CNN. (a) LSTM. (b) Cell‐CNN (normal cell). (c) LeNet‐5 and its variant. (d) Cell‐CNN (reduction cell).](images/c09f006.png)

[**Figure 9.6**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0006) The structure of used NNs, including LSTM, LeNet‐5 as well as its variant (deeper and more filters), and cell‐based CNN. (a) LSTM. (b) Cell‐CNN (normal cell). (c) LeNet‐5 and its variant. (d) Cell‐CNN (reduction cell).

 

#### 9.2.4.2 Benchmark Datasets

As listed in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001), 17 widely used datasets are adopted in the experiments. The first 10 datasets including MNIST [\[52\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0052) as well as its variants [\[57\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0057) and Cifar10‐bw [\[58\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0058) are used in the experiments in training AE and SAE. The next six datasets are collected from the UCR time series classification archive [\[59\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0059) and used in the experiments of training LSTMs. Besides, the last dataset Cifar10 [\[58\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0058) is used in the experiments of CNNs.

![Table 9.1  Characteristics of 17 Chosen Benchmark Datasets.](images/c09-i0157.png)

[**Table 9.1**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-tbl-0001)  Characteristics of 17 Chosen Benchmark Datasets.

 

#### 9.2.4.3 Compared Algorithms

Since the experiments are conducted on AE, SAE, LSTM, and CNNs, different comparison approaches have to be selected for different NNs.

 

***Algorithms for Training AE*** The following comparison approaches are chosen for training the AE:

*   SGD [\[4\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004). Stochastic GD;
*   Adam [\[6\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006). A method for stochastic optimization;
*   NSGA‐II [\[44\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0044). NSGA‐II with SBX operator;
*   NSGA‐II (+gradient). Based on NSGA‐II, update all offspring solutions by SGD for one step at each generation;
*   NSGA‐II (+gradient![normal bar 0](images/c09-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mn>0</mn></math>). Based on NSGA‐II, update all offspring solutions by SSGD for one step at each generation;
*   GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>SSGD). GEMONN without updating the Pareto optimal solutions by SSGD;
*   GEMONN (single). GEMONN without optimizing sparsity by [Eq. (9.16)](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0016);
*   GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>S). GEMONN without considering sparsity by Eqs. ([9.13](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0013)) and ([9.14](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0014));
*   GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>G). GEMONN without using gradient information by Eqs. ([9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0008)), ([9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0009)), ([9.11](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0011)), and ([9.12](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0012)).

SGD and Adam are two most popular gradient‐based approaches for training DNNs with millions of weights, which can be used as baselines to validate whether the performance of GEMONN is promising or not. NSGA‐II, NSGA‐II (+gradient), and NSGA‐II (+gradient![normal bar 0](images/c09-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mn>0</mn></math>) are used to verify the effectiveness of the proposed genetic operator gSBX, since the other components of NSGA‐II and GEMONN, i.e., solution evaluation, mating selection, and environmental selection, are completely the same. The remaining GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>SSGD), GEMONN(single), GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>S), and GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>G) are designed for ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of the novel strategies proposed in GEMONN.

 

***Approaches for Training SAE*** The following state‐of‐the‐art approaches are used for training SAE:

*   SDAE [\[60\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0060). Stacked denoising AEs;
*   SCAE [\[61\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0061). Stacked contractive AEs;
*   SSAE [\[62\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0062). Stacked sparse AEs;
*   EUDNN [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011). An evolutionary approach for training unsupervised DNNs.

As introduced in [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011), SDAE, SCAE, and SSAE are three state‐of‐the‐art gradient‐based approaches for training SAE, which incorporate various problem independent regularization terms to decrease the network complexity for alleviating overfitting. Besides, the evolutionary approach EUDNN is considered as the state‐of‐the‐art, which can effectively train large‐scale DNNs with the help of dimensionality reduction. As a result, the comparison between GEMONN and the chosen algorithms is meaningful and convincing.

 

***Algorithms for Training LSTM and CNNs*** Only SGD and Adam are considered for training LSTM and CNNs in the comparative studies, since these two approaches are very popular and effective for optimizing the large number of weights together. Besides, existing EAs, including EUDNN, are not well suited for training them due to their poor performance resulted from the curse of dimensionality.

 

#### 9.2.4.4 Parameter Settings

The parameter settings for all the compared approaches are given below.

 

***Parameters in Training AE*** The number of hidden units of the AE is set to 500, which means that the total number of weights to be optimized is ![left-parenthesis 28 asterisk 28 plus 1 right-parenthesis asterisk 500](images/c09-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>500</mn></math>. Besides, the following settings are used in the compared approaches:

*   SGD and Adam. The learning rate varies in ![StartSet 0.1 comma 0.01 comma 0.001 EndSet](images/c09-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.001</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>; the batch size is set to 64; and the maximal number of training steps is set to ![50 asterisk 500](images/c09-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>50</mn><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>500</mn></math>, to be consistent with the evolutionary approaches.
*   NSGA‐II and its variants. The population size is set to 50; the maximum number of generations is set to 500.
*   GEMONN and its variants. The population size is set to 50 and the maximum generation is set to 500.

As a result, all the compared approaches have the same number of function evaluations that calculates the output and the gradient over all the training samples for fairness.

 

***Parameters in training SAE*** The number of units in each layer of SAE is empirically set to \[![i n p u t](images/c09-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, 500, 400, 300, 200, 100, ![o u t p u t](images/c09-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></math>\], where ![i n p u t](images/c09-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></math> is the dimension of features and ![o u t p u t](images/c09-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></math> is the number of classes of the dataset. The following parameter settings are used in the comparative studies, which also ensures that all the compared approaches consume the same number of function evaluations:

*   SDAE, SCAE, and SSAE. Following the settings in [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011), the SGD is chosen as the training approach, where the learning rate varies in ![StartSet 0.1 comma 0.01 comma 0.001 EndSet](images/c09-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.001</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, and the batch size is set to 64; the maximum number of training epochs is set to ![50 asterisk 500](images/c09-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>50</mn><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>500</mn></math>; the binary corrupted level of SDAE, the sparsity of SSAE, the coefficient of the contractive term in SCAE is set to ![StartSet 0.1 comma 0.3 comma 0.5 comma 0.7 EndSet](images/c09-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.7</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, respectively.
*   EUDNN. The population size is set to 50; the maximum iteration is set to 500; other parameters follow the original settings in the literature.
*   GEMONN. The population size is set to 50; maximum generation is set to 500.

 

***Parameters in Training LSTM and CNNs*** The sizes of the input layer, hidden layer, and output layer of a 2‐layer LSTM are set to ![i n p u t](images/c09-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, 100, and ![o u t p u t](images/c09-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></math>, respectively, and the parameters in CNNs are presented in [Section 9.2.4.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0019). The following settings are used in the compared approaches:

*   SGD and Adam. The learning rate varies in ![StartSet 0.1 comma 0.01 comma 0.001 EndSet](images/c09-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.001</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, and the batch size is set to 64 for LSTM and CNNs; The maximum number of training epochs is set to ![50 asterisk 100](images/c09-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>50</mn><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>100</mn></math> for LSTM and ![50 asterisk 500](images/c09-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>50</mn><mo>&#42;</mo><mn>500</mn></math> for CNNs.
*   GEMONN. The population size is set to 50; and the maximum number of generations is set to 100 for LSTM and 500 for CNNs.

All models and the gradient‐based approaches are implemented in Pytorch [\[63\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0063), and GEMONN as well as variants of NSGA‐II are implemented in Numpy [\[64\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0064). These experiments were performed on a Windows 10 computer with an Intel i7‐8700k CPU and an NVIDIA 1080 GPU. The source code of the proposed approach is made available from [https://github.com/smartdonckey/GEMONN](https://github.com/smartdonckey/GEMONN).

 

#### 9.2.4.5 Experimental Results on AE

[Figure 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0007) presents the solutions obtained by all algorithms under comparison in the objective space. It can also be found that the performance of SGD and Adam highly relies on the learning rate, as the solutions obtained by SGD (0.1) outperform SGD (0.01) and SGD (0.001), while Adam (0.1) is also much worse than Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001). Moreover, the solutions obtained by SGD and Adam are not sparse at all, which may affect the generalization of the model and result in overfitting.

![Figure 9.7 The final solutions obtained by the compared approaches on the MNIST dataset, where “SGD (0.1)” denotes the SGD with a learning rate of 0.1.](images/c09f007.png)

[**Figure 9.7**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0007) The final solutions obtained by the compared approaches on the MNIST dataset, where “SGD (0.1)” denotes the SGD with a learning rate of 0.1.

On the other hand, the solutions obtained by NSGA‐II have poor convergence in terms of the MSE and we cannot find any valuable solution due to the poor search ability of the existing genetic operators. With the assistance of the gradient information, the solutions obtained by NSGA‐II (+gradient![normal bar 0](images/c09-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mn>0</mn></math>) are better than those obtained by NSGA‐II, which verifies the importance of introducing gradient information into EAs. Nevertheless, the performance of NSGA‐II and its variants is much worse than the gradient‐based approaches and the proposed GEMONN.

The proposed GEMONN exhibits quite competitive performance compared to SGD, Adam, and NSGA‐II. On the one hand, it can be seen that the solutions acquired by GEMONN are very promising, whose MSE is just worse than those obtained by Adam (0.001) and Adam (0.01) but much better than those obtained by the other approaches. On the other hand, the sparsity of the solutions acquired by GEMONN is similar to those obtained by NSGA‐II but much better than those obtained by SGD and Adam. In short, the AE trained by the proposed GEMONN can have a relatively low MSE with satisfactory sparsity.

To investigate the convergence speed of the compared approaches, [Fig. 9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0008) depicts the decline in MSE of all the compared approaches, with the increase of the number of function evaluations, where the observation is consistent with [Fig. 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0007). More specifically, GEMONN outperforms NSGA‐II and most gradient‐based approaches, while it converges slower than Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001).

![Figure 9.8 Performance changes in MSE of the compared approaches on the MNIST dataset.](images/c09f008.png)

[**Figure 9.8**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0008) Performance changes in MSE of the compared approaches on the MNIST dataset.

As a result, solutions obtained by the proposed GEMONN have better sparsity but worse training loss than those obtained by Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001). To further investigate which solutions are better for classification, an FC layer is tailored for the AE and trained in a supervised manner. [Figure 9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0009) presents the mean correct classification rate (CCR) [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011) on test set obtained by SGD, Adam, and the proposed GEMONN, averaged over 30 runs. Besides, a three‐layer FC network with the same size is directly trained for the classification task and used as the baseline. By contrast, the results of NSGA‐II are ignored since the obtained CCR values are quite poor. It can be observed from [Fig. 9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0009) that the mean CCR values obtained by GEMONN are better than all the other compared approaches including Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001), though the solutions found by Adam (0.01) and Adam (0.001) are with lower MSE than GEMONN as shown in [Fig. 9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0008). Therefore, it can be inferred that the AEs trained by Adam overfit the training set to some extent, whereas the sparse AEs obtained by GEMONN can alleviate overfitting.

![Figure 9.9 The mean CCR values of the proposed GEMONN against SGD, Adam, and the baseline for training the AE tailed by a classification layer. The tick labels “A–J” denote the datasets of MNIST, MNIST‐basic, MNIST‐rot, MNIST‐back‐rand, MNIST‐back‐image, MNIST‐rot‐back‐image, rectangles, rectangles‐image, convex, and Cifar10‐bw, respectively.](images/c09f009.png)

[**Figure 9.9**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0009) The mean CCR values of the proposed GEMONN against SGD, Adam, and the baseline for training the AE tailed by a classification layer. The tick labels “A–J” denote the datasets of MNIST, MNIST‐basic, MNIST‐rot, MNIST‐back‐rand, MNIST‐back‐image, MNIST‐rot‐back‐image, rectangles, rectangles‐image, convex, and Cifar10‐bw, respectively.

For visual observation of the difference between the sparsity of the AEs obtained by the compared approaches, [Fig. 9.10](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0010) draws the connections between the input layer and hidden layer of the AEs obtained by Adam (0.01), Adam (0.001), SGD (0.1), and GEMONN on the MNIST dataset, where a darker color indicates a denser connection between weights. It is obvious that the AE obtained by GEMONN is much sparser than those obtained by the gradient‐based approaches. Moreover, [Fig. 9.11](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0011) plots the connections between the input layer and the hidden layer of the AE obtained by GEMONN at different generations on the MNIST dataset. For better visualization, each graphic in [Fig. 9.11](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0011) consists of 500 binary images, where each image has ![28 times 28](images/c09-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn></math> pixels and each pixel indicates whether the corresponding input unit is connected to a hidden unit or not. Besides, a gray pixel indicates a connection between the input unit and a hidden unit, while a white dot indicates there is no connection. As can be seen from [Fig. 9.11](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0011), the AE is not sparse at the beginning, while it gradually becomes sparse as the population evolves. As a consequence, the proposed GEMONN can effectively control the sparsity of the obtained NN, and such a sparse nature is crucial for preventing the model from overfitting.

![Figure 9.10 Connections between the input and hidden layers of the AEs obtained by Adam (0.01), Adam (0.001), SGD (0.1), and GEMONN on the MNIST dataset. A darker color indicates a denser connection between weights. (a) Adam (0.01). (b) Adam (0.001). (c) SGD (0.1). (d) GEMONN.](images/c09f010.png)

[**Figure 9.10**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0010) Connections between the input and hidden layers of the AEs obtained by Adam (0.01), Adam (0.001), SGD (0.1), and GEMONN on the MNIST dataset. A darker color indicates a denser connection between weights. (a) Adam (0.01). (b) Adam (0.001). (c) SGD (0.1). (d) GEMONN.

![Figure 9.11 Connections between the input and hidden layers of the AE obtained by GEMONN at different generations on the MNIST dataset. A gray pixel indicates an input unit is connected to a hidden unit, while a white pixel indicates there is no connection. (a) 1st generation. (b) 10th generation. (c) 100th generation. (d) 500th generation.](images/c09f011.png)

A gray pixel indicates an input unit is connected to a hidden unit, while a white pixel indicates there is no connection. (a) 1st generation. (b) 10th generation. (c) 100th generation. (d) 500th generation.

Afterward, the effectiveness of the novel strategies proposed in GEMONN is verified by ablation studies. First, GEMONN is compared to GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>SSGD) on the MNIST dataset to verify the effectiveness of the SSGD based the update strategy for Pareto optimal solutions. According to the solutions obtained by GEMONN and GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>SSGD) shown in [Fig. 9.12](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0012)(a), it is clear that the solutions obtained by GEMONN dominate most solutions obtained by GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>SSGD), hence the effectiveness of SSGD is confirmed. Second, [Fig. 9.12](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0012)(b) depicts the effectiveness of considering the optimization of sparsity within GEMONN. As can be seen that the final solutions of GEMONN (single) have higher training CCR values than that of GEMONN on all 10 datasets, however, GEMONN can obtain better test CCR values than GEMONN (single). The crucial reason is that GEMONN (single) encounters the overfitting problem to some extent due to the optimization not considering the sparsity restriction. According to the above comparisons in Figs. [9.8](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0008), [9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0009), and [9.12](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0012)(b), it is indeed an effective way to mitigate the overfitting by considering sparsity in optimization. Third, GEMONN is compared to GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>G) and GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>S) on the MNIST dataset to verify the effectiveness of the gradient information in the proposed genetic operator. As can be seen from [Fig. 9.13](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0013)(a), the solutions obtained by GEMONN are superior over those obtained by GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>G) and GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>S) in terms of both the sparsity and MSE. Besides, GEMONN converges significantly faster than GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>G) and GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>S) in terms of the hypervolume indicator (HV) [\[55\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0055), as shown in [Fig. 9.13](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0013)(b). Therefore, the effectiveness of the novel strategies proposed in GEMONN can be verified.

![Figure 9.12 The validation of proposed strategies by comparing the performance of GEMONN and its variants. (a) Solutions obtained by GEMONN and GEMONN (minusSSGD) on the MNIST dataset. (b) Comparison between GEMONN and GEMONN (single) in terms of training and test CCR values.](images/c09f012.png)

[**Figure 9.12**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0012) The validation of proposed strategies by comparing the performance of GEMONN and its variants. (a) Solutions obtained by GEMONN and GEMONN (![minus](images/c09-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>SSGD) on the MNIST dataset. (b) Comparison between GEMONN and GEMONN (single) in terms of training and test CCR values.

![Figure 9.13 Comparison between the performance of GEMONN and its variants on the MNIST dataset. (a) Solutions obtained by GEMONN and its variants. (b) Convergence profiles of HV of GEMONN and its variants.](images/c09f013.png)

[**Figure 9.13**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0013) Comparison between the performance of GEMONN and its variants on the MNIST dataset. (a) Solutions obtained by GEMONN and its variants. (b) Convergence profiles of HV of GEMONN and its variants.

Lastly, a parameter sensitivity analysis of the population size ![upper P o p](images/c09-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> and distribution index ![eta](images/c09-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> in GEMONN is conducted. [Figure 9.14](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0014)(a) shows the HV values obtained by GEMONN on four datasets MNIST, MNIST‐rot, rectangles, and convex with different population sizes, where it can be seen that GEMONN can obtain a relatively good performance when the population size is larger than 50. It is not necessary to set ![upper P o p](images/c09-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> to 100 for a slightly higher HV value at the expense of a doubled number of fitness evaluations. The results of sensitivity analysis of the distribution index ![eta](images/c09-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> in GEMONN on four datasets TwoPatterns, ECG5000, UWaveGestureLibraryX, and InsectWingbeatSound are plotted in [Fig. 9.14](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0014)(b). From this figure, we can see that the proposed GEMONN can obtain the best performance with the distribution index being equal to 15 or 20. Thus, the recommended ![eta equals 20](images/c09-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math> in [\[35\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0035) is also suitable and effective for GEMONN.

![Figure 9.14 Parameter sensitivity analysis to population size and distribution index. (a) Sensitivity to population size. (b) Sensitivity to distribution index.](images/c09f014.png)

[**Figure 9.14**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0014) Parameter sensitivity analysis to population size and distribution index. (a) Sensitivity to population size. (b) Sensitivity to distribution index.

 

#### 9.2.4.6 Experimental Results on SAE

[Table 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0002) lists the CCR values of the SAEs obtained by GEMONN, EUDNN, SSAE, SCAE, and SDAE on the nine Datasets, where each cell in the table records the mean and standard deviation of the CCR values obtained in 30 independent runs. #### 9.2.4.7 Experimental Results on LSTM and CNNs

The comparison between the proposed GEMONN and gradient‐based approaches in training LSTM is presented in [Table 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0004). The results are calculated based on 30 independent runs, and the Wilcoxon rank sum test is also employed. Note that due to the poor performance of Adam (0.1) and SGD (0.001), only the results of Adam (0.001), Adam (0.01), SGD (0.01), and SGD (0.1) are listed in the table. As can be seen, the overall performance of GEMONN is better than the gradient‐based approaches, having achieved the largest average CCR values on four out of six datasets. Besides, Adam (0.01) and SGD (0.1) obtain the largest average CCR values on the remaining two datasets. In short, the performance of GEMONN is significantly better than Adam (0.001) as well as SGD (0.01) and competitive to Adam (0.01) and SGD (0.1). In addition, it is worth to note that the performance of Adam is sensitive to the learning rate since Adam (0.01) outperforms Adam (0.001) on ECG5000 and ElectricDevicess, but Adam (0.001) outperforms Adam (0.01) on FordA and UWaveGestureLibraryX. By contrast, the GEMONN does not contain the learning rate or any other sensitive parameter, which is also a superiority of evolutionary approaches over gradient‐based approaches.

The comparative results between GEMONN and the gradient‐based approaches in training CNNs on Cifar10 dataset are shown in [Fig. 9.16](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0016), where the mean test accuracy over 30 independent runs is plotted. Note that the result of SGD (0.001) is not given due to its poor performance. From this figure, it can be observed that GEMONN outperforms gradient‐based approaches on LeNet‐5, and the performance of GEMONN is also slightly better than the opponents on LeNet‐deeper. However, Adam (0.001) and Adam (0.01) get the best performance on Vgg16‐variant as well as Cell‐CNN, while GEMONN obtains a competitive performance. It is worth noting that the performance of GEMONN degenerates with the architecture of CNN becoming complex since the proportion of convolutional operation parameters increases from 5% to 98%. Essentially, the weights of a whole CNN can be divided into two parts, including the feature extraction (convolutional) part and the classifier (FC) part. Compared to weights of the FC layers, convolutional operations have much fewer weights due to the intrinsic merit of local connection and weight‐sharing, where most weights of convolutional layers should not be optimized to zero during the training process [\[66\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0066). To gain a deep insight into the weights of each part obtained by GEMONN, [Fig. 9.17](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0017) depicts the percentage of nonzero weights in four CNNs obtained by GEMONN and Adam. It is clear that the weights of convolutional layers obtained by the proposed approach are much sparser than that of Adam; hence, the final performance of GEMONN may be slightly worse than the best gradient‐based approaches. Nevertheless, EMONN still holds a competitive performance compared to SGD and Adam.

## 9.3 Action Command Encoding‐Based Surrogate‐Assisted Evolutionary Algorithm for Neural Architecture Search

NAS appeared in the 1980s [\[67\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0067) and manifested an explosive growth in recent years [\[23\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0023), where various optimizers have been adopted to automatically determine the desired hyperparameters and topologies of neural networks especially CNNs. For example, NEAT [\[29\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0029) optimizes both the topologies and weights of feedforward neural networks by genetic algorithm; The work in [\[68\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0068) adopts the tree‐structured Parzen estimator (TPE) [\[69\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0069) to optimize the hyperparameters of CNNs, which represents the search space as an expression graph and optimizes the loss function by sampling hyperparameters in the graph; NAS [\[17\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0017) uses a controller recurrent neural network to generate the hyperparameters and topologies of CNNs and trains the controller by a policy gradient method [\[70\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0070); NAO [\[21\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0021) embeds the hyperparameters and topologies of CNNs into a continuous space by using an LSTM [\[50\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0050), then optimizes it through GD. As can be seen, there have been many optimizers adopted in NAS, such as EAs (e.g., NEAT), Bayesian optimization (e.g., TPE), RL (e.g., NAS), and GD (e.g., NAO). However, only a few encoding schemes have been designed to provide an effective search space to be explored by these optimizers. In addition, although these search methods can generate better architectures than hand‐crafted ones, the performance is improved at the expense of computational resources, where many search methods are criticized for the high computational cost of the search process or the large complexity of the found architectures. In this section, we would like to take a step forward along this line of research, aiming to improve the performance of NAS by presenting a novel encoding scheme, and we also would like to propose an effective EA for NAS with the assistance of the encoding scheme due to the various merits of EAs. However, since EAs are population‐based optimizers, it will further aggravate the expensive computational cost in NAS.

To this end, this section introduces an action command encoding‐based surrogate assisted EA, termed ACEncoding, for NAS by designing a novel encoding scheme and an effective surrogate model. In the proposed action command encoding scheme, an architecture is constructed by some action commands and each action command is specified by three adjoined integers. By predefining a series of action commands including adding a layer, adding a connection, and cloning a local module, the proposed encoding scheme can use multiple action commands to construct complex architectures in a generative manner. Considering that architectures are represented by a variable‐length sequence of integers within a finite range, thus the surrogate model, called Seq2Rank, converts the sequence to a fixed‐length vector by a Seq2Seq model [\[71\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0071), then uses a RankNet [\[72\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0072) to predict the rankings of architectures.

In the following, we first present the mathematical formulation of NAS, then the action command encoding method, the performance evaluator‐based surrogate model, and the framework of the proposed ACEncoding are subsequently presented. Finally, experimental comparisons between the ACEncoding and state‐of‐the‐art approaches for searching CNNs are presented and discussed.

In this chapter, we adopt the bi‐objective optimization problem formulation for NAS, where the number of model parameters is used to measure the model complexity.

 

### 9.3.2 Action Command Encoding Scheme

 

#### 9.3.2.1 Action Commands in the Encoding Scheme

The proposed action command encoding scheme is inspired by the process of gene expression, where each architecture is constructed by a series of action commands and each action command is encoded by three integers. Regarding an architecture as a directed acyclic graph ![upper G equals left-parenthesis upper V comma upper E right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the action command encoding scheme does not directly encode the layer set ![upper V](images/c09-i0325.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> or connection set ![upper E](images/c09-i0326.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> like existing encoding schemes; instead, the architecture grows from empty according to the action commands in the encoding. In the encoding scheme, the following two basic action commands are defined:

1.  (1) Adding a new layer to the architecture.
2.  (2) Adding a new connection to the architecture.
    
    Obviously, these two action commands are enough to represent arbitrary topologies, which is the same as the graph‐based encoding.
    
    However, the encoding will be very long when representing large architectures with dense connections; hence, the following two action commands are also considered in the encoding scheme:
    
3.  (3) Adding a new layer in parallel with an existing one, i.e., the two layers have the same predecessors and successors.
4.  (4) Adding a new layer after an existing one, i.e., the successors of the new layer are set to the same as the existing layer, then the successor of the existing layer is set to the new layer.

These two action commands can generate some complex topologies like the widely used block‐based topology consisting of two parallel layers [\[56\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0056); hence, we believe that they are helpful to find desired architectures more efficiently. Note that the combination operation is omitted here, which is fixed to the element‐wise addition as suggested in many existing encoding schemes \[[21](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0021), [73](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0073), [74](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0074)\]. It is obvious that the graph‐based encoding should use many operations (i.e., adding a new layer and adding multiple connections) to achieve each of these two action commands, especially when the existing layer is connected to many other layers.

Moreover, it has been well recognized that many successful architectures, including GoogLeNet, ResNet, and those generated by block‐based encoding, are composed of repeated modules [\[75\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0075). Therefore, the following two action commands are designed to repeat the local modules in the architecture:

1.  (5) Cloning an existing local module and locating the two local modules in parallel, i.e., the two modules have the same predecessors and successors.
2.  (6) Cloning an existing local module and locating the two local modules in sequence, i.e., the successors of the new module are set to the same as the existing module, then the successor of the existing module is set to the new module.

Here, a local module is defined as a set of layers connected in a chain‐like structure with no branching. Besides, another action command is designed to represent the dense block like those in DenseNet:

1.  (7) Making an existing local module a densely connected block, i.e., each layer is connected to all the others in the module.

By using these seven action commands, the proposed encoding scheme can represent arbitrary topologies and encode some popular blocks in a short sequence. Since these action commands are designed according to the topologies of some popular architectures, the proposed encoding scheme is free to be extended by more action commands for representing the topologies of other effective architectures. Note that each action command does not necessarily appear in the encoding, as an action command will be weeded out during the search process if it always brings a bad performance to the architecture. Besides, it is noteworthy that some basic action commands (e.g., adding a layer or connection) have been adopted in the mutation operator of EA‐based search methods \[[22](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0022), [76](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0076)\], but these action commands cannot be achieved by other optimizers. By contrast, the encoding scheme encodes these action commands in a sequence that can be explored by different optimizers, where an EA, RL, and GD are employed in the experiments.

 

#### 9.3.2.2 Decoding Process of the Proposed Action Command Encoding Scheme

[Table 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0005) lists the *codon* of each action command, where each action command is represented by three integers with different meanings. The first integer in each codon varies from 1 to 7 denoting the index of an action command, while the second and third integers can be one of the three variables ![upper T](images/c09-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, ![upper I](images/c09-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math>, and ![upper L](images/c09-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>. ![upper T](images/c09-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> denotes the type of layer to be added, which varies from 1 to 10 denoting one of the following 10 operations as suggested in [\[21\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0021): (1) ![1 times 1](images/c09-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolution; (2) ![3 times 3](images/c09-i0332.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> convolution; (3) ![1 times 3 plus 3 times 1](images/c09-i0333.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolution; (4) ![1 times 7 plus 7 times 1](images/c09-i0334.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolution; (5) ![2 times 2](images/c09-i0335.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></math> max pooling; (6) ![3 times 3](images/c09-i0336.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> max pooling; (7) ![5 times 5](images/c09-i0337.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math> max pooling; (8) ![2 times 2](images/c09-i0338.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></math> average pooling; (9) ![3 times 3](images/c09-i0339.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> average pooling; (10) ![5 times 5](images/c09-i0340.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math> average pooling. Note that all the operations are tailed by batch normalization. ![upper I](images/c09-i0341.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> denotes the index of an existing layer; note that the first two indices denote the input layer and output layer rather than the generated convolutional or pooling layers. ![upper L](images/c09-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> denotes the length of a local module with chain‐like structure, which consists of ![upper L plus 1](images/c09-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> layers starting from an existing layer.

![Table 9.5  Codon of Each Action Command Defined in the Proposed Encoding Scheme, Where Each Action Command Is Represented by Three Integers. The Variable upper T Denotes the Type of Layer, upper I Denotes the Index of an Existing Layer, and upper L Denotes the Length of Local Module.](images/c09-i0347.png)

[**Table 9.5**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-tbl-0005)  Codon of Each Action Command Defined in the Proposed Encoding Scheme, Where Each Action Command Is Represented by Three Integers. The Variable ![upper T](images/c09-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> Denotes the Type of Layer, ![upper I](images/c09-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> Denotes the Index of an Existing Layer, and ![upper L](images/c09-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> Denotes the Length of Local Module.

[Figure 9.18](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0018) depicts an example to illustrate the decoding process of the encoding scheme, where the sequence contains six action commands determined by 18 integers. The initial architecture has two inputs and an output, and it grows according to the following action commands to form an architecture having 9 layers and 12 connections: Adding a convolutional layer, adding a pooling layer, adding a connection, adding a pooling layer, adding a convolutional layer, and cloning a module. It is worth noting that the action commands do not specify the successor when adding a layer, where the successor is set to the output layer by default (e.g., the connection between the convolutional layer and the output layer shown in [Fig. 9.18](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0018)(a)). If this layer is specified as the predecessor of other layers by the subsequent action commands, the default connection between this layer and the output layer is omitted.

![Figure 9.18 An illustration of the decoding process of the proposed action command encoding scheme. (a) Adding a convolutional layer. (b) Adding a pooling layer and a connection. (c) Adding a pooling layer and a convolutional layer. (d) Cloning a module having two layers.](images/c09f018.png)

[**Figure 9.18**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0018) An illustration of the decoding process of the proposed action command encoding scheme. (a) Adding a convolutional layer. (b) Adding a pooling layer and a connection. (c) Adding a pooling layer and a convolutional layer. (d) Cloning a module having two layers.

In order to provide a finite search space, the variables ![upper I](images/c09-i0368.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper L](images/c09-i0369.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> in the codon are restricted to be less than a maximum value. This maximum value is set to 30 in the experiments, which is enough to represent a relatively large architecture. In addition, since some large values of ![upper I](images/c09-i0370.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> or ![upper L](images/c09-i0371.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> may lead to invalid action commands, they are revised by specific strategies in the decoding process. First, if the layer index ![upper I](images/c09-i0372.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> is larger than the number of existing layers ![upper N](images/c09-i0373.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, ![upper I](images/c09-i0374.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> is changed to ![mod left-parenthesis upper I minus 1 comma upper N right-parenthesis plus 1](images/c09-i0375.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>mod</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Second, if the module length ![upper L](images/c09-i0376.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> exceeds the maximum length of the module (i.e., reaching the output layer or a layer having multiple branches), ![upper L](images/c09-i0377.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> is changed to the maximum length of the module. Third, if the architecture becomes cyclic after adding a connection, the connection is reversed. The procedure of the decoding process of ACEnoding is summarized in Algorithm 9.3.

 

#### 9.3.2.3 Remarks

It can be found from [Fig. 9.18](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0018) that the proposed action command encoding scheme constructs an architecture with a relatively complex topology by using 18 variables. On the contrary, the adjacent matrix‐based encoding requires ![left-bracket 8 times left-parenthesis 7 minus 1 right-parenthesis right-bracket slash 2 equals 28](images/c09-i0378.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>28</mn></math> variables to represent the same topology, the graph‐based encoding requires 6 variables to store the layers and ![12 times 2 equals 24](images/c09-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>12</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></math> variables to store the connections, and the block‐based encoding needs to use four blocks determined by ![5 times 4 equals 20](images/c09-i0380.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math> variables to represent a similar architecture with fewer connections. The shorter encoding is owing to the delicate action commands that inherit the advantages of both graph‐based encoding and block‐based encoding, which provide a more compact search space that facilitates the optimization of architectures. The trade‐off between the length of encoding and the complexity of the represented architecture is automatically balanced by optimizers in the search process, where a bias toward the first four action commands in [Table 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0005) leads to more complex architectures and a bias toward the last three action commands makes the encoding shorter. The main difference between the proposed action command encoding scheme and existing encoding schemes are summarized in the following.

*   *Action command encoding scheme vs. hyperparameter‐based encoding and adjacent matrix‐based encoding*. The hyperparameter‐based encoding and adjacent matrix‐based encoding can only represent the hyperparameters and topologies of architectures, respectively, while the proposed action command encoding scheme can represent both of them. Besides, the proposed encoding scheme specifies a topology by using a series of action commands stored in a sequence, which is much shorter than the adjacent matrix.
*   *Action command encoding scheme vs. graph‐based encoding*. The proposed action command encoding scheme is equivalent to the graph‐based encoding when using only the first two action commands, which are enough to represent arbitrary topologies. By contrast, the proposed encoding scheme can represent specific complex topologies by the other action commands, which cannot be represented by the graph‐based encoding using a short sequence.
*   *Action command encoding scheme vs. block‐based encoding*. Both the proposed action command encoding scheme and the block‐based encoding can represent complex topologies using a short encoding. However, the topologies that can be represented by block‐based encoding are limited by the topology of a single block, whereas arbitrary topologies can be represented by the proposed encoding scheme.

 

### 9.3.3 Performance Evaluator‐Based Surrogate Model

 

#### 9.3.3.1 Architecture Embedding

The general architecture of Seq2Rank is illustrated in [Fig. 9.19](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0019). As can be seen, the model for architecture embedding consists of a FC layer for word embedding and an LSTM layer used in the Seq2Seq model. To begin with, an architecture represented by the proposed action command encoding scheme is tokenized by regarding the codon of each action command as a token; besides, an `<SOS>` token and an `<EOS>` token are attached to the start and end of each sequence, respectively, and an `<MOS>` token is also required to split the action commands for normal cell and reduction cell if the cell structure is adopted. Then, each token is converted to one‐hot representation and fed to the embedding layer to obtain a word vector. Afterward, a Seq2Seq model is trained by maximizing the following conditional probability:

In practice, a number of architectures should be evaluated via training and validation at the beginning of the search process, then they are used to train the RankNet.
