### 9.3.4 Framework of ACEncoding

To simultaneously optimize the accuracy and complexity of neural architecture in NAS, the proposed ACEncoding employs NSGA‐II as the optimizer due to its high competitiveness in solving bi‐objective optimization problems [\[77\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0077). Compared with existing work on NSGA‐II for NAS, the proposed ACEncoding is characterized with two key aspects: an effective action command encoding scheme for NAS, and an efficient performance evaluator‐based strategy for accelerating the search. Specifically, Algorithm 9.4 presents the main steps of the proposed ACEncoding with the surrogate model Seq2Rank under NSGA‐II, which mainly consists of seven steps.

First, train a Seq2Seq model based on an amount of sequential data in advance. Second, randomly generate a population ![upper P](images/c09-i0397.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> consisting of ![upper P o p](images/c09-i0398.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> solutions which represent corresponding neural architectures, and decode and evaluate the solutions in ![upper P](images/c09-i0399.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> after training their corresponding architectures to compute their objective values in Eq. ([9.3.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0033)). Then, the surrogate model, i.e., the Seq2Rank performance evaluator, is initially trained with the initial population's information (including all architecture' encoding and performance) based on the pretrained Seq2Seq model. Fourth, the binary tournament selection [\[24\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0024) is applied to the population ![upper P](images/c09-i0400.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> to mate individuals in the population and generate the parent population ![upper P prime](images/c09-i0401.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. Fifth, an offspring population ![upper P Subscript n e w](images/c09-i0402.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></math> is produced from the parent population ![upper P prime](images/c09-i0403.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> by implementing the crossover and mutation operators proposed in NSGA‐Net [\[24\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0024). Sixth, determine whether the solutions in ![upper P Subscript n e w](images/c09-i0404.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></math> at the current generation need to train their architecture for evaluation: if yes, decode and evaluate the solutions in ![upper P Subscript n e w](images/c09-i0405.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></math> after training their corresponding architectures to compute their objective values in Eq. ([9.3.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0033)); otherwise, directly obtain the architecture performance of all solutions in ![upper P Subscript n e w](images/c09-i0406.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></math> by the surrogate model Seq2Rank. Finally, the main population ![upper P](images/c09-i0407.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and the offspring population ![upper P Subscript n e w](images/c09-i0408.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></math> will be concatenated together, and the standard environmental selection operation in NSGA‐II [\[44\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0044) is used to select ![upper P o p](images/c09-i0409.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi></math> better solutions as the new main population ![upper P](images/c09-i0410.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>. The second to the seventh step will repeat until the evolution termination criteria is satisfied, after which the non‐dominated individuals will be output.

 

### 9.3.5 Experimental Studies

 

#### 9.3.5.1 Performance Verification of Action Command Encoding

Actually, the action command encoding scheme devised in the proposed ACEncoding can be used for any other optimizers, including RL and gradient optimization. To validate the effectiveness of the devised action command encoding scheme in encoding, we compared the devised encoding scheme with NSGA‐Net, MetaQNN [\[82\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0082) and NAO [\[21\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0021), where NSGA‐Net is based on an EA and the adjacent matrix‐based encoding, MetaQNN is based on RL and the hyperparameter‐based encoding, and NAO is based on GD and the block‐based encoding. Hence, it is reasonable to adopt these three methods to compare the proposed action command encoding scheme with other encoding schemes on different optimizers. The parameter settings mainly follow those in the original papers of the three methods, the details of which are given in the following.

*   *Structure of CNN*. The widely used cell structure is adopted in ACEncoding to decrease the search space. Specifically, a normal cell and a reduction cell are encoded by the proposed encoding scheme independently, and the whole CNN consists of three normal cells and two reduction cells stacked alternately. For the hyperparameters in the convolutional and pooling layers, the filter size is determined by the encoding, the number of filters is always set to 16, and the stride size is set to 2 for the layers directly connected to the reduction cell's inputs and 1 for all the other layers.
*   *ACEncoding and NSGA‐Net*. The only difference between NSGA‐Net and NSGA‐Net is the adopted encoding scheme, where NSGA‐Net adopts the adjacent matrix‐based encoding. When integrating with the proposed action command encoding, the optimizer randomly initializes a population with 40 architectures having 10–20 action commands for each cell, and then evolves the population for 25 generations to generate 1000 architectures in total. Since the crossover and mutation operators in NSGA‐Net are tailored for the binary adjacent matrix, new crossover and mutation operators are designed for the proposed action command encoding scheme. To be specific, the crossover operator randomly selects an anchor point from the encodings of two parent architectures and exchanges the action commands after the anchor point of the two encodings to generate two offspring architectures. The offspring architectures are then mutated by one of the three operations, including adding a random action command, randomly deleting an action command, and randomly changing the variables of an action command. The crossover probability is 1 and the mutation probability is 0.1.
*   *ACEncoding with RL as the optimizer, termed ACEncoding under RL*. MetaQNN iteratively generates architectures according to a ![upper Q](images/c09-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐table and updates the ![upper Q](images/c09-i0412.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐table according to the performance of the generated architectures via ![upper Q](images/c09-i0413.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐learning. When integrating with the proposed action command encoding, each action command is regarded as a state and the ![upper Q](images/c09-i0414.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐table stores the value ![upper Q left-parenthesis s Subscript i Baseline comma s Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0415.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denoting the reward of selecting action command ![s Subscript j](images/c09-i0416.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> after action command ![s Subscript i](images/c09-i0417.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>. To generate an architecture, the agent sequentially selects action commands via the ![epsilon](images/c09-i0418.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐greedy strategy according to the ![upper Q](images/c09-i0419.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐table, until the termination state is selected or 20 action commands have been selected. This procedure repeats twice to generate the normal cell and reduction cell of an architecture, and the generated architecture is evaluated and stored in a replay dictionary for periodically updating the ![upper Q](images/c09-i0420.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐values between action commands in the ![upper Q](images/c09-i0421.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐table. The ![upper Q](images/c09-i0422.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐learning rate is set to 0.1, the discount factor is set to 1 (i.e., there are no over‐prioritize short‐term rewards), and the parameter ![epsilon](images/c09-i0423.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is set to 1, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 when 200, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 850, 900, 950, and 1000 architectures have been evaluated.
*   *ACEncoding with GD as the optimizer, termed ACEncoding under GD*. NAO adopts an encoder LSTM to embed the architecture into a continuous space and takes the continuous representation as input to predict its performance by a feedforward neural network. Thus, better continuous representation can be obtained by moving the input along the gradient direction induced by the performance, and the updated continuous representation is fed into a decoder LSTM to generate a new architecture. When integrating with the proposed action command encoding, the optimizer randomly initializes 600 architectures having 20 action commands for each cell, as the length of the decoder is fixed in NAO. Then, these architectures are evaluated and used to train the two LSTMs and the feedforward neural network jointly. Afterward, 200 new architectures are generated by performing GD on the best 200 architectures. The last step repeats twice to form 1000 architectures generated in total. The sizes of the embedding layer, the hidden layer of the LSTMs, and the hidden layer of the feedforward neural network are set to 64, 128, and 200, respectively, and the models are trained using Adam [\[6\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006) for 1000 epochs with a learning rate of 0.001.
*   *Performance evaluation strategy*. All the above three methods generate 1000 architectures during the whole search process. Each architecture is evaluated via training and validation without using parameter sharing or surrogate model, where the 50,000 images in CIFAR‐10 are randomly split into a training set of 45,000 samples and a validation set of 5000 samples. Each architecture is trained by SGD with a batch size of 128, a momentum of 0.9, and a learning rate ranging from 0.1 to 0.001 following a single‐period cosine schedule. The training samples are normalized and randomly augmented by several data pre‐processing techniques, including random crop (i.e., padding each image by 4 pixels and cropping a random ![32 times 32](images/c09-i0424.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>32</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn></math> patch), horizontal flipping [\[13\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0013), and cutout (with a mask length of 16) [\[84\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0084). Besides, the scheduled path dropout (with a probability of 0.2) [\[56\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0056) and an auxiliary classifier (appended to the architecture at 2/3 depth with a constant factor of 0.4) [\[16\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0016) are adopted in the training process.

[Figure 9.20](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0020) plots the minimum validation error during the search process of the original NSGA‐Net, MetaQNN, and NAO and those integrated with the proposed action command encoding scheme, where NSGA‐Net with the devised encoding scheme is actually ACEncoding. It can be found that the proposed action command encoding scheme is competitive to the adjacent matrix‐based encoding on NSGA‐Net, while the devised encoding scheme converges obviously faster than the hyperparameter‐based encoding on MetaQNN and the block‐based encoding on NAO. Therefore, it can be concluded that the proposed action command encoding scheme is suitable for different optimizers including EAs, RL, and GD, and it is competitive to or more effective than existing encoding schemes.

![Figure 9.20 Minimum validation error during the search process of the original NSGA‐Net (a), MetaQNN (b), and NAO (c) and those integrated with the proposed action command encoding scheme on CIFAR‐10.](images/c09f020.png)

[**Figure 9.20**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0020) Minimum validation error during the search process of the original NSGA‐Net (a), MetaQNN (b), and NAO (c) and those integrated with the proposed action command encoding scheme on CIFAR‐10.

 

#### 9.3.5.2 Performance Comparison on CIFAR‐10

[Table 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0006) presents the test error of 31 CNNs found by human experts and 17 NAS methods. It can be observed that the CNNs obtained by ACEncoding have 2.80% to 3.16% test errors and 2.4M to 3.2M parameters, which are quite competitive with the other CNNs listed in the table. As for ACEncoding, the test error of the obtained CNN is slightly higher than the CNN obtained by ACEncoding without Seq2Rank; by contrast, the search cost can decrease to 1.5 GPU days from 7 GPU days. Furthermore, the CNN obtained by the proposed ACEncoding is enlarged by setting the number of filters to 96, denoted as ACEncoding (more filters), which can lead to a test error of 2.32%, better than all the other CNNs in the table.

![Table 9.6  Comparison of Performance Between the CNNs Found by Human Experts and Neural Architecture Search Methods on CIFAR‐10.](images/c09-i0425.png)

[**Table 9.6**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-tbl-0006)  Comparison of Performance Between the CNNs Found by Human Experts and Neural Architecture Search Methods on CIFAR‐10.

[Figure 9.21](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0021) depicts the test error and number of parameters of the CNNs listed in [Table 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0006). It can be found that there are four CNNs having the best trade‐offs between test error and complexity, where two of them are obtained by the proposed ACEncoding, one of them is obtained by NASNet, and the remaining one is wide ResNet. It should be noted that NASNet obtains the CNN by searching for 2000 GPU days, whereas the proposed ACEncoding consumes only 1.5 GPU days. Although the wide ResNet is manually designed with no search cost, its test error is much higher than the other three CNNs. Besides, [Fig. 9.22](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0022) plots the test error and search cost of the CNNs, where the best trade‐off CNN found by the proposed ACEncoding has larger search cost but lower test error than the other trade‐off CNNs. In short, the proposed ACEncoding can strike a balance among the search performance, the complexity of architectures, and the computational cost of search process.

It can be seen that the architectures have more than 10 layers with many connections. For adjacent matrix‐based encoding and graph‐based encoding, they require a long sequence of variables to represent such complex architectures. The transferability of the architectures found by the proposed ACEncoding and its variants is then verified on CIFAR‐100 [\[58\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0058), where the same CNNs are trained by the 50,000 training samples of CIFAR‐100 and tested on the 10,000 test samples. According to the results listed in [Table 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0007), the CNNs obtained by the proposed ACEncoding and its variants also have competitive test errors and complexities to the others. Besides, the CNN generated based on the second best architecture found by the proposed ACEncoding is evaluated, which has higher complexity but lower test error than the other CNNs obtained by its variants.

#### 9.3.5.5 Performance Verification of Seq2Rank

The proposed performance evaluator Seq2Rank is compared to two existing surrogate models for predicting the performance of architectures, namely, E2EPP [\[88\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0088) and Peephole [\[89\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0089). E2EPP is an end‐to‐end performance predictor based on random forest [\[90\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0090), which is effective to a limited number of training samples and can directly handle the discrete variables without embedding. Peephole holds a similar pipeline to the proposed Seq2Rank, which embeds the architecture by an LSTM with embedding layer and predicts the performance by a feedforward neural network. However, Peephole concatenates all the hidden states but not using mean pooling or attention mechanism, and it predicts the validation accuracy rather than the ranking of each architecture. More importantly, Seq2Rank uses the Seq2Seq model to learn a continuous representation in an unsupervised manner, while Peephole directly trains the whole model in a supervised manner. For the models in Peephole and Seq2Rank, the sizes of the embedding layer, the hidden layer of the LSTM, and the two hidden layers of the feedforward neural network are set to 62, 120, 60, and 30, respectively, and the models are trained using SGD for 25 epochs with a learning rate of 0.1.

A number of 10,000 architectures represented by the devised action command encoding are randomly generated to form the dataset, where different numbers of samples are used as training samples and the rest are used as test samples. [Table 9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0009) lists the performance of E2EPP, Peephole, and Seq2Rank in terms of the Kendall's Tau metric, which is calculated by [\[91\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0091)

Obviously, the value of Kendall's Tau ranges from ![minus](images/c09-i0441.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>1 to 1 and a higher value corresponds to a higher accuracy. It can be found from the table that Peephole always has a worse performance than Seq2Rank, and E2EPP outperforms Seq2Rank only with 1000 training samples due to the superiority of random forest on small training sets. To summarize, it can be verified that Seq2Rank is more suitable for predicting the performance of architectures represented by the devised encoding than some existing surrogate‐assisted performance evaluators.

## 9.4 Summary

This chapter presents a gradient guide multi‐objective evolutionary algorithm (GEMONN) and an action command encoding‐based surrogate‐assisted EA (ACEncoding) for the training of DNNs and NAS, respectively. Specifically, the proposed GEMONN focuses on designing a powerful genetic operator gSBX to directly optimize the weights of DNNs, by means of taking advantage of the gradient information. Moreover, the network sparsity is also optimized together with the training loss, which can reduce the network complexity and alleviate overfitting. Experimental results on single‐layer NNs, deep‐layer NNs, recurrent NNs, and CNNs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GEMONN. In short, this work not only introduces a novel approach for training deep NNs but also enhances the performance of EAs in solving large‐scale optimization problems.

For the proposed ACEncoding, a novel encoding scheme and a performance evaluator are presented for NAS. The proposed encoding scheme defines a set of action commands and encodes each architecture in a sequence consisting of the codons of multiple action commands. The proposed encoding scheme inherits the advantages of existing encoding schemes that can represent complex architectures as a relatively short sequence and has shown better effectiveness than some popular encoding schemes in EAs, RL, and GD. The proposed performance evaluator Seq2Rank adopts a Seq2Seq model to convert the variable‐length encoding of the action command into a fixed‐length sequence and then predicts the ranking of the architecture determined by the encoding via RankNet. The proposed performance evaluator has been empirically verified to be better than some existing surrogate models in predicting the performance of architectures represented by the proposed ACEncoding.
